sections.heading: Accounts and access
sections.text: # Accounts and access

sections.heading: Create a local account
sections.text:
## Create a local account

A local account signs in with a username and password and is always an administrator. Give everybody else access through single sign-on and [roles](#roles).

1.  Open Admin → Accounts → Users and select **\+ Add user**.
2.  Enter Display name and Username, then choose **Add**.
3.  Securely hand over the one-time password before dismissing the panel. The recipient must choose their own password at first sign-in. If it is lost, reset it; you cannot read it back.

sections.heading: Reset, disable or sign out
sections.text:
## Reset, disable or sign out

Choose **Manage** on the person's row.

-   **Reset password:** sign out existing sessions and issue a temporary password.
-   **Disable account:** sign out and block access; keep the account’s name on its past changes.
-   **Enable account:** allow new sign-ins without restoring old sessions.
-   **Revoke sessions:** sign out without changing the password. This does not block future access.
-   **Rename:** change the display name only.

Smeltr asks you to confirm before it resets a password or disables an account. Your own row has no Reset password: a local account uses Change password in the account menu at the top right, which shows your name. A single sign-on account changes its password at the provider.

sections.heading: Change session lifetimes
sections.text:
## Change session lifetimes

1.  Open Admin → System → Sessions.
2.  Set Idle timeout and Maximum session age, observing the units displayed alongside each field.
3.  Select **Save sessions**.

By default, a session ends after 30 minutes without activity or 12 hours after sign-in. You can set both limits from two minutes to 30 days. Idle timeout cannot exceed Maximum session age. Changes apply on each session's next request; shortening a limit can sign people out immediately. A leader restart clears all in-memory sessions, not account records.

sections.heading: Recover access when nobody can sign in
sections.text:
## Recover access when nobody can sign in

If you've lost your admin password and nobody else can sign in, recover access on the leader host.

1.  Stop the leader and verify there is no other instance using its data directory.
2.  Start the same binary, configuration and data under the same account, once, with the following environment setting.

```
SMELTR_RECOVER_ADMIN=1 SMELTR_CONFIG_FILE=/absolute/path/to/smeltr.toml /absolute/path/to/smeltr
```

Read the username and temporary password from the leader’s process console or service log, then sign in and change the password. Remove SMELTR\_RECOVER\_ADMIN from the service environment before the next restart; leaving it enabled resets the account again every time. This recovery procedure requires access to the leader host.

sections.heading: Sign in through single sign-on
sections.text:
## Sign in through single sign-on

People can sign in through your organization's identity provider over [OpenID Connect](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html) (OIDC). Local accounts keep working whatever is set here, so keep at least one local administrator as a way in when the provider is down.

1.  Open Admin → Accounts → Single sign-on and copy the **Redirect URI**. It is the leader's own address followed by `/api/auth/oidc/callback`.
2.  At your provider, register a web application (a confidential client) with that redirect URI. Have the provider name each person's groups in a `groups` claim of the ID token.
3.  Back in Smeltr, turn on **Enabled** and enter the provider's **Issuer URL**, the **Client ID** and the **Client secret**. If your provider names groups in another claim, set it under Advanced.
4.  Select **Save**.

The issuer must be an `https://` URL, or an `http://` URL to `localhost` or a loopback address, for a local test provider. Saving reads the provider's discovery document and keys, so a wrong issuer is refused when you save. The client and the groups claim are only tried at the first sign-in, so sign in once to check them. The client secret is stored encrypted and never shown again; changing the issuer or client ID forgets it, so enter the new client's secret with them.

The sign-in screen then offers **Sign in with SSO**, with **Sign in with username** beside it for local accounts. The first time somebody signs in through the provider, Smeltr creates their account. Accounts lists them with SSO as their sign-in, and the email or username the provider gives them under their name. To sign in, a person must belong to at least one group that has a role. **Refused sign-ins** on the Roles tab lists everyone turned away, with the groups the provider sent.

The provider owns an SSO account's password, so it has no Reset password. To stop somebody signing in, remove them from every group that has a role, or disable their account in Smeltr.

Account, role and session actions take effect immediately; they are not pipeline changes waiting for branch deployment.

sections.heading: Give people access with roles
sections.text:
## Give people access with roles

An SSO account can do only what its roles give it. A role is named for one group in the provider's groups claim, and gives whoever holds that group one level in each area: the shared configuration or a worker group.

-   **viewer** reads the area's configuration.
-   **editor** also saves to it on a branch, and captures, previews and reads its samples.
-   **deployer** also approves and deploys changes to it.

Anybody holding an area also reads the shared configuration, which every group draws on. The Map and Status pages show only the groups a person holds. A change is shown only to someone who can view every area it touches; changing it takes an editor, and deploying it a deployer, in each of them. A change to shared counts as shared alone. Rolling back from History, or selecting **Release**, moves every group, so it takes a deployer in shared and in every group. Group lists name only the groups a person holds. A role marked **Administrator** gives everything, Admin included.

1.  Open Admin → Accounts → Roles and select **\+ Add role**.
2.  Enter the group exactly as the provider names it.
3.  Choose a level for each area, or tick Administrator, and select **Save**.

A change to a role applies on each holder's next request. A change to somebody's groups at the provider applies within a few minutes, while they stay signed in, when the provider issues refresh tokens and its refreshes carry an ID token; otherwise at their next sign-in. A refresh the provider refuses, or one that leaves them in no group with a role, signs them out. To shut somebody out at once, disable their account in Users, or remove them from those groups at the provider and then revoke their sessions. Users lists each person's roles beside their name.

sections.heading: Backup and recovery
sections.text:
# Backup and recovery

A complete recovery needs both the leader data and its matching **secrets encryption key**, which decrypts stored secrets. Keep separate, protected copies of both.

sections.heading: Take a consistent offline backup
sections.text:
## Take a consistent offline backup

Stop the leader before copying its files so the backup is consistent. Schedule a maintenance window. Workers running in separate processes normally keep running their current configuration, but workers configured to stop when the leader is unreachable may stop. Browser sessions end. In standalone mode, stopping Smeltr also stops its worker and data processing.

Complete this checklist in order:

-   Record the installed version, checksum or container-image ID, configuration file, environment settings, and service account. Keep the matching executable or container image for recovery.
-   Stop the leader through its service manager or gracefully terminate the foreground process. Confirm it has exited before copying files.
-   Copy the entire leader.storage.data\_dir: `leader.db`, any accompanying SQLite files, `repos/` and `tls/`. Do not select just the database or just Git. Each start that finds `leader.db` sound also keeps a copy beside it as `leader.db.previous`.
-   Back up the exact leader.secrets.key separately under restricted access. Label it so you can match it to the data backup. Also keep the service configuration and any private certificate authority or proxy configuration needed to restore access.
-   Encrypt and restrict both backups, preserve ownership and permissions, and verify checksums. Restart the original leader and verify login and heartbeats.

The key lives outside the data directory by default. Keep it separate so a stolen data backup does not also provide the key to decrypt stored secrets. TLS private keys inside the data directory also make that backup sensitive.

sections.heading: Restore without creating two leaders
sections.text:
## Restore without creating two leaders

1.  Stop or isolate the original leader and prevent its automatic restart.
2.  On the replacement host, install the same binary version or container-image ID first. Restore the complete data directory and matching secrets encryption key to the configured paths, preserving restrictive permissions.
3.  Restore the configuration and verify DNS, public origin, ports and certificate names. Do not initialize an empty leader over the recovery target.
4.  Start it as the original service account. Sign in again; a backup holds no sessions. If you lose account access, use [administrator recovery](/docs/accounts#recovery).
5.  Check Git history, worker groups, certificate status, and any errors on the Secrets page. Confirm workers reconnect and compare each worker's reported Commit with the restored main commit.

A restored Git history may be older than the fleet's cached configuration. Review that difference before allowing production workers to fetch from it.

sections.heading: Test a restore safely
sections.text:
## Test a restore safely

Restore into a network-isolated environment with no production workers and no access to production sources or destinations. Use disposable worker state and non-production credentials. Check login, history, secret usability, trust and a sample deployment, then record the measured recovery time. A restored leader is not passive: do not expose a test restore to the production fleet.

sections.heading: Availability and worker state
sections.text:
## Availability and worker state

A standalone worker keeps its state in `worker/` beneath the leader data directory. Include that directory in the stopped-process backup. An isolated restore also starts that worker when `worker.enabled` is true, so block access to production data systems before starting it.

Run one leader. If it is lost, restore a backup using the procedure above; Smeltr does not currently switch automatically to another leader. Preserve worker state across upgrades, including its identity, credential, trust files and local configuration repository. Never start two workers from the same copied identity. A rebuilt host should enroll afresh.

sections.heading: Capture a sample
sections.text:
# Capture a sample

Capture a few real records to build and test your pipeline. You can inspect the records as they arrive and stop as soon as you have enough.

sections.heading: Choose a capture target
sections.text:
## Choose a capture target

1.  Work on your draft branch. Configure a [source](/docs/sources) and its credentials.
2.  Open Build → Resources → Samples, choose **\+ Add sample**, then **Capture**. The pipeline editor has the same **Capture** button above its list of samples. The sample you capture there becomes the editor's sample.
3.  Choose the worker **Group** and **Capture target**.

The capture uses the source configuration on your branch. A worker already reading that source takes samples from the records flowing through it. Otherwise it opens a separate reader without saving a new reading position.

A Kafka or Event Hubs capture reads in real time by default. To read older records, open **Advanced** and set **Start at**. Existing source reading positions will remain unchanged.

![Capture setup with the Network security group, panw-firewalls source, a raw-text filter, a 200-record limit, a 30-second limit, and Start.](/capture-form-light.png)

Choose a capture target, narrow the sample with an optional filter, and set record and time limits before starting.

sections.heading: Collect records
sections.text:
## Collect records

1.  Leave **Keep records where** empty for all records, or enter a condition such as `_raw.includes("error")`.
2.  Set **At most** to the total number of records you want, up to 1,000, and choose a time limit. Workers share the total.
3.  Select **Start**. Inspect the incoming records and worker counts. Select a worker chip to view only that worker's records.
4.  Wait for the capture to finish, or select **Stop capture** to keep what has arrived so far.

At a source, the filter runs before the pipeline. It can read `_raw` and fields the source provides; fields your parser creates are not available yet.

When you capture at a destination, the filter reads each record as the route's pipeline delivered it, so it can use fields your parsers created. When several routes deliver there, the capture keeps records only from routes where the filter can run. Before you start, the dialog lists the other routes and why each is skipped.

The filter does not support array `map` and `filter` calls.

![Capture in progress, showing incoming firewall records from two workers, the record limit, time remaining, and Stop capture button.](/capture-running-light.png)

Capture in progress using sample traffic. Worker counts show where the records came from; select a worker to inspect its records.

sections.heading: Save and test
sections.text:
## Save and test

Enter a name under **Save as** and select **Save sample**. Open the saved sample in your pipeline, run it, and inspect the output. Save an expected result as a test, following [the Build page](/build#test-heading). Choose **Edit** on a sample's row under Build → Resources → Samples to change it.

You need at least one captured record to save. Choose **Discard** if the records are not useful. Capture only enough to test the case you care about: saved samples become part of the versioned configuration.

sections.heading: Capture a blocked source
sections.text:
## Capture a blocked source

Capture works on a blocked source or destination. Select it on the Map and choose **Capture**. A blocked worker shows the records holding it up with `__exception.message` first, and other workers still show new records.

sections.heading: If no records arrive
sections.text:
## If no records arrive

-   Read the reason shown for each worker. Check its connection and credentials if it failed.
-   Try without a filter, send a known record, and capture again.
-   At a destination, read the message under the filter. If it says no route can use the filter, change or clear the filter.
-   Check that the selected group has online workers and that the source has records available during the capture window.

You can sample Smeltr metrics and logs even before you deploy that source. They describe the process serving the capture. The worker may refuse a logs capture when another reader already holds the log buffer; the worker's reason explains this.

sections.heading: Certificates and TLS
sections.text:
# Certificates and TLS

TLS encrypts connections and checks the server’s identity. A certificate authority (CA) signs server certificates. Clients must trust that authority before accepting its certificates.

sections.heading: Choose the trust model
sections.text:
## Choose the trust model

|  | TLS at the leader | TLS at a proxy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Certificate served by | Smeltr | Reverse proxy or ingress |
| Setting | `leader.tls.enabled = true` | `leader.tls.enabled = false`; keep upstream private |
| Worker trust | Enrollment codes establish trust in the leader CA | System trust; configure private CA trust separately |
| Browser trust | Verify the CA fingerprint, then install its public certificate | Trust the proxy certificate; install a private CA if needed |
| Certificate changes | Admin → System → Leader certificate | At the proxy or ingress |

sections.heading: Obtain and verify the public CA
sections.text:
## Obtain and verify the public CA

For direct TLS the generated CA is at `tls/ca.pem` beneath leader.storage.data\_dir. Obtain that public file through a trusted host-management channel for initial browser setup. Once signed in, Admin → System → Leader certificate also provides **Download ca.pem** and the authority fingerprint. Never distribute the CA private key.

```
openssl x509 -in /var/lib/smeltr/tls/ca.pem -noout -subject -dates -fingerprint -sha256
```

Verify the certificate names against the public URL and any worker-only DNS names. Add worker-only names with leader.tls.extra\_san, restart for startup-setting changes, and check the certificate shown in the UI. Do not use a certificate warning bypass as the production setup procedure.

sections.heading: Keep certificates in the list
sections.text:
## Keep certificates in the list

Open Admin → Certificates and choose **\+ Add certificate**. Enter a Name, paste the full certificate chain and its private key, both PEM, and choose **Add**. For a private authority, end the chain with its root. The private key is stored encrypted and never shown again.

To renew a certificate, choose **Replace** and paste the new version. If the leader serves it, the leader switches to the new version; there's no need to choose it again. Connection identities that present it are pointed at the new version in a change, which reaches workers when you deploy it. The certificate the leader serves cannot be deleted.

To have the leader issue one instead, choose **Issued by this leader**, enter the DNS names and IP addresses it is for under **Issued for**, choose how long it lasts under **Valid for**, and choose **Add**. The leader signs it with its own authority, so a client verifies it against the leader's [ca.pem](#download). When a third of its life remains (30 days of 90, about four months of a year), or after you [rotate the authority](#rotation), the leader issues the next version on its own, valid for the same length of time. Workers keep the old version until you update the identities: the Issues page lists each connection identity presenting an older version. Choose **Update identities** on the certificate's row, which opens a change that points them at the newest version, and deploy that change before the old version expires.

sections.heading: Names a certificate must cover
sections.text:
## Names a certificate must cover

A certificate this leader serves must cover the name your browser reaches it by. If this leader runs its own worker, it must also cover the address that worker reaches it by: 127.0.0.1, unless [worker.leader.url](/docs/reference#worker.leader.url) says otherwise. Public authorities don't issue certificates for 127.0.0.1, so to serve a public certificate, set worker.leader.url to a URL on one of the certificate's names, such as `https://smeltr.example.com`, then restart.

sections.heading: Choose where the certificate comes from
sections.text:
## Choose where the certificate comes from

Admin → System → Leader certificate shows the authority and the certificate this leader serves, and a **Source** chooser with the one in force marked.

| Source | Where the certificate comes from |
| --- | --- |
| Leader issued | The leader's own authority signs it. **Issue a new one** replaces it under the same authority. |
| Uploaded | An administrator picks a certificate from **Admin → Certificates**, or adds one there with **add a certificate**, and selects **Serve this certificate**. See [Names a certificate must cover](#names). |
| ACME | The leader orders it from a certificate authority and renews it. [Order a certificate over ACME](#acme). |

A new certificate from the same authority is served at once.

A new authority has to reach the workers first. The page shows the switch in progress while the leader hands the authority to them, and which workers have it. The leader serves the new certificate as soon as every worker has it, or at the cutover time the page shows, which you can change.

-   **Cut over now** serves it without waiting.
-   **Abandon switch** cancels the switch.

Browsers must be told to trust a new authority separately. If the page says the socket refused the reload, restart the leader. Replace proxy certificates at the proxy.

sections.heading: Order a certificate over ACME
sections.text:
## Order a certificate over ACME

Let's Encrypt and other certificate authorities issue certificates automatically over ACME. The authority checks that each name on the certificate reaches this leader, then issues it. The leader renews it on its own. Each order is a new version of the **acme** entry in Admin → Certificates, which connection identities can present too; move them to a new version with **Update identities**, as for an issued certificate.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
### Before you start

-   Every name on the certificate points at this leader in DNS, unless you use DNS-01. A public authority such as Let's Encrypt won't issue for `localhost` or a private address.
-   With the TLS-ALPN-01 challenge, the default, port 443 on each name must reach this leader.
-   With the HTTP-01 challenge, port 80 on each name must reach this leader. The leader listens on leader.tls.acme\_http\_port only while it orders. That setting is 80 unless something forwards 80 to another port.
-   With the DNS-01 challenge, nothing has to reach this leader, so it works for a leader on a private network. The zones that hold the names must be in your Cloudflare account. DNS-01 can't prove an IP address.
-   If this leader runs its own worker, read [Names a certificate must cover](#names) first.

sections.heading: Order it
sections.text:
### Order it

1.  Under Source, choose **ACME**.
2.  Pick the **Directory**: Let's Encrypt, or Other to type another authority's URL.
3.  Check **Names**. They start as this leader's own names, without localhost.
4.  Enter a **Contact email**. The authority sends notices about the account there.
5.  Agree to the terms of service.
6.  Select **Get certificate**. The first certificate from an authority is a switch, as described above.

sections.heading: Renewal
sections.text:
### Renewal

With ACME in force, the page shows when the certificate renews.

-   The leader renews when one-third of the certificate's life remains, e.g. 30 days of a 90-day certificate.
-   If an order fails, the page shows why, and the leader tries again every hour.
-   **Save** keeps your changes for the next renewal. **Renew now** orders a certificate right away.
-   A renewal under a new root is a switch, like the first order.

The leader stops renewing once you choose another source.

sections.heading: Advanced settings
sections.text:
### Advanced settings

Under **Advanced**:

-   **Challenge** picks TLS-ALPN-01, HTTP-01 or DNS-01. For DNS-01, **API token** takes a Cloudflare token with Zone · Zone · Read and Zone · DNS · Edit on those zones. The leader stores it encrypted and never shows it again.
-   **Authority** takes the root a private authority issues under, as PEM. It is needed only when the platform does not already trust that root.
-   **EAB key ID** and **EAB HMAC key** are for an authority that requires an account with it. It gives you both. The leader stores the HMAC key encrypted and never shows it again.

sections.heading: Rotate the authority
sections.text:
## Rotate the authority

1.  Back up the leader state and key; inventory offline workers and workers using explicit worker.leader.ca files.
2.  Under Rotate authority, set **Wait for the fleet** and select **Start rotation**.
3.  The leader publishes the incoming authority on heartbeats while it still signs under the old one. Ensure workers have received it. Explicit CA-file overrides require manual maintenance; update browser trust separately.
4.  Only after verifying client readiness choose **Cut over now**, or allow the deadline to do so automatically. The leader retires the old authority and withdraws enrollment codes naming it.
5.  Verify heartbeats and browser access after cutover. Before cutover, **Abandon rotation** cancels the pending rotation.

A worker that missed the incoming authority can lose the ability to verify the leader at cutover and require re-enrollment. The deadline is an automatic cutover, not merely a reminder. Do not start rotation without a plan for offline workers.

sections.heading: Expression reference
sections.text:
# Expression reference

An expression computes one value from a record's fields. Use expressions in Eval, Code, Drop and If steps, step filters, and route conditions.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

A name reads the field of that name on the record being processed, and operators and functions compute from those values. A method call and a function call are one call. Every value has a type, and the pipeline compiles only when every expression's types fit.

-   `let host: str = "web-01"`: `host.length()` → `6`
-   `let host: str = "web-01"`: `length(host)` → `6`

sections.heading: Types
sections.text:
### Types

A name's first write sets its type. A name's type is fixed for the whole pipeline. A declaration, `name: T = e`, states it, and `e as T` converts a value to another type.

Code

```
y = 1;
ratio: f64 = 3;
let label: str = "checkout";
service = label;
```

Input

```
{
  "id": 7
}
```

→

Output

```
{
  "id": 7,
  "y": 1,
  "ratio": 3.0,
  "service": "checkout"
}
```

After that, three kinds of write treat a value of another type differently:

| Write | What it converts | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x = e` | Nothing. It accepts null, and an `i64` into an `f64` name. | `r: f64 = 1.5; r = 2;` stores `2.0` |
| `x: T = e` | A field a parser did not declare, record by record. It also changes the type of `x`. | `n: i64 = extra;` turns `"5"` into `5` |
| `e as T` | Any value. | `"5" as i64` is `5`; `2.7 as i64` is `3` |

Code

```
ratio: f64 = 1.5;
ratio = 2;
count: i64 = extra;
rounded = 2.7 as i64;
```

Input

```
{
  "extra": "5"
}
```

→

Output

```
{
  "extra": "5",
  "ratio": 2.0,
  "count": 5,
  "rounded": 3
}
```

After a JSON or Key/value parser, you can copy a field the parser does not declare as it is: `copy = extra;`. Its type is only known per record, so to calculate with it, give it a type first, as in `extra: str = extra;`, or convert the value: `(extra as str) + "!"`.

| Type | Holds | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bool` | `true` or `false`. | `true` → `true` |
| `i64` | A 64-bit signed integer. A result that does not fit is null, with an `Overflow` exception. | `443` → `443` |
| `f64` | A 64-bit floating-point number. `/` on two numbers always gives one. | `1.5` → `1.5` |
| `str` | Text, always valid UTF-8. Positions and lengths count characters. | `"GET"` → `"GET"` |
| `bytes` | Bytes, not read as text. Text functions refuse them; `decode` reads them as text in a named encoding. They write as base64, and `toString` names another form. |  |
| `datetime` | An instant in UTC, to the microsecond, written as ISO 8601. | `"2024-05-01T12:00:00Z".parseTime()` → `"2024-05-01T12:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `duration` | A signed span, to the microsecond, written as its count of microseconds. | `duration(90, "s")` → `90000000` |
| `variant` | A value whose type is known only per row, such as a field of an open object that no declaration names. | `p = json("{\"port\": 443}")`: `p.port` → `443` |
| `array<T>` | Elements of one type, as many as each row has. | `[200, 404]` → `[200,404]` |
| `{name: T, ...}` | Named fields. `{ip: str}` holds only the fields it names; `{ip: str, ...}` also keeps the others. See [Objects](#objects). | `{ip: "10.0.0.1", port: 443}` → `{"ip":"10.0.0.1","port":443}` |

Any other mismatch is an error when you save, and the error names the fix:

-   `x: i64 = "5";` does not compile. Write `"5" as i64`.
-   `n: i64 = 1; n = 2.5;` does not compile. Write `2.5 as i64`, or`n: f64 = 2.5`.

An expression whose types do not fit on any row does not compile.

Does not compile:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| `"10" * 2` | Text and a number have no common type. Convert first: `"10".parseInt() * 2`. |

sections.heading: Null
sections.text:
### Null

A declared field a record lacks reads as null, and a name no step declares or writes does not compile. Arithmetic on null gives null. A condition reads null as false: a ternary takes the value after `:`, an If step its else branch, and a step whose filter is null leaves the record unchanged. `??` gives a fallback for null. Writing `null` to a field removes it.

-   `let host: str = null`: `host.length()` → `null`
-   `let host: str = null`: `host ?? "unknown"` → `"unknown"`
-   `let message: str = null`: `!message.startsWith("debug")` → `true` // a negated test is true when the field is null
-   `let message: str = null`: `message != null && !message.startsWith("debug")` → `false`

sections.heading: Fields
sections.text:
## Fields

Every record has these fields. A source's own fields are on its [source page](/docs/sources), and the fields a destination reads are on its [destination page](/docs/destinations). Smeltr never delivers a field at the record's root whose name starts with `__`.

| Field | Type | Set by | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `_raw` | `str` | source | The text the source received, decoded with the source's `encoding`. A parser reads it. The destination delivers it with the record unless a step sets it to `null`. A source whose `encoding` is `none` gives no `_raw`. |
| `__source.name` | `str` | source | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | source | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `smeltr.exception` | `struct` | Smeltr | The exceptions of a record answered tag or deliver: `route`, `pipeline`, and `exceptions`, a list of each one's `step`, `kind` and `message`. |

sections.heading: Naming a field
sections.text:
## Naming a field A bare name is letters, digits, `_` and `$`, dotted. `source.ip` is one column. A name is the same name wherever it stands: read, written, or passed. `$` is the record itself, an [object](#objects): `$.source.ip` and `source.ip` are one read. A field whose name holds any other character is written `$["..."]`, so `$["source.ip"]` is a different field: one key with a dot in it. `$["..."]` takes a string literal and names a field, not a value: `$["x-y"].z` is the one field `x-y.z`, as `a.b` is. `$[k]` with `k` a value reads whichever field `k` names on that row, as any object's `o[k]` does. On a named field, a fixed string key follows the same path: `geo["city"]` reads `geo.city`. A declared field a record lacks reads as null. | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | `.` | the field of that dotted name, or a child of an object | `geo = {"city": "Oslo", "lat": 59}`: `geo.city` → `"Oslo"`
`source.ip = "10.0.0.1"`: `source.ip.startsWith("10.")` → `true` // one flat column | | `$[]` | a field of the record by its name, for one a bare spelling cannot hold | `$["user-agent"] = "curl"`: `$["user-agent"].toUpperCase()` → `"CURL"` | Does not compile: | | | | --- | --- | | `@timestamp` | `@` cannot start a bare name. Write `$["@timestamp"]`. |

sections.heading: Objects
`object.keys()`
sections.text:
### `object.keys()`

The object's keys, as an array of strings, in the order the record writes them. A field holding null is left out.

-   `{"a": 1, "b": 2}.keys()` → `["a","b"]`

sections.heading: `object.entries()`
sections.text:
### `object.entries()`

Each key with its value, as `{key, value}`, in the order of `keys`. Every value must be of one type. Other languages call this `items`.

-   `{"a": 1, "b": 2}.entries()` → `[{"key":"a","value":1},{"key":"b","value":2}]`

sections.heading: `fromEntries(pairs)`
sections.text:
### `fromEntries(pairs)`

An object of an array of `{key, value}`. A later key replaces an earlier one, and a null key is left out.

-   `fromEntries([{"key": "a", "value": 1}, {"key": "a", "value": 2}])` → `{"a":2}`

sections.heading: `object.omit(key, ...)`
sections.text:
### `object.omit(key, ...)`

The object without those keys.

-   `{"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}.omit("a", "c")` → `{"b":2}`

sections.heading: Statements
sections.text:
## Statements

A statement ends with a semicolon, and a block in braces holds statements. The language has these statements:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| `name = e;` | Writes the value of `e` to `name`, a field of the record or a local. `e` must have `name`'s type, an `i64` widens to an `f64`, and `null` fits any type. Writing `null` to a field removes it. |
| `name: T = e;` | Gives `name` the type `T` and writes `e`. This also converts the type declaration to `T`. |
| `name: T;` | Declares the type of `name` in advance. Use before parse functions to coerce types and improve performance. |
| `let name = e;` | Binds a local variable scoped to this block. It never reaches the record, and it takes the type of `e`. `let name: T = e;` gives it a type. |
| `$ = e;` | Replaces the whole record with the [object](#objects) `e`. |
| `Object.assign(o, e);` | Writes each field of the object `e` into the object `o`, converting each value to the type of its field in `o`. `Object.assign($, e)` writes into the record. |
| `if (c) { … } else { … }` | Runs the first block where `c` is true, and the `else` block where it is false or null. `else if` chains. |
| `switch (e) { case v: … default: … }` | Compares `e` with each `case` value, in order, with `==`. Runs from the first that matches through every case after it, until a `break`. `default` matches when no case does, and comes last. |
| `for (let x of a) { … }` | Runs the block once per element of the array `a`, with `x` that element. |
| `while (c) { … }` | Runs the block while `c` is true. The code step has a time budget, 100 ms by default and configured by `SMELTR_LOOP_BUDGET_MS`, to prevent infinite loop stalls. When it runs out, a loop still running stops and marks each record whose condition is still true with a `LoopBudgetExceeded` exception. |
| `break;` | Leaves the innermost loop or `switch`. |
| `continue;` | Ends this trip of the innermost loop and starts the next. |
| `function f(p: T): R { … }` | A local function. A parameter or result with no type takes its value's type. The body's last expression, written without a semicolon, is its value. |
| `return e;` | Ends the function with the value `e`. |
| `try { … } catch (e) { … } finally { … }` | Runs the block until a record's first exception that loses a value. The write that failed keeps the name's old value. A `catch` then runs on that record, with the exception cleared; `e.kind` is its kind and `e.message` its text. `finally` runs on every record that entered the `try`. A `try` needs a `catch`, a `finally` or both. |
| `catch (e: K1 \| K2) { … }` | Runs on the records holding one of the kinds it names, and clears only those. Several catches are tried in order; a catch with no type takes every kind left, and comes last. |
| `throw e;` | In a `catch`, puts the caught exception back on the record, for an outer `try` or its exception answer. |
| `delete(a, b.c);` | Removes each named field from the record. A field bound outside an `if`, loop or `try` cannot be deleted inside one; write `a = null` there. |
| `move(from, to);` | Renames the field `from` to `to`, and removes `from`. |
| `drop();` | Discards the record. |
| `unroll(a);` | Replaces the record with one record per element of the array field `a`, each holding its element at `a`. `unroll(a, true)` keeps the record's other fields on each. It stands outside every `if`, loop and `try`. |

sections.heading: Parse and lookup
sections.text:
## Parse and lookup

The parse functions read text into an object, as a Parser step does, and `lookup` reads a lookup table, as a Lookup step does. A call stands where a statement writes its object: `Object.assign($, f(…))`, `$ = f(…)`, `x = f(…)` and `x: T = f(…)`, or a `let`. Smeltr reads everything but the text and the key when the pipeline compiles, so you write it as literals. A parse function converts a field that a declared type names to it; every other field keeps the type the format gives, which is `str` for all but JSON.

sections.heading: `json(text, {splitDots, formats})`
sections.text:
### `json(text, {splitDots, formats})`

The object the JSON `text` holds. It reads lenient JSON too, such as a trailing comma, raw control characters and `\xHH` escapes.

| Option | Holds | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `splitDots` | Whether a key holding dots is split into a nested path: `a.b` becomes `{a: {b}}`. | `false` |
| `formats` | The text format of each `datetime` field, by name: `{ts: "%d/%m/%Y"}`. The specifiers are `parseTime`'s. | any format the parser recognizes |

sections.heading: `kv(text, {pairSep, kvSep, quote, escapes, nextKey, splitDots, formats})`
sections.text:
### `kv(text, {pairSep, kvSep, quote, escapes, nextKey, splitDots, formats})`

An object of the `key=value` pairs in `text`. Every value is a `str`.

| Option | Holds | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pairSep` | The character between one pair and the next. | a space |
| `kvSep` | The character between a key and its value. | `=` |
| `quote` | The character around a value that holds `pairSep`; `null` for none. | `"` |
| `escapes` | Whether a backslash escapes any character in any value, quoted or not: `\n`, `\r` and `\t` are control characters and any other `\x` is `x`. Without it, only `\"` and `\\` inside quotes are escapes. | `false` |
| `nextKey` | Whether an unquoted value runs to the `pairSep` before the next key: in `level=info debug x=1`, `level` is `info debug`. Off, a value ends at the first `pairSep` and `debug` is a bare key, `debug=true`. | `true` |
| `splitDots` | Whether a key holding dots is split into a nested path: `a.b` becomes `{a: {b}}`. | `true` |
| `formats` | The text format of each `datetime` field, by name: `{ts: "%d/%m/%Y"}`. The specifiers are `parseTime`'s. | any format the parser recognizes |

sections.heading: `cef(text, {splitDots, formats})`
sections.text:
### `cef(text, {splitDots, formats})`

An object of the ArcSight CEF record in `text`: the seven header fields as `version`, `deviceVendor`, `deviceProduct`, `deviceVersion`, `deviceEventClassId`, `name` and `severity`, and each extension key as written. Text before `CEF:` is skipped. Every value is a `str`.

| Option | Holds | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `splitDots` | Whether a key holding dots is split into a nested path: `a.b` becomes `{a: {b}}`. | `false` |
| `formats` | The text format of each `datetime` field, by name: `{rt: "%b %d %Y %H:%M:%S"}`. The specifiers are `parseTime`'s. | any format the parser recognizes |

sections.heading: `csv(text, [headers], {delimiter, quote, escape, squeeze, trim, splitDots, formats})`
sections.text:
### `csv(text, [headers], {delimiter, quote, escape, squeeze, trim, splitDots, formats})`

An object of one CSV line's columns, named by `headers` in order. A `null` header skips its column. Every value is a `str`.

| Option | Holds | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `delimiter` | The character between columns. | `,` |
| `quote` | The character that quotes a column, which may then hold the delimiter. | `"` |
| `escape` | The character that escapes a quote, or itself, inside a quoted column. `null` reads a doubled quote as one. | `null` |
| `squeeze` | Whether a run of delimiters is one, as aligned columns write. | `false` |
| `trim` | Whether spaces around each unquoted column are dropped. | `false` |
| `splitDots` | Whether a key holding dots is split into a nested path: `a.b` becomes `{a: {b}}`. | `false` |
| `formats` | The text format of each `datetime` field, by name: `{ts: "%d/%m/%Y"}`. The specifiers are `parseTime`'s. | any format the parser recognizes |

sections.heading: `grok(text, [patterns], {patterns, splitDots, formats})`
sections.text:
### `grok(text, [patterns], {patterns, splitDots, formats})`

An object of the fields the first matching pattern captures. Each `%{NAME:field}` captures `field`. Every value is a `str`.

| Option | Holds | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `patterns` | Your own patterns by name, `{NAME: "regex"}`, which the patterns may use as `%{NAME}`. | none |
| `splitDots` | Whether a key holding dots is split into a nested path: `a.b` becomes `{a: {b}}`. | `true` |
| `formats` | The text format of each `datetime` field, by name: `{ts: "%d/%m/%Y"}`. The specifiers are `parseTime`'s. | any format the parser recognizes |

sections.heading: `lookup(table, key, {match, column, first, all, fields, formats})`
sections.text:
### `lookup(table, key, {match, column, first, all, fields, formats})`

An object of the `fields` read from the row of the lookup table `table` that `key` matches. A field with no match and no default is left out.

| Option | Holds | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `match` | How `key` matches the key column: `"exact"`, `"cidr"` or `"regex"`. | `"exact"` |
| `column` | The key column. A MaxMind database has none. | required, except for a MaxMind database |
| `first` | `true`: the first matching row, in table order. | `false`: the most exact match |
| `all` | `true`: every matching row; each field is an array. | `false` |
| `fields` | Each output named for its column, `"column"`, or for its column and its default, `["column", "default"]`. | required |
| `formats` | The text format of each `datetime` field, by name: `{ts: "%d/%m/%Y"}`. The specifiers are `parseTime`'s. | any format the parser recognizes |

sections.heading: Comparison and logic
sections.text:
## Comparison and logic The operators that answer a question or pick a value rather than compute one. None belongs to a single type: comparison works across numbers, text, instants and spans, and `??` takes a value of any type. Both operands of a comparison must have the same type, except that an `i64` beside an `f64` widens to `f64`. Ordering works on numbers, text, instants and spans. Text orders by Unicode code point, so it is case-sensitive: `"Z" < "a"` is `true`. `bool` and `bytes` take `==` and `!=` only. Comparisons always return a boolean. Equality is true when both values are null, and false when only one is null. `!=` gives the opposite result. Ordering (`<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`) is false if either value is null; null is not converted to zero. `!`, `&&` and `||` read null as false and always return a boolean. For example, `!null` is `true`, `true && null` is `false`, and `false || null` is `false`. Non-null operands must be booleans; numbers and strings are not converted to true or false. `??` tests null and nothing else, so `0` and `""` pass through: `"" ?? "fallback"` is `""`. It binds looser than `&&` and `||`, so `a ?? b && c` is `a ?? (b && c)`. Every branch must compile. Branches whose types do not meet, such as a `str` and an `i64`, give a `variant`. A `variant`, a value read from an open object `{...}` or made from one, has a type only per row. `== null`, `!= null`, `isNull` and `??` compile on it, and so does a read by a `str` or `i64` key, as `v.k`, `v[k]` or `v[0]`. A read gives a `variant`, null where the row's value holds nothing; a negative index counts from the end. Any other operator, condition or function argument needs a type first, as in `n: i64 = v`. A ternary whose branches are a `variant` and another type is a `variant`: each row keeps the value of the branch it took. Null and an empty array are different. A conditional array value that selects null stays null: `== null` is true and `??` uses its fallback. The length of a null array is null; `length([])` is `0`. | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | `==` | equal | `404 == 404` → `true`
`null == null` → `true`
`null == 0` → `false` | | `!=` | not equal | `404 != 200` → `true`
`null != 0` → `true`
`null != null` → `false` | | `<` | less | `1.5 < 2` → `true`
`null < 1` → `false` | | `<=` | less or equal | `2 <= 2` → `true`
`null <= 1` → `false` | | `>` | greater | `duration(1, "s") > duration(999, "ms")` → `true`
`1 > null` → `false` | | `>=` | greater or equal | `2 >= 3` → `false`
`null >= null` → `false` | | `&&` | both / and | `"GET" == "GET" && 200 < 300` → `true`
`true && false` → `false`
`true && null` → `false` | | `\|\|` | either / or | `true \|\| false` → `true`
`false \|\| null` → `false`
`true \|\| null` → `true` | | `!` | not | `!true` → `false`
`!null` → `true` | | `??` | the left value unless it is null | `"nope".parseInt() ?? -1` → `-1` throws `CoercionRefused` // the left is null, so the fallback stands in
`(true ? null : [1, 2]) ?? [9]` → `[9]` // a null array value uses the fallback
`[] ?? [9]` → `[]` // an empty array is already a value | | `?:` | ternary; if true, then take the first, otherwise take the second | `200 < 300 ? "ok" : "bad"` → `"ok"`
`true ? 1 : 2.5` → `1.0` // the branches widen to a common type
`null ? "yes" : "no"` → `"no"` | Does not compile: | | | | --- | --- | | `"10" < 9` | Text and a number have no common type. Convert first: `"10".parseInt() < 9` is `false`. | | `true > false` | `bool` has no ordering. | | `0 \|\| 200 < 300` | There is no truthiness: `\|\|` takes `bool` operands. |

sections.heading: `value.isNull()`
sections.text:
### `value.isNull()`

`(any)` → `bool`

True when the value is null or the field is absent.

A declared field a record lacks reads as null, so `isNull(user.id)` is how you test for absence.

-   `"".isNull()` → `false`
-   `"nope".parseInt().isNull()` → `true` throws `CoercionRefused`
-   `"smeltr".at(99).isNull()` → `true` throws `IndexOutOfRange`
-   `isNull("")` → `false` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: Conversion
sections.text:
## Conversion

Reading one type as another. A parse whose text does not convert is null on that row and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception on the record; it never returns an approximation. Blank text is null and throws nothing. Text that reads as an instant is read with [parseTime](#parseTime).

sections.heading: `value.toString(form = "base64")`
sections.text:
### `value.toString(form = "base64")`

`(i64/f64/bool/str/bytes/datetime/duration)` → `str`; `(bytes, str)` → `str`

Renders a number, bool, datetime or duration as text, exactly as the JSON output would. Bytes render in the form named: `"base64"`, `"hex"` (two lowercase digits a byte) or `"binary"` (eight `0`s and `1`s a byte, high bit first). A form it does not know is null and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception.

-   `404.toString()` → `"404"`
-   `"1998-08-30T12:00:00Z".parseTime().toString()` → `"1998-08-30T12:00:00.000000Z"`
-   `duration(1, "s").toString()` → `"1000000"` // a span writes as its microsecond count
-   `"café".encode("utf-8").toString()` → `"Y2Fmw6k="` // bytes write as base64 where no form is named, as the JSON output writes them
-   `"café".encode("utf-8").toString("hex")` → `"636166c3a9"`
-   `toString(404)` → `"404"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.parseInt(radix = 10)`
sections.text:
### `value.parseInt(radix = 10)`

`(str)` → `i64`; `(str, i64)` → `i64`

Parses a whole string as an integer. Surrounding whitespace is allowed; trailing junk is not.

-   `"42".parseInt()` → `42`
-   `" 42 ".parseInt()` → `42` // surrounding space is ignored
-   `"12abc".parseInt()` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused` // not `12`: the whole text must be a number
-   `"0x1f".parseInt(16)` → `31` // an explicit radix, 2 to 36
-   `parseInt("ff", 16)` → `255` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.parseHex()`
sections.text:
### `value.parseHex()`

`(str)` → `i64`

Parses a hexadecimal string, with or without a `0x` prefix. An alias for `parseInt(value, 16)`.

-   `"0x1f".parseHex()` → `31`
-   `"ff".parseHex()` → `255` // the `0x` is optional
-   `"zz".parseHex()` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused`
-   `parseHex("ff")` → `255` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.parseFloat()`
sections.text:
### `value.parseFloat()`

`(str)` → `f64`

Parses a whole string as a floating-point number.

-   `"3.5".parseFloat()` → `3.5`
-   `"1e3".parseFloat()` → `1000.0` // an `f64` always writes a decimal point, so it cannot be read back as an integer
-   `"3.5kb".parseFloat()` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused`
-   `parseFloat("3.5")` → `3.5` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.parseBytes(form = "base64")`
sections.text:
### `value.parseBytes(form = "base64")`

`(str)` → `bytes`; `(str, str)` → `bytes`

Reads text back into the bytes `toString` wrote, in the form named: `"base64"` (padded or not), `"hex"` (either case) or `"binary"`.

-   `"Y2Fmw6k=".parseBytes().decode("utf-8")` → `"café"`
-   `"636166c3a9".parseBytes("hex").toString()` → `"Y2Fmw6k="`
-   `"not base64!".parseBytes()` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused`
-   `parseBytes("Y2Fmw6k=").toString("hex")` → `"636166c3a9"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `bytes.decode(encoding)`
sections.text:
### `bytes.decode(encoding)`

`(bytes, str)` → `str`

Reads bytes as text in the encoding named: a WHATWG label such as `"utf-8"`, `"utf-16le"` or `"latin1"`, or `"auto"`, which detects as a source's `encoding` does. Bytes that do not decode become U+FFFD. An encoding it does not know is null and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception.

-   `"6361 66e9".replaceAll(/ /, "").parseBytes("hex").decode("latin1")` → `"café"`
-   `"Y2Fmw6k=".parseBytes().decode("auto")` → `"café"`
-   `"Y2Fmw6k=".parseBytes().decode("klingon")` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused`
-   `decode(parseBytes("Y2Fmw6k="), "utf-8")` → `"café"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `text.encode(encoding)`
sections.text:
### `text.encode(encoding)`

`(str, str)` → `bytes`

The text's bytes in the encoding named, by the labels `decode` takes. `"auto"` names no encoding to write. A character the encoding cannot spell makes the result null and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception.

-   `"café".encode("latin1").toString("hex")` → `"636166e9"`
-   `"hi".encode("utf-16le").toString("hex")` → `"68006900"`
-   `"日本".encode("latin1")` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused`
-   `encode("café", "utf-8").toString("hex")` → `"636166c3a9"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: Numbers
sections.text:
## Numbers `i64` and `f64`. An `i64` beside an `f64` widens to `f64`. An arithmetic `i64` result never wraps. The bitwise operators take `i64` only and work over all 64 bits. An `i64` result that does not fit, from `+`, `-`, `*`, negation, `abs`, `idiv`, `round`, `floor`, `ceil` or `trunc`, is null on that row and throws an `Overflow` exception on the record: `9223372036854775807 * 2` is null, not a wrapped negative. A value divided by zero with `/`, `%` or `idiv` is null on that row and throws a `DivideByZero` exception on the record. A null divided by zero is null and throws nothing. An `f64` result that is not finite, such as `1e308 * 10`, throws no exception. JSON has no spelling for it, so the output omits the field. Bitwise operands are signed and already 64 bits wide, so there is no narrowing step and no unsigned shift. The shift count is taken modulo 64, and bits pushed off the end are gone: `1 << 65` is `2`, and `(1 << 62) << 2` is `0`. | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | `+` | add numbers | `200 + 1` → `201` | | `-` | subtract numbers | `1000 - 1` → `999` | | `-` | negate | `-(41)` → `-41` | | `*` | multiply | `1.5 * 4` → `6.0` | | `/` | divide, always `f64` | `1500 / 1000` → `1.5`
`1 / 0` → `null` throws `DivideByZero` // by zero is null, not infinity | | `%` | remainder, signed like the left operand | `-5 % 3` → `-2`
`5 % -3` → `2` // the sign comes from the left operand, not the right
`5 % 0` → `null` throws `DivideByZero` // a zero divisor is null, as dividing by zero is | | `**` | power | `3 ** 8` → `6561.0`
`2 ** 3 ** 2` → `512.0` // right-associative, so `2 ** (3 ** 2)` | | `&` | bits set in both | `0xff & 0x0f` → `15` // `11111111 & 00001111` = `00001111` | | `\|` | bits set in either | `6 \| 3` → `7` // `110 \| 011` = `111` | | `^` | bits set in exactly one | `6 ^ 3` → `5` // `110 ^ 011` = `101` | | `~` | every bit flipped, so `~n` is `-n - 1` | `~0` → `-1` // `000…0` flipped is `111…1`, all 64 bits set
`~6` → `-7` // `000…0110` flipped is `111…1001` | | `<<` | shift toward the high end | `1 << 8` → `256` | | `>>` | shift toward the low end, sign-preserving | `-8 >> 1` → `-4`
`256 >> 4` → `16` | Does not compile: | | | | --- | --- | | `1.5 & 1` | Bitwise operators take `i64` only. |

sections.heading: `value.abs()`
sections.text:
### `value.abs()`

`(i64/f64)` → `the value's type`

Absolute value, keeping the input's type.

-   `(-3).abs()` → `3`
-   `abs(-2.5)` → `2.5` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `min(a, b, ...)`
sections.text:
### `min(a, b, ...)`

`(i64/f64, i64/f64, ...)` → `i64 when every argument is, else f64`

The smallest of its arguments: an `i64` when every argument is one, else an `f64`.

-   `min(200, 64)` → `64`
-   `status = 404`: `min(status, 500)` → `404`
-   `min(200, 64, 128)` → `64` // any number of arguments
-   `min(3, 5.5)` → `3.0` // one `f64` argument widens the result, so the answer is `3.0` and not `3`
-   `status = 404`: `status.min(500)` → `404` // the same call, written as a method

sections.heading: `max(a, b, ...)`
sections.text:
### `max(a, b, ...)`

`(i64/f64, i64/f64, ...)` → `i64 when every argument is, else f64`

The largest of its arguments: an `i64` when every argument is one, else an `f64`.

-   `max(200, 64)` → `200`
-   `max(64, 200, 128)` → `200` // any number of arguments
-   `max(3, 2.5)` → `3.0` // the integer wins, and the answer is still `3.0` and not `3`
-   `status = 404`: `status.max(500)` → `500` // the same call as `max(status, 500)`, written as a method

sections.heading: `value.clamp(lo, hi)`
sections.text:
### `value.clamp(lo, hi)`

`(i64/f64, i64/f64, i64/f64)` → `i64 when every argument is, else f64`

The value pulled into `lo..hi`: `lo` when it is below, `hi` when it is above, itself in between. An `f64` if any argument is one.

-   `width = 150`: `width.clamp(0, 100)` → `100`
-   `width = -20`: `width.clamp(0, 100)` → `0`
-   `width = 64`: `width.clamp(0, 100)` → `64`
-   `(1).clamp(0.5, 2)` → `1.0` // one `f64` bound widens the result even when the value is kept, so the answer is `1.0` and not `1`
-   `(1).clamp(10, 0)` → `null` // an inverted range satisfies nothing, so it is null rather than one of the ends
-   `width = 150`: `clamp(width, 0, 100)` → `100` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.round()`
sections.text:
### `value.round()`

`(f64)` → `i64`

The nearest integer. A tie rounds away from zero, as `as i64` does.

-   `2.4.round()` → `2`
-   `2.5.round()` → `3` // a tie rounds away from zero
-   `-2.5.round()` → `-3` // a literal binds the method before the minus: `-(2.5.round())`
-   `(-2.5).round()` → `-3` // parenthesized, the value itself rounds
-   `round(2.5)` → `3` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.floor()`
sections.text:
### `value.floor()`

`(f64)` → `i64`

The largest integer no greater than the value.

-   `2.9.floor()` → `2`
-   `floor(-2.1)` → `-3` // down, away from zero

sections.heading: `value.ceil()`
sections.text:
### `value.ceil()`

`(f64)` → `i64`

The smallest integer no less than the value.

-   `2.1.ceil()` → `3`
-   `ceil(-2.9)` → `-2` // up, toward zero

sections.heading: `value.trunc()`
sections.text:
### `value.trunc()`

`(f64)` → `i64`

The fraction dropped, toward zero.

-   `2.9.trunc()` → `2`
-   `trunc(-2.9)` → `-2` // toward zero, which is where it differs from `floor`

sections.heading: `idiv(a, b)`
sections.text:
### `idiv(a, b)`

`(i64/f64, i64/f64)` → `i64 when every argument is, else f64`

Integer division, truncating toward zero: the pair of `%`.

-   `idiv(7, 2)` → `3`
-   `idiv(-7, 2)` → `-3` // toward zero, so `idiv(a, b) * b + a % b` is `a`

sections.heading: Sequences
sections.text:
## Sequences A string and an array both have a length and positions, and the same functions reach into either. Positions count from zero and a negative one counts from the end; positions and lengths count Unicode characters, so a slice can never land mid-character. For arrays and strings, `x[i]` is `at(x, i)`, including negative positions and out-of-range results. A position past either end reads null and throws an `IndexOutOfRange` exception on the record. On a named field, a fixed string key is part of the [field name](#names): `geo["city"]` reads `geo.city`. | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | `[]` | the element of an array at that position; negative counts from the end | `fields = "a,b,c".split(",")`: `fields[2]` → `"c"`
`fields = "a,b,c".split(",")`: `fields[-1]` → `"c"` // the last element
`fields = "a,b,c".split(",")`: `fields[5]` → `null` throws `IndexOutOfRange` // past the end of an array is null | | `[]` | the character of a string at that position | `method = "GET"`: `method[0]` → `"G"`
`method = "GET"`: `method[99]` → `null` throws `IndexOutOfRange` // past the end of a string is null | | `[]` | the child of an object under that name | `geo = {"city": "Oslo", "lat": 59}`: `geo["city"]` → `"Oslo"` // a name, not a position |

sections.heading: `value.length()`
sections.text:
### `value.length()`

`(str/bytes/array)` → `i64`

Characters in a string, bytes in a `bytes` value, or elements in an array.

-   `line = "disk full"`: `line.length()` → `9`
-   `"🔥 alert".length()` → `7` // characters, not bytes and not UTF-16 units: an emoji counts once
-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",").length()` → `3` // elements, for an array
-   `line = "disk full"`: `length(line)` → `9` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.slice(start[, end])`
sections.text:
### `value.slice(start[, end])`

`(str, i64)` → `str`; `(str, i64, i64)` → `str`; `(array of scalars, i64)` → `the array's type`; `(array of scalars, i64, i64)` → `the array's type`

A substring, or part of an array, from `start` up to but not including `end`. A string is indexed by characters. A negative index counts from the end; `end` defaults to the length.

-   `line = "error: disk full"`: `line.slice(7)` → `"disk full"`
-   `"1998-08-30".slice(0, 4)` → `"1998"` // `end` is exclusive
-   `path = "/api/v2/things"`: `path.slice(-6)` → `"things"` // a negative start counts from the end
-   `"a,b,c,d".split(",").slice(1, 3)` → `["b","c"]` // arrays slice the same way
-   `line = "error: disk full"`: `slice(line, 7)` → `"disk full"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.at(index)`
sections.text:
### `value.at(index)`

`(str, i64)` → `str`; `(array of scalars, i64)` → `the element type`

One element of an array, one character of a string, or one field of a declared object.

For arrays and strings, `value[index]` is the same as `value.at(index)`.

On a named field, `payload["status"]` resolves as `payload.status`. A declared field a record lacks reads as null. This named-path form differs from calling `at` on an object value.

An object value passed to `at` needs a declared field set and a literal key. An unknown key does not compile. For a declared array of objects, `tags[0]["name"]` reads a field of one element.

-   `"smeltr".at(0)` → `"s"`
-   `"smeltr".at(-1)` → `"r"` // a negative index counts from the end
-   `"smeltr".at(99)` → `null` throws `IndexOutOfRange` // past either end of a string is null
-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",")[-1]` → `"c"` // `[...]` is `at`, negative index included
-   `at("smeltr", 0)` → `"s"` // the same call, written as a function
-   `payload.status = 200`: `payload["status"]` → `200` // a fixed string key on a named field

sections.heading: `value.indexOf(search)`
sections.text:
### `value.indexOf(search)`

`(str, str)` → `i64`; `(array of scalars, value)` → `i64`

Where `search` first occurs in a string, or which element of an array equals it. `-1` when it does not. Other languages call this `find`.

-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.indexOf(",")` → `1`
-   `"GET /health".indexOf("POST")` → `-1` // `-1`, not null
-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",").indexOf("c")` → `2`
-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `indexOf(line, ",")` → `1` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.includes(search)`
sections.text:
### `value.includes(search)`

`(str, str)` → `bool`; `(array of scalars, value)` → `bool`

Whether a string contains `search`, or an array contains an element equal to it.

-   `msg = "connection reset by peer"`: `msg.includes("reset")` → `true`
-   `"GET,HEAD".split(",").includes("HEAD")` → `true` // arrays too
-   `msg = "connection reset by peer"`: `includes(msg, "reset")` → `true` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: Strings
sections.text:
## Strings

A `str` is text, always valid UTF-8. `+` joins two. [length](#length), [slice](#slice), [at](#at), [indexOf](#indexOf) and [includes](#includes) take a string or an array.

There is no implicit stringification: a number has to go through `toString()` before it can be joined to text.

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+` | join text | `"GET" + " /health"` → `"GET /health"` |

Does not compile:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| `"a" + 1` | No implicit stringification. Write `"a" + (1).toString()`. |

sections.heading: `value.lastIndexOf(search)`
sections.text:
### `value.lastIndexOf(search)`

`(str, str)` → `i64`

Where `search` last occurs, or `-1`. Useful for splitting on the final separator.

-   `"/api/v2/things".lastIndexOf("/")` → `7`
-   `"a.b.c".lastIndexOf(".")` → `3`
-   `lastIndexOf("/api/v2/things", "/")` → `7` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.startsWith(prefix)`
sections.text:
### `value.startsWith(prefix)`

`(str, str)` → `bool`

Whether the string begins with `prefix`.

-   `path = "/api/v2/things"`: `path.startsWith("/api/")` → `true`
-   `"GET /health".startsWith("POST")` → `false`
-   `path = "/api/v2/things"`: `startsWith(path, "/api/")` → `true` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.endsWith(suffix)`
sections.text:
### `value.endsWith(suffix)`

`(str, str)` → `bool`

Whether the string ends with `suffix`.

-   `"app.log.gz".endsWith(".gz")` → `true`
-   `endsWith("app.log.gz", ".gz")` → `true` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.toUpperCase()`
sections.text:
### `value.toUpperCase()`

`(str)` → `str`

Uppercased. Unicode-aware, so a character can expand.

-   `level = "warn"`: `level.toUpperCase()` → `"WARN"`
-   `"straße".toUpperCase()` → `"STRASSE"` // Unicode-aware, so one character can become two
-   `level = "warn"`: `toUpperCase(level)` → `"WARN"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.toLowerCase()`
sections.text:
### `value.toLowerCase()`

`(str)` → `str`

Lowercased, Unicode-aware. Lowercase both sides to compare them without regard to case.

-   `"WARN".toLowerCase()` → `"warn"`
-   `"Get".toLowerCase() == "get"` → `true`
-   `toLowerCase("WARN")` → `"warn"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.trim()`
sections.text:
### `value.trim()`

`(str)` → `str`

Whitespace removed from both ends. Other languages call this `strip`.

-   `raw = " disk full "`: `raw.trim()` → `"disk full"`
-   `"\ttabbed\n".trim()` → `"tabbed"` // every kind of whitespace, not just spaces
-   `raw = " disk full "`: `trim(raw)` → `"disk full"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.trimStart()`
sections.text:
### `value.trimStart()`

`(str)` → `str`

Whitespace removed from the start only. Other languages call this `lstrip` or `ltrim`.

-   `" indented".trimStart()` → `"indented"`
-   `trimStart(" indented")` → `"indented"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.trimEnd()`
sections.text:
### `value.trimEnd()`

`(str)` → `str`

Whitespace removed from the end only. Other languages call this `rstrip` or `rtrim`.

-   `"trailing ".trimEnd()` → `"trailing"`
-   `trimEnd("trailing ")` → `"trailing"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.padStart(length, pad = " ")`
sections.text:
### `value.padStart(length, pad = " ")`

`(str, i64)` → `str`; `(str, i64, str)` → `str`

Pads the front with `pad` — a space by default — until the string is `length` characters. Already long enough is returned unchanged. Other languages call this `rjust`.

-   `"7".padStart(3, "0")` → `"007"`
-   `"5".padStart(3)` → `" 5"` // the default pad is a space
-   `id = 42`: `id.toString().padStart(5, "0")` → `"00042"`
-   `"toolong".padStart(3, "0")` → `"toolong"` // never truncates
-   `"x".padStart(2000000000)` → `null` // a result over 16 MiB is null and throws nothing
-   `padStart("7", 3, "0")` → `"007"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.padEnd(length, pad = " ")`
sections.text:
### `value.padEnd(length, pad = " ")`

`(str, i64)` → `str`; `(str, i64, str)` → `str`

Pads the end with `pad`, a space by default, until the string is `length` characters. Already long enough is returned unchanged. Other languages call this `ljust`.

-   `"id".padEnd(5, ".")` → `"id..."`
-   `"hi".padEnd(4)` → `"hi "` // the default pad is a space
-   `padEnd("id", 5, ".")` → `"id..."` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.repeat(count)`
sections.text:
### `value.repeat(count)`

`(str, i64)` → `str`

The string repeated `count` times.

-   `"ab".repeat(3)` → `"ababab"`
-   `"x".repeat(0)` → `""`
-   `"x".repeat(-1)` → `null` // a negative count, or a result over 16 MiB, is null
-   `repeat("ab", 3)` → `"ababab"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.md5()`
sections.text:
### `value.md5()`

`(str/bytes)` → `str`

The MD5 hash of the bytes, or of a text's UTF-8 bytes, in lowercase hex. A fingerprint for spotting repeats, never a security check.

-   `"abc".md5()` → `"900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72"`

sections.heading: `value.sha1()`
sections.text:
### `value.sha1()`

`(str/bytes)` → `str`

The SHA-1 hash of the bytes, or of a text's UTF-8 bytes, in lowercase hex.

-   `"abc".sha1()` → `"a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d"`

sections.heading: `value.sha256()`
sections.text:
### `value.sha256()`

`(str/bytes)` → `str`

The SHA-256 hash of the bytes, or of a text's UTF-8 bytes, in lowercase hex.

-   `"abc".sha256()` → `"ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad"`

sections.heading: `value.sha512()`
sections.text:
### `value.sha512()`

`(str/bytes)` → `str`

The SHA-512 hash of the bytes, or of a text's UTF-8 bytes, in lowercase hex.

-   `"abc".sha512().slice(0, 16)` → `"ddaf35a193617aba"` // the first 16 of 128 digits

sections.heading: Regular expressions
sections.text:
## Regular expressions

A pattern is written as a literal, `/[0-9]+/`, and compiled once, when the pipeline is compiled, not per row. The flags are `i` to ignore case, `m` to let `^` and `$` match at each line, and `s` to let `.` match a newline.

sections.heading: `value.test(/pattern/)`
sections.text:
### `value.test(/pattern/)`

`(str, /pattern/)` → `bool`

Whether the pattern matches anywhere in the value, as a `bool`. Use it in a `Drop` condition or a route.

-   `"GET /health".test(/^GET/)` → `true`
-   `"id=abc".test(/^id=[0-9]+$/)` → `false`
-   `"Error: nope".test(/error/i)` → `true`
-   `test("GET /health", /^GET/)` → `true` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.match(/pattern/)`
sections.text:
### `value.match(/pattern/)`

`(str, /pattern/)` → `array(str)`

The whole match followed by each capture group, as an array — or null when nothing matches.

Element 0 is the whole match, so a capture group is at 1.

-   `"2026-08-30".match(/([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)/)` → `["2026-08-30","2026","08","30"]`
-   `"v=17".match(/v=([0-9]+)/).at(1)` → `"17"`
-   `"nothing here".match(/[0-9]+/)` → `null`
-   `match("2026-08-30", /([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)/)` → `["2026-08-30","2026","08","30"]` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.replaceFirst(/pattern/, replacement)`
sections.text:
### `value.replaceFirst(/pattern/, replacement)`

`(str, /pattern/, str)` → `str`

The value with the first match replaced. `$1`, `$<name>` and `$&` in the replacement refer back to the match.

-   `"a1b2".replaceFirst(/[0-9]/, "#")` → `"a#b2"` // the first match only
-   `"2026-08-30".replaceFirst(/([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)-([0-9]+)/, "$3/$2/$1")` → `"30/08/2026"` // capture groups, reordered
-   `replaceFirst("user=alice", /user=(.+)/, "user=***")` → `"user=***"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `value.replaceAll(/pattern/, replacement)`
sections.text:
### `value.replaceAll(/pattern/, replacement)`

`(str, /pattern/, str)` → `str`

The value with every match replaced.

-   `"a1b2".replaceAll(/[0-9]/, "#")` → `"a#b#"` // every match, where `replaceFirst` takes one
-   `"user=alice".replaceAll(/user=(.+)/, "user=***")` → `"user=***"`
-   `replaceAll("a1b2", /[0-9]/, "#")` → `"a#b#"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: Arrays
sections.text:
## Arrays

An `array<T>` holds elements of the one type `T`. `filter` keeps the elements whose condition is true and `map` computes a value for each element. [length](#length), [slice](#slice), [at](#at), [indexOf](#indexOf) and [includes](#includes) take an array or a string.

`+` joins two arrays of the same element type. It never appends a single element, since `xs + y` would be ambiguous when `y` is itself an array; [push](#push) appends.

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+` | join two arrays | `line = "a,b"`;`more = "c,d"`: `line.split(",") + more.split(",")` → `["a","b","c","d"]` |

Does not compile:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| `["a", "b"] + "c"` | `+` joins two arrays; use `push` to append an element. |

sections.heading: `array.map(item => expression)`
sections.text:
### `array.map(item => expression)`

A new array with one computed value for each element. The source array is unchanged.

It compiles in an Eval or Code step. In a route condition, a delivery condition or a capture filter it does not compile.

The arrow takes one parameter. Its body is one expression, or a block whose last expression is the value. An arrow may call local functions and hold another arrow.

-   `[1, 2, 3].map(x => x * 2)` → `[2,4,6]`
-   `map([1, 2, 3], x => x * 2)` → `[2,4,6]` // the same call in function form

sections.heading: `array.filter(item => condition)`
sections.text:
### `array.filter(item => condition)`

A new array of the elements whose condition is true. It filters elements inside a record; a Drop step discards the whole record.

It compiles in an Eval or Code step. In a route condition, a delivery condition or a capture filter it does not compile.

The arrow takes one parameter. Its body is one expression, or a block whose last expression is the value. An arrow may call local functions and hold another arrow.

A null condition counts as false. When no element matches, the result is an empty array.

-   `[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(x => x > 2)` → `[3,4]`
-   `[1, 2].filter(x => x > 9)` → `[]`
-   `filter([1, 2, 3], x => x > 1).map(x => x * 2)` → `[4,6]` // filter and then transform the kept elements

sections.heading: `value.split(delimiter)`
sections.text:
### `value.split(delimiter)`

`(str, str)` → `array(str)`; `(str, /pattern/)` → `array(str)`

Splits a string into an array on a literal delimiter or a regex. An empty delimiter splits into characters.

-   `"GET /health HTTP/1.1".split(" ")[2]` → `"HTTP/1.1"` // index the array with `[...]` -- one field out of a delimited line
-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",")` → `["a","b","c"]`
-   `"a1b22c".split(/[0-9]+/)` → `["a","b","c"]` // a regex separator splits on runs
-   `"abc".split("")` → `["a","b","c"]`
-   `line = "GET /health HTTP/1.1"`: `split(line, " ")[2]` → `"HTTP/1.1"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `array.join(separator)`
sections.text:
### `array.join(separator)`

`(array of scalars, str)` → `str`

The elements as one string, separated by `separator`.

-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",").join(" | ")` → `"a | b | c"`
-   `"a,b".split(",").join("")` → `"ab"`
-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `join(line.split(","), " | ")` → `"a | b | c"` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `array.push(value, ...)`
sections.text:
### `array.push(value, ...)`

`(array, value, ...)` → `the array's type`

The array with every value appended. A null value is a position, as it is in `["a", null]`.

-   `line = "a,b"`: `line.split(",").push("c")` → `["a","b","c"]`
-   `x = [] as array<str>`: `x.push("a")` → `["a"]` // `[]` has no element type of its own, so the name that holds it declares one
-   `line = "a,b"`: `line.split(",").push("c", "d", "e")` → `["a","b","c","d","e"]` // every value in one call -- a loop that pushes rebuilds the whole array each time round
-   `line = "a,b"`: `line.split(",").push(parseInt("x").toString())` → `["a","b",null]` throws `CoercionRefused` // a null value is a position, so every value keeps its place
-   `line = "a,b"`: `line.split(",").push("c").join(" | ")` → `"a | b | c"` // the new array comes back, so it goes straight into the next call
-   `line = "a,b"`: `push(line.split(","), "c")` → `["a","b","c"]` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `array.insert(index, value, ...)`
sections.text:
### `array.insert(index, value, ...)`

`(array, i64, value, ...)` → `the array's type`

The array with every value inserted before `index`. `push` is this with the position at the end.

An index past either end clamps. A null index makes the result null. A null value takes a position.

-   `line = "a,b,d"`: `line.split(",").insert(2, "c")` → `["a","b","c","d"]`
-   `line = "a,b"`: `line.split(",").insert(-1, "z")` → `["a","z","b"]` // `-1` is the last element, so the value lands before it -- to append, use `push`
-   `line = "a,b"`: `line.split(",").insert(1, "x", "y")` → `["a","x","y","b"]`
-   `line = "a,b"`: `line.split(",").insert(1, parseInt("x").toString())` → `["a",null,"b"]` throws `CoercionRefused` // a null value is a position here too
-   `line = "a,b,d"`: `insert(line.split(","), 2, "c")` → `["a","b","c","d"]` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `array.remove(index)`
sections.text:
### `array.remove(index)`

`(array of scalars, i64)` → `the array's type`

The array without the element at `index`. The elements after it move up one.

A null array or index makes the result null.

-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",").remove(1)` → `["a","c"]`
-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",").remove(-1)` → `["a","b"]` // `-1` is the last element, as it is for `at`
-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",").remove(5)` → `["a","b","c"]` // an index outside the array removes nothing

sections.heading: `array.resize(size)`
sections.text:
### `array.resize(size)`

`(array of scalars, i64)` → `the array's type`

The array with exactly `size` positions: its first `size`, or its own followed by positions that hold nothing.

A negative or null size, or a null array, makes the result null.

-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",").resize(2)` → `["a","b"]`
-   `line = "a,b,c"`: `line.split(",").resize(4)` → `["a","b","c",null]` // a new position holds nothing until a write fills it
-   `resize([] as array<str>, 2)` → `[null,null]` // sized before any data arrives; each position holds nothing until a write fills it

sections.heading: `array.concat(other, ...)`
sections.text:
### `array.concat(other, ...)`

`(array of scalars, array of scalars, ...)` → `the array's type`

One array with every element of all of them, in order. `a + b` is the same call.

-   `line = "a,b"`: `line.split(",").concat(["c", "d"])` → `["a","b","c","d"]`
-   `line = "a,b"`: `line.split(",").concat(["c"], ["d", "e"])` → `["a","b","c","d","e"]` // any number of arrays, in one pass
-   `line = "a,b"`: `concat(line.split(","), ["c", "d"])` → `["a","b","c","d"]` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `array.sort(descending)`
sections.text:
### `array.sort(descending)`

`(array of scalars)` → `the array's type`; `(array of scalars, bool)` → `the array's type`

The elements in order: text by its bytes, numbers by value, `false` before `true`. `descending` is optional. Equal elements keep their order and nulls go last. Other languages call this `sorted`.

-   `["b", "c", "a"].sort()` → `["a","b","c"]`
-   `[3, 1, 2].sort(true)` → `[3,2,1]` // descending
-   `[2, null, 1].sort()` → `[1,2,null]` // nulls last

sections.heading: Dates and times
sections.text:
## Dates and times A datetime is an instant in UTC, microsecond-resolution, and serializes as ISO 8601. `now()` is read once per record, so every route a record takes sees the same instant. There is no local time zone: a log line's own offset is read when it is parsed and kept nowhere else. [Comparison](#tests) orders instants: `start < end` is true when `start` is earlier. | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | `+` | advance an instant | `"1998-08-30".parseTime() + duration(90, "s")` → `"1998-08-30T00:01:30.000000Z"`
`now() + duration(1, "h") > now()` → `true` // `now()` is read once per record, so both of these are the same instant | | `-` | wind an instant back | `"1998-08-30".parseTime() - duration(1, "d")` → `"1998-08-29T00:00:00.000000Z"` | | `-` | the span between two instants | `"1998-08-31".parseTime() - "1998-08-30".parseTime() == duration(1, "d")` → `true` | Does not compile: | | | | --- | --- | | `"1998-08-30T12:00:00Z".parseTime() + "1998-08-30T12:00:00Z".parseTime()` | Two instants have no sum. Subtract them for a span. | The clock

sections.heading: `now()`
sections.text:
### `now()`

`()` → `datetime`

The current instant. Captured once per record, so every route a record takes sees the same value.

-   `now().year() >= 2026` → `true`

Reading text

sections.heading: `value.parseTime([format][, reference = now()])`
sections.text:
### `value.parseTime([format][, reference = now()])`

`(str)` → `datetime`; `(str, str)` → `datetime`; `(str, datetime)` → `datetime`; `(str, str, datetime)` → `datetime`

Parses text into a datetime. With no format, a run of digits is a compact date when it reads as one (`YYYYMMDD` or `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS`), else a Unix epoch whose unit comes from its magnitude — seconds below 10^11, then milliseconds, microseconds and nanoseconds at each further thousand — and other text is matched against the common shapes — ISO 8601, `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`, `YYYY/MM/DD HH:MM:SS`, syslog's `Mon D HH:MM:SS`, and Apache's `[D/Mon/YYYY:HH:MM:SS +ZZZZ]`. Give a `strftime` format to pin it, and a reference instant to fix the year a syslog stamp does not carry. A parser's declared `datetime` field is this call: the bare type detects, and `{"type":"datetime","format":...}` pins. Other languages call this `strptime`.

The reference is a datetime, not a year — usually the field carrying when the record was collected. Pass none and it is `now()`, which is what makes the no-argument form right for a live stream.

A yearless stamp takes the reference's year, and rolls back a year rather than landing in the future: parsed against 1 January 1999, `Dec 31` is 1998. That also means an anchor \*earlier\* than the stamp reads as the year before it.

Text that does not parse is null on that row and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception on the record. An impossible date is such text, never a silently shifted one: `1998-02-30` does not become 2 March.
