A zone name is not one offset: `CST` is six hours behind UTC in Chicago and eight ahead in Shanghai, and one pipeline reads both. `%z` takes the fixed set the table names. Replace any other name with the offset that source means — `replaceAll(/CEST/, "+0200")` — and the choice sits beside the source it belongs to.

Reading what it finds

-   `"1998-08-30T12:00:00Z".parseTime()` → `"1998-08-30T12:00:00.000000Z"`
-   `"1998-08-30 12:34:56".parseTime().hour()` → `12`
-   `"904478400".parseTime()` → `"1998-08-30T12:00:00.000000Z"` // ten digits of seconds; the same instant in milliseconds, `904478400000`, reads the same
-   `"904478400000".parseTime() == "904478400".parseTime()` → `true`
-   `"19980830".parseTime()` → `"1998-08-30T00:00:00.000000Z"` // eight digits that read as a date are that date, not a count of seconds

Pinning the shape

-   `"30/08/1998".parseTime("%d/%m/%Y")` → `"1998-08-30T00:00:00.000000Z"`
-   `"2026-08-30 12:00:00 CEST".parseTime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused` // a zone name outside the set `%z` takes is null, never a guess
-   `"2026-08-30 12:00:00 CEST".replaceAll(/CEST/, "+0200").parseTime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")` → `"2026-08-30T10:00:00.000000Z"` // give the name the offset it means for this source, then parse
-   `"1000".parseTime("%Q")` → `"1970-01-01T00:00:01.000000Z"` // auto-detect reads four digits as seconds; `%Q` says milliseconds and `%s` says seconds

Yearless stamps

-   `"Feb 3 04:05:06".parseTime() == "Feb 3 04:05:06".parseTime(now())` → `true` // no reference means `now()`, which is where a yearless stamp gets its year
-   `"02-03 04:05:06".parseTime("%m-%d %H:%M:%S")` → `"2026-02-03T04:05:06.000000Z"` // a shape auto-detect does not know; the year comes from `now()`
-   `"Dec 31 23:59:00".parseTime("1999-01-01T00:05:00Z".parseTime())` → `"1998-12-31T23:59:00.000000Z"` // a December line read five minutes into January is last year's, not next year's

-   `parseTime("1998-08-30T12:00:00Z")` → `"1998-08-30T12:00:00.000000Z"` // the same call, written as a function

`parseTime(value, format)` takes these, and only these. Every other byte of the format must match the text literally, and text left over when the format runs out makes the result null rather than a partial read. Auto-detect tries an ordered list of formats built from the same specifiers, so every rule below holds for `parseTime(value)` too.

Format specifiers for parseTime:

| The date |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `%Y` | The year, exactly four digits. There is no two-digit year: every century pivot is wrong for someone. | `"2026-08-30".parseTime("%Y-%m-%d")` → `"2026-08-30T00:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `%m` | Month number, `1`\-`12`, with or without a leading zero. | `"8/2026".parseTime("%m/%Y")` → `"2026-08-01T00:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `%d` | Day of month, `1`\-`31`, with or without a leading zero. A day past the month's end is null. | `"2026-02-30".parseTime("%Y-%m-%d")` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused` // February has no 30th |
| `%e` | Day of month with an optional leading space, as in `Aug 3`. | `"Aug 3 2026".parseTime("%b %e %Y")` → `"2026-08-03T00:00:00.000000Z"` |
| The time of day |
| `%H` | Hour on a 24-hour clock, `0`\-`23`. `24` is ISO 8601's end-of-day and is allowed only at a zero minute, second and fraction. | `"2026-08-30 24:00:00".parseTime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")` → `"2026-08-31T00:00:00.000000Z"` // the midnight that closes the date |
| `%I` | Hour on a 12-hour clock, `1`\-`12`. Pair it with `%p`. | `"2026-08-30 02:00 PM".parseTime("%Y-%m-%d %I:%M %p")` → `"2026-08-30T14:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `%M` | Minute, `0`\-`59`, two digits. | `"2026-08-30 00:45".parseTime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")` → `"2026-08-30T00:45:00.000000Z"` |
| `%S` | Second, `0`\-`60`, two digits. `60` is a leap second and lands on the following minute. | `"2016-12-31 23:59:60".parseTime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")` → `"2017-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `%f` | Fractional seconds. Every digit is read and the first six kept, so a nanosecond stamp is truncated rather than refused; a shorter run is a position, not a count. | `"2026-08-30 00:00:00.123456789".parseTime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%f")` → `"2026-08-30T00:00:00.123456Z"` |
| The offset |
| `%z` | A UTC offset — `Z`, `+HH`, `+HHMM` or `+HH:MM` — or one of the named zones `UT`, `UTC`, `GMT`, `EST`, `EDT`, `CST`, `CDT`, `MST`, `MDT`, `PST`, `PDT`. Any other name is null. Without `%z` the text reads as UTC. | `"2026-08-30T00:00:00+05".parseTime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z")` → `"2026-08-29T19:00:00.000000Z"` // A whole-hour offset without its minutes |
| Names and AM/PM |
| `%b` | An English month name, abbreviated or full. The same specifier as `%B`. | `"30 August 2026".parseTime("%d %b %Y")` → `"2026-08-30T00:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `%B` | An English month name, abbreviated or full. The same specifier as `%b`. | `"30 Aug 2026".parseTime("%d %B %Y")` → `"2026-08-30T00:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `%a` | An English weekday name, abbreviated or full. Consumed and discarded — it is never checked against the date. | `"Sun, 30 Aug 2026".parseTime("%a, %d %b %Y")` → `"2026-08-30T00:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `%A` | An English weekday name, abbreviated or full. The same specifier as `%a`. | `"Sunday 30 Aug 2026".parseTime("%A %d %b %Y")` → `"2026-08-30T00:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `%p` | `AM` or `PM`, either case. Reads `%I`; `12 AM` is midnight and `12 PM` is noon. | `"2026-08-30 12:00 AM".parseTime("%Y-%m-%d %I:%M %p")` → `"2026-08-30T00:00:00.000000Z"` |
| `%s` | Seconds since the Unix epoch, with an optional sign and fraction. It names the whole instant, so the format holds no other specifier. | `"1000.5".parseTime("%s")` → `"1970-01-01T00:16:40.500000Z"` // auto-detect would read a count this small as seconds too; the specifier says so outright |
| `%Q` | Milliseconds since the Unix epoch, with an optional sign and fraction. It names the whole instant, so the format holds no other specifier. | `"1000".parseTime("%Q")` → `"1970-01-01T00:00:01.000000Z"` // auto-detect reads a count this small as seconds |
| `%%` | A literal percent sign. | `"2026 100%".parseTime("%Y 100%%")` → `"2026-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z"` |

sections.heading: `value.parseDuration()`
sections.text:
### `value.parseDuration()`

`(str)` → `duration`

Parses text into a duration: the count of microseconds `toString()` writes, whole or as a decimal rounded to the microsecond. Text that is no count is null.

-   `"90000000".parseDuration().countIn("s")` → `90.0`
-   `duration(250, "ms").toString().parseDuration() == duration(250, "ms")` → `true` // what `toString()` writes reads back as the same span
-   `"soon".parseDuration()` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused`

A part of the instant

sections.heading: `value.year()`
sections.text:
### `value.year()`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

The calendar year.

-   `"1998-08-30".parseTime().year()` → `1998`

sections.heading: `value.month()`
sections.text:
### `value.month()`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

The month, 1 to 12.

-   `"1998-08-30".parseTime().month()` → `8`

sections.heading: `value.day()`
sections.text:
### `value.day()`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

The day of the month.

-   `"1998-08-30".parseTime().day()` → `30`

sections.heading: `value.hour()`
sections.text:
### `value.hour()`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

The hour, 0 to 23, in UTC.

-   `"1998-08-30 12:34:56".parseTime().hour()` → `12`

sections.heading: `value.minute()`
sections.text:
### `value.minute()`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

The minute, 0 to 59.

-   `"1998-08-30 12:34:56".parseTime().minute()` → `34`

sections.heading: `value.second()`
sections.text:
### `value.second()`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

The second, 0 to 59.

-   `"1998-08-30 12:34:56".parseTime().second()` → `56`

sections.heading: `value.millisecond()`
sections.text:
### `value.millisecond()`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

The millisecond within the second, 0 to 999.

-   `"1998-08-30T12:00:00.250Z".parseTime().millisecond()` → `250`

sections.heading: `value.dayOfWeek()`
sections.text:
### `value.dayOfWeek()`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

The day of the week: 1 is Monday, 7 is Sunday.

-   `"1998-08-31".parseTime().dayOfWeek()` → `1`

Epoch counts

sections.heading: `value.epochMillis()`
sections.text:
### `value.epochMillis()`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

Milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

-   `"1998-08-30 12:00:00".parseTime().epochMillis()` → `904478400000`

sections.heading: `epochSeconds(value)`
sections.text:
### `epochSeconds(value)`

`(datetime)` → `i64`

The Unix timestamp: whole seconds since the epoch, rounded down. A time before the epoch is negative and rounds away from zero.

-   `epochSeconds(parseTime("1998-08-30T12:00:00Z"))` → `904478400`

sections.heading: `fromEpochMillis(millis)`
sections.text:
### `fromEpochMillis(millis)`

`(i64)` → `datetime`

A datetime from milliseconds since the Unix epoch, for a producer that already sends one.

-   `fromEpochMillis(904478400000)` → `"1998-08-30T12:00:00.000000Z"`

sections.heading: `fromEpochSeconds(seconds)`
sections.text:
### `fromEpochSeconds(seconds)`

`(i64)` → `datetime`

A datetime from seconds since the Unix epoch. A count past the datetime range is null.

-   `fromEpochSeconds(904478400)` → `"1998-08-30T12:00:00.000000Z"`

sections.heading: Durations
sections.text:
## Durations

A duration is a signed span, microsecond-resolution. Subtracting two datetimes produces one. It serializes as a bare count of microseconds, `toString()` produces the same text, and `parseDuration()` reads it back.

[Comparison](#tests) orders spans: `age > duration(5, "m")` is true when `age` is longer than five minutes.

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `+` | add two spans | `duration(30, "m") + duration(45, "s") == duration(1845, "s")` → `true` |
| `-` | the difference of two spans | `duration(1, "h") - duration(30, "m") == duration(30, "m")` → `true` |
| `*` | scale a span | `duration(90, "s") * 2 == duration(3, "m")` → `true` |
| `/` | the ratio of two spans | `duration(1, "h") / duration(1, "m")` → `60.0` |
| `/` | divide a span | `duration(1, "h") / 4 == duration(15, "m")` → `true` |

Does not compile:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| `duration(1, "y")` | A year varies in length, so a span cannot be counted in one. Days are fixed: `duration(365, "d")`. |

sections.heading: `duration(count, unit)`
sections.text:
### `duration(count, unit)`

`(i64/f64, str)` → `duration`

A span of `count` units. The unit is `"ns"`, `"us"`, `"ms"`, `"s"`, `"m"`, `"h"`, `"d"`, `"w"` or a long name, and the count may be fractional.

A span is held to the microsecond, so anything finer truncates toward zero: `duration(1500, "ns")` is one microsecond and `duration(1, "ns")` is a zero span. A fractional count of any unit rounds the same way.

There is no month or year: how long either one is depends on which one, and a span is a count with no calendar attached to answer that. A week is seven days, so it is here.

A literal unit is checked when the pipeline compiles: `duration(1, "y")` does not compile. A unit computed per row that names no unit makes the result null. A span too large to hold is null.

-   `duration(90, "s").toString()` → `"90000000"`
-   `duration(250, "ms").toString()` → `"250000"`
-   `duration(1.5, "d").toString()` → `"129600000000"`
-   `duration(1000, "ns").toString()` → `"1"` // a thousand nanoseconds is one microsecond, exactly
-   `duration(2, "w") == duration(14, "d")` → `true` // a week is exactly seven days
-   `duration(90, "s") > duration(1, "minute")` → `true`

sections.heading: `duration.countIn(unit)`
sections.text:
### `duration.countIn(unit)`

`(duration, str)` → `f64`

The whole span counted in one unit, as an `f64`, not a remainder.

-   `duration(90, "s").countIn("m")` → `1.5`
-   `duration(36, "h").countIn("d")` → `1.5`
-   `duration(1, "d").countIn("h")` → `24.0`
-   `duration(1, "s").countIn("us")` → `1000000.0` // the unit the wire form counts in
-   `duration(14, "d").countIn("w")` → `2.0`
-   `started = "1998-08-30 12:00:00".parseTime()`;`ended = "1998-08-30 12:30:00".parseTime()`: `(ended - started).countIn("m")` → `30.0`
-   `countIn(duration(90, "s"), "m")` → `1.5` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: Addresses and networks
sections.text:
## Addresses and networks

An address is text. A function parses it and writes it back as text. Text that is not an address makes the result null and throws no exception. Space around an address is ignored. To match an address against a table of blocks, use a lookup.

sections.heading: `text.isIp()`
sections.text:
### `text.isIp()`

`(str)` → `bool`

The text is an address, v4 or v6. Text that is not one is `false`. Null stays null.

-   `"10.1.2.3".isIp()` → `true`
-   `"fe80::1".isIp()` → `true`
-   `"10.1.2".isIp()` → `false`
-   `isIp("10.1.2.3")` → `true` // the same call, written as a function

sections.heading: `text.ipVersion()`
sections.text:
### `text.ipVersion()`

`(str)` → `i64`

`4` or `6`.

-   `"10.1.2.3".ipVersion()` → `4`
-   `"::1".ipVersion()` → `6`
-   `"example.com".ipVersion()` → `null`

sections.heading: `text.ipNormalize()`
sections.text:
### `text.ipNormalize()`

`(str)` → `str`

The address in one spelling. Leading zeros go. IPv6 is lowercase and its longest run of zero groups is compressed. Two spellings of one address come out the same.

-   `"2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001".ipNormalize()` → `"2001:db8::1"`
-   `" 10.1.2.3 ".ipNormalize()` → `"10.1.2.3"`
-   `"010.1.2.3".ipNormalize()` → `null` // a dotted quad takes no leading zero

sections.heading: `text.ipScope()`
sections.text:
### `text.ipScope()`

`(str)` → `str`

Where the address reaches: `unspecified`, `loopback`, `link-local`, `multicast`, `private` or `public`. Private is RFC 1918 and `fc00::/7`.

-   `"10.1.2.3".ipScope()` → `"private"`
-   `"8.8.8.8".ipScope()` → `"public"`
-   `"127.0.0.1".ipScope()` → `"loopback"`
-   `"fe80::1".ipScope()` → `"link-local"`
-   `"224.0.0.1".ipScope()` → `"multicast"`
-   `"::".ipScope()` → `"unspecified"`
-   `"fd12::1".ipScope()` → `"private"`

sections.heading: `address.inCidr(block, ...)`
sections.text:
### `address.inCidr(block, ...)`

`(str, str, ...)` → `bool`

The address is in one of the blocks. A block of the other family holds nothing. A bare address is a block of one.

-   `"10.1.2.3".inCidr("10.0.0.0/8")` → `true`
-   `"10.1.2.3".inCidr("192.168.0.0/16", "10.0.0.0/8")` → `true` // any number of blocks
-   `"10.1.2.3".inCidr("::/0")` → `false` // the other family
-   `"10.1.2.3".inCidr("10.1.2.3")` → `true` // a bare address is a block of one
-   `"10.1.2.3".inCidr("10.0.0.0/33")` → `null` // a block that does not parse

sections.heading: `address.cidrNetwork(prefix)`
sections.text:
### `address.cidrNetwork(prefix)`

`(str, i64)` → `str`

The address masked to `prefix` bits, written as a block. Group by it to count per subnet.

-   `"10.1.2.3".cidrNetwork(24)` → `"10.1.2.0/24"`
-   `"10.1.2.3".cidrNetwork(12)` → `"10.0.0.0/12"`
-   `"2001:db8:abcd::1".cidrNetwork(32)` → `"2001:db8::/32"`
-   `"10.1.2.3".cidrNetwork(33)` → `null` // past the width of the address

sections.heading: `communityId(srcIp, srcPort, dstIp, dstPort, transport, seed)`
sections.text:
### `communityId(srcIp, srcPort, dstIp, dstPort, transport, seed)`

`(str, i64, str, i64, str)` → `str`; `(str, i64, str, i64, i64)` → `str`; `(str, i64, str, i64, str, i64)` → `str`; `(str, i64, str, i64, i64, i64)` → `str`

The flow's [Community ID](https://github.com/corelight/community-id-spec), version 1. `transport` is an IANA protocol number, 0 to 255, as a number or as text, or one of these names in any case: `icmp`, `igmp`, `tcp`, `udp`, `gre`, `icmpv6` (or `ipv6-icmp`), `eigrp`, `ospf`, `pim`, `sctp`. Any other name is null. TCP, UDP and SCTP need both ports, 1 to 65535; for ICMP and ICMPv6 the ports are the type and the code; any other protocol has no ports. Both addresses must be IPv4 or both IPv6. `seed` is optional, 0 to 65535, 0 by default. Both directions of a flow give one ID.

-   `communityId("128.232.110.120", 34855, "66.35.250.204", 80, "tcp")` → `"1:LQU9qZlK+B5F3KDmev6m5PMibrg="`
-   `communityId("66.35.250.204", 80, "128.232.110.120", 34855, 6)` → `"1:LQU9qZlK+B5F3KDmev6m5PMibrg="` // the reply, with the protocol's number
-   `communityId("128.232.110.120", 34855, "66.35.250.204", 80, "tcp", 123)` → `"1:hTSGlFQnR58UCk+NfKRZzA32dPg="` // a seed
-   `communityId("128.232.110.120", 0, "66.35.250.204", 80, "tcp")` → `null` // TCP needs both ports
-   `communityId("10.0.0.1", 5, "10.0.0.2", 6, "quic")` → `null` // not a protocol name it knows

sections.heading: URLs, domains and user agents
sections.text:
## URLs, domains and user agents

Text that does not read is null and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception on the record; blank text is null and throws nothing.

sections.heading: `text.urlDecode()`
sections.text:
### `text.urlDecode()`

`(str)` → `str`

`%XX` as the byte it names and `+` as a space, as a form field is encoded, and the bytes read as UTF-8; a byte that is not UTF-8 becomes U+FFFD. A `%` that two hex digits do not follow stays a `%`, so every text reads.

-   `"a%20b+c%C3%A9".urlDecode()` → `"a b cé"`
-   `"100%".urlDecode()` → `"100%"` // a bare % stays

sections.heading: `text.htmlStrip()`
sections.text: ### `text.htmlStrip()` `(str)` → `str` The text without its markup. A tag goes, in any case. A block-level tag, start or end, becomes a line break: `address`, `article`, `aside`, `blockquote`, `br`, `dd`, `div`, `dl`, `dt`, `fieldset`, `figcaption`, `figure`, `footer`, `form`, `h1` to `h6`, `header`, `hgroup`, `hr`, `li`, `nav`, `noscript`, `ol`, `output`, `p`, `pre`, `section`, `table`, `tbody`, `td`, `tfoot`, `th`, `thead`, `tr` and `ul`. A comment, a `` or `` declaration, and a `

sections.heading: `text.parseUrl()`
sections.text:
### `text.parseUrl()`

`(str)` → `{domain: str, fragment: str, path: str, extension: str, port: i64, query: str, scheme: str, user_info: str, username: str, password: str}`

A URL's parts as an object: `domain`, `fragment`, `path`, `extension`, `port`, `query`, `scheme`, `user_info`, `username` and `password`. Text that reads as an RFC 3986 URI or relative reference, such as a bare path, has its path, query, fragment and user info decoded. An `http`, `https`, `ftp`, `file` or `jar` URL that does not, holding a space or a `|` say, is split as written, undecoded. `extension` is what follows the last `.` of the path's last segment. `username` is the user info up to its first `:`, all of it where there is none, and `password` what follows that `:`. A part the URL lacks is null. Other languages call this `urlparse`.

-   `"https://www.example.com:8443/files/report.pdf?x=1#top".parseUrl()` → `{"domain":"www.example.com","fragment":"top","path":"/files/report.pdf","extension":"pdf","port":8443,"query":"x=1","scheme":"https"}`
-   `"http://user:pw@host/a%20b".parseUrl().path` → `"/a b"` // a part read on its own
-   `"/search/index.html?q=x".parseUrl()` → `{"path": "/search/index.html", "extension": "html", "query": "q=x"}` // a path alone
-   `"not a url".parseUrl()` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused`

sections.heading: `host.registeredDomain()`
sections.text:
### `host.registeredDomain()`

`(str)` → `{domain: str, registered_domain: str, top_level_domain: str, subdomain: str}`

The host, the name registered under its public suffix, that suffix and what is left, as an object of `domain`, `registered_domain`, `top_level_domain` and `subdomain`. The suffixes are the ICANN section of the Public Suffix List, compiled in. A host with no known suffix does not read.

-   `"www.foo.example.co.uk".registeredDomain()` → `{"domain":"www.foo.example.co.uk","registered_domain":"example.co.uk","top_level_domain":"co.uk","subdomain":"www.foo"}`
-   `"co.uk".registeredDomain()` → `{"domain":"co.uk","top_level_domain":"co.uk"}` // a suffix alone
-   `"intranet.local".registeredDomain()` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused` // no known suffix

sections.heading: `text.parseUserAgent()`
sections.text:
### `text.parseUserAgent()`

`(str)` → `{name: str, version: str, os: {name: str, version: str, full: str}, device: {name: str}}`

The browser, operating system and device a User-Agent header names, as an object of `name`, `version`, `os.name`, `os.version`, `os.full` and `device.name`. The rules are uap-core's, compiled in. `name` and `device.name` are `Other` where no rule matches, and `os` is null where none names an operating system. `os.full` is `os.name`, then `os.version` where there is one.

-   `"Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/120.0.6099.109 Safari/537.36".parseUserAgent()` → `{"name":"Chrome","version":"120.0.6099.109","os":{"name":"Windows","version":"10","full":"Windows 10"},"device":{"name":"Other"}}`
-   `"curl/8.4.0".parseUserAgent().name` → `"curl"` // one part

sections.heading: Exceptions and try
sections.text:
## Exceptions and try

A calculation that cannot give a value leaves its field null and marks the record with an exception: text that is not a number, a division by zero, an overflow. Each exception has a kind, such as `CoercionRefused` or `DivideByZero`. A conversion that fails, such as `"five" as i64`, gives null and marks the record with a `CoercionRefused` exception. A parser's declared field that the parser cannot read as its type also gives null, and marks the record with an `UnparsableField` exception. An exception no `catch` takes stays on the record to the end of the pipeline, where its [exception answers](/docs/routing/exceptions#answers) apply.

A function's entry says when it throws one. Each kind belongs to a category. The group's [exception answers](/docs/routing/exceptions#answers) answer a kind or its category, and a route may override them. By default an encoding exception is ignored, since its value is kept, a delivery exception blocks, and every other kind is tagged.

-   `10 / 0` → `null` throws `DivideByZero`
-   `"many".parseInt()` → `null` throws `CoercionRefused`
-   `9223372036854775807 + 1` → `null` throws `Overflow`

| Kind | Category | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Unparsable` | parse | A parser got nothing from the record: malformed JSON, an unterminated CSV quote, a Grok pattern that matched nothing. |
| `UnparsableField` | parse | One declared field could not be read as its declared type while the rest of the record parsed. That field is null. |
| `KeyContradiction` | parse | Two keys of a record contradict after flattening, such as the same key twice. One is kept. |
| `CoercionRefused` | parse | A value could not convert to the type asked for, as in `parseInt("many")`. The result is null. |
| `Overflow` | math | `i64` arithmetic overflowed. The result is null. |
| `DivideByZero` | math | A division by zero. The result is null, not Infinity. |
| `NaN` | math | A parse met `NaN`, `Infinity` or a number past `f64`'s range. That key has no value. |
| `LoopBudgetExceeded` | limits | A `while` loop hit its time budget with the record's condition still true. |
| `IndexOutOfRange` | limits | An array read or write, or a string read, named a position the value does not have. The read is null and the write does nothing. |
| `InvalidUtf8` | encoding | Bytes that did not decode under the source's encoding were replaced with U+FFFD. |
| `GuessedEncoding` | encoding | A source set to `auto` recognized neither UTF-8 nor UTF-16 and guessed the encoding. The text may well be right. |
| `Unmatched` | delivery | No route or delivery condition took it. |
| `Unprocessable` | delivery | No pipeline could finish the record: one crashed on its batch, or the record does not fit the memory budget alone. |
| `Refused` | delivery | A destination refused the record. |

A `try` block stops at a record's first exception that loses a value. The write that failed does not happen, so the field keeps what it held. Its `catch` then runs on that record, with the exception cleared. `catch (e)` names the exception: `e.kind` is its kind and `e.message` its text. When one statement leaves several, `e.kind` is the first and `e.message` holds all their texts, and the `catch` clears them all. A `finally` block runs on every record that entered the `try`. A `try` needs a `catch`, a `finally` or both.

Code

```
try {
  count = parseInt(text);
} catch (e) {
  count = 0;
  problem = e.kind;
  detail = e.message;
} finally {
  checked = true;
}
```

Input

```
{
  "text": "many"
}
```

→

Output

```
{
  "checked": true,
  "count": 0,
  "detail": "text is \"many\", which could not convert to i64 in count",
  "problem": "CoercionRefused",
  "text": "many"
}
```

A typed catch, such as `catch (e: DivideByZero | NaN)`, runs on the records holding a kind it names and clears only those kinds. A `try` can have several catches, and it tries them in order. A catch with no type takes every kind left, and comes last. A kind no catch names stays on the record, for an outer `try` or its exception answer. `throw e` in a catch puts the exception back on the record, which goes on to the next `try` out, or to its exception answer when there is none. A catch reads `e` and cannot change it. A `try` catches every kind but the encoding and delivery ones. An encoding exception repairs its value instead, so the block goes on and no `catch` takes it.

sections.heading: Delivery
sections.text:
# Delivery

Smeltr advances a source's reading position after every chosen destination accepts the record or completes the configured action for a refused record. Smeltr retries unreachable destinations. These rules apply across [destination types](/docs/destinations).

sections.heading: Delivery at a glance
sections.text:
## Delivery at a glance

*Diagram: Delivery and recovery. When a destination accepts a record, that delivery is complete. If it is unreachable, Smeltr retries and pauses input when buffers fill. If it refuses a record, Smeltr follows your chosen action: hold and retry, send it elsewhere for investigation, or count and drop it.*

Choose any normal Smeltr destination to receive refused records for investigation and later replay. Selecting it for this job makes it a dead-letter destination; it is not a separate destination type. Smeltr waits for every selected destination to confirm receipt. If one is unavailable, the input streams sending records to it can still be paused.

Each destination writes the record in its own [format](/docs/destinations#formats). An unreachable destination can keep the source paused until delivery succeeds. For records a destination refuses, the [configured action](#refused) determines what happens next.

sections.heading: Hold and retry
sections.text:
## Hold and retry

When a destination is unreachable, delivery retries. Connection failures, authentication failures, and throttling need attention at the receiving service or its connection settings. As buffers fill, Smeltr pauses the input streams sending records to that destination. Sources with independent delivery paths can continue.

For Kafka inputs, Smeltr saves its reading position only after the required deliveries finish or the **drop** action discards the record. While the source is paused, Smeltr reads nothing more from Kafka, so records it has not read wait there for as long as the topic's [retention](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#topicconfigs_retention.ms) keeps them. Allow enough for the outage and the time needed to catch up. Worker memory has a fixed limit and does not replace this storage. Smeltr cannot reread local logs and metrics from a retained Kafka topic.

An unreachable destination does not automatically switch to a standby destination. Dead-letter delivery handles records that a destination refuses, using its [configured refusal action](#refused).

sections.heading: Handle refused records
sections.text:
## Handle refused records

A record a destination cannot accept is `Refused`. Examples include a mapping conflict, an oversized message, or a text record missing its required field. An **answer** is the configured action for that refusal: block, deliver, or drop. Set the group's answer under **Exceptions** on the Routes page, or one destination's under **Exceptions** in its card.

![A destination's Exceptions: a refused record is delivered to kafka-dlq.](/destination-overrides-light.png)

A destination's Exceptions hold only Refused. Here they send the record to kafka-dlq.

-   **block (default):** keep the record and send it again while the source waits.
-   **deliver:** send it to the destinations you pick, where it stays for investigation and later replay. Each must be configured and reachable.
-   **drop:** count the refused record and continue.

A connection or authentication failure needs its own fix. A refusal action does not repair an unreachable service. Use pipeline filtering for records you intentionally want to discard.

sections.heading: Keep refused records for investigation
sections.text:
## Keep refused records for investigation

You can send a refused record to another destination, such as a Kafka topic, so you can inspect it and try sending it again after fixing the problem. This is often called a **dead-letter queue**. Any normal Smeltr destination can serve this role: you designate it by selecting it for the **deliver** action. Prepare the destination and its credentials before deploying the change.

If you pick several destinations, all of them must confirm acceptance. For a Kafka source, Smeltr waits for these confirmations before saving its reading position past that record. You still need to investigate why the original destination refused it.

sections.heading: If the destination for refused records also fails
sections.text:
### If the destination for refused records also fails

If it is unreachable, Smeltr retries and can pause the input streams sending records to it as buffers fill. If it refuses the record, its own configured action applies: block, deliver elsewhere, or drop. You can pass records through several destinations, but the path must never loop back to an earlier one. Each destination along the path writes the record in its own format.

Inspect a saved record before planning replay. It holds the record in the [format](/docs/destinations#formats) of the destination that kept it.

sections.heading: Recover and replay
sections.text:
## Recover and replay

After fixing a connection or receiving service, watch delivery resume and the source backlog drain. Records saved for investigation stay there until you arrange to send them through again, a process called replay. Smeltr does not automatically send them back to the original destination.

1.  Inspect the refusal and a saved record. Fix the mapping, pipeline, permissions, or capacity that caused it.
2.  Choose which saved records to retry. If they are in Kafka, use a separate source and consumer group, and select an explicit range of record positions or times. See [Kafka source reads](/docs/sources/kafka). Keep the retained records until you verify recovery.
3.  Build the recovery route on a branch. Use saved samples to test its output and delivery conditions. Send records to the intended destination and check that the route cannot feed them back into the same input topic.
4.  Plan for redelivery. Preserve stable document IDs when using Elasticsearch dedupe or overwrite, and check how downstream consumers handle duplicates.
5.  Review and deploy the recovery route. Verify the worker commit, actual destination records, rejection counts, and remaining backlog before widening the replay window.
6.  Retire the temporary recovery route after you have accounted for its selected records.

For missing output, follow [No records arriving](/docs/troubleshooting#no-output). To check a working path end to end, use [the tutorial's delivery check](/docs/first-pipeline#verify).

sections.text:

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

*Diagram: From a source to its destinations, and back to the commit. The reader polls a batch from the source and tracks its position. Transform routes the batch and runs its pipelines. Egress, one per destination, writes each destination's records and retries until they land. Each destination acknowledges its records, and once every destination the batch reached has acknowledged it, the reader commits the batch's position to the source.*

A position is committed only after every destination the batch reached has acknowledged it, oldest batch first. After a restart or a retry a record can arrive twice, but it is not lost. Smeltr metrics and logs sources keep no position.

What happens to a record decides when its batch's position commits. Until it commits, a restart reads the batch again.

| The record | The position commits |
| --- | --- |
| Is acknowledged by every destination it was sent to | Once every older batch has committed too. |
| Is dropped by a step, or picked by no deliver rule | With its batch. |
| Reaches a destination that does not answer | Only once it lands. Egress retries, and a destination that stays down pauses the sources feeding it. |
| Carries an exception | By the answer to it, as below. A pipeline's exceptions are answered by its route's `exceptions` over the group's; Unmatched and Unprocessable by the group's; Refused by the destination's over the group's. |

| Answer | The position commits |
| --- | --- |
| `ignore`, `tag` | Once the destinations the record goes on to acknowledge it. |
| `drop` | With its batch. |
| `deliver` | Once every destination named acknowledges the record. |
| `block` | Not until the record goes through. A refused record is sent again until the destination takes it; any other stops its source until a new config is deployed. |

Unmatched, Unprocessable and Refused block unless an answer says otherwise, and take no `ignore` or `tag`. [Exceptions](/docs/routing/exceptions#answers) covers each answer.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

A destination is one entry of the bundle's Destinations array. Every kind takes these settings:

`id`  string required

The destination's name, unique among destinations. Routes and other destinations' answers name it.

Examples:

- `events-out`
- `siem-archive`

`exceptions`  answers default the group's answer, `block` unless it gives another

What happens to a record this destination refuses: block keeps it and sends it again until the destination takes it, drop lets it go, and deliver sends it to other destinations. See [Handle refused records](/docs/delivery#refused).

Examples:

- `{"kinds": {"Refused": "drop"}}`
- `{"kinds": {"Refused": "block"}}`

sections.heading: Formats
sections.text:
## Formats

A destination's `format` decides what it writes of each record. Routes and exception answers name only destinations, so one record can reach two destinations in two forms.

| format | What it writes |
| --- | --- |
| json, ndjson, parquet, avro, csv | The record as the pipeline wrote it. |
| text | The text of the field `field` names, `_raw` by default. The destination refuses a record without that field. |
| bytes | One field's bytes, once per source record. The destination's `field` names the field, and defaults to `__source.bytes`: each record's bytes as the source received them, before any pipeline ran. Those bytes let you [replay](/docs/delivery#recovery) records: a source that reads them back gets what the original source got. |

Each kind writes only some formats:

| Destination | format |
| --- | --- |
| HTTP | json (default), text, bytes (base64 in a batch: [bodies](/docs/destinations/http#bodies)) |
| Kafka | json (default), text, bytes, avro |
| Elasticsearch | json |
| Splunk HEC, event endpoint | json (default), text |
| Splunk HEC, raw endpoint | json (default), text, bytes |
| S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob, SFTP | ndjson (default), json, parquet, avro, csv, text, bytes |
| Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake | parquet, as the table's data files |

sections.heading: Fields
sections.text:
## Fields

Smeltr never delivers a record field whose name starts with `__`. A pipeline sets `__destination` fields to steer a record, and each kind reads only its own:

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__destination.topic` | `str` | The Kafka topic or Event Hub a destination writes the record to. Null means the default value for that destination. |
| `__destination.index` | `str` | The index an Elasticsearch or Splunk HEC destination files the record under. Null means the destination's default index. A Splunk HEC destination on the `raw` endpoint refuses a record naming an index other than its own. |
| `__destination.id` | `str` | The Elasticsearch document ID, used when the destination's document ID setting is `dedupe` or `overwrite`. When it is null, the destination's id field names the field that gives it, and with neither the document is sent with no ID. |
| `__destination.prefix` | `str` | What an S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage destination's object key starts with, taken as it is. Null means the destination's own prefix, with its time placeholders filled in. |

sections.heading: Add a destination
sections.text:
## Add a destination

1.  Select the worker group and work on a branch.
2.  Open Build → Destinations and choose **\+ Add destination**.
3.  Choose its type, give it a unique id and fill in its settings, then choose **Add**. Save the page.
4.  Connect it to a route's delivery path, whose condition selects the records it receives from a [source](/docs/sources). [Follow the routing example](/docs/first-pipeline#route).
5.  [Review and deploy](/docs/review), then [verify it](#verify).

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

1.  Check that the intended workers are online and run the deployed commit.
2.  Send a record you can recognize through a source and a route to the destination.
3.  Check Status and Logs for source, routing or destination errors.
4.  Find the record at the destination and check its fields.

A preview of a saved sample checks the pipeline, not the live connection.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**No records arrive**

Follow [No records arriving](/docs/troubleshooting#no-output) to check input, worker configuration, routing, filtering and delivery in order.

**TLS verification fails**

Check the server name and the authority in the connection identity. If the server uses a private CA, the connector must trust it.

sections.heading: Azure Blob Storage
sections.text:
# Azure Blob Storage

Writes batches of records as blobs in an Azure Blob Storage container.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Writes as the worker host's managed identity.

```
{
  "id": "archive",
  "type": "azureBlob",
  "account": "acmelogs",
  "container": "events"
}
```

![The Azure Blob Storage form on the Destinations page: id archive, account acmelogs, container events, format ndjson.](/azure-blob-destination-form-light.png)

The same destination on the Destinations page.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   [Create the storage account and container](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/blobs/storage-quickstart-blobs-portal).
-   Choose how it signs in, and give that identity permission to write blobs to the container. A key, signature or client secret goes in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
    -   the worker host's [managed identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview), or a [service principal](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/howto-create-service-principal-portal), either given a role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor (see [assign a role for blob data](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/blobs/assign-azure-role-data-access));
    -   an [account key](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/common/storage-account-keys-manage); or
    -   a [shared access signature](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview) allowed to create and write blobs.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`account`  string required

The storage account.

Examples:

- `acmelogs`
- `acmeprodaudit01`

`container`  string required

The container.

Examples:

- `events`
- `audit-logs`

`accessKey`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the account's access key. Set at most one of `accessKey`, `sasToken`, `clientSecret` and `managedIdentityClientId`; with none, the host's managed or workload identity is used.

Examples:

- `AZURE_ACCESS_KEY`
- `{"secret": "azure-access-key","version": 1}`

`sasToken`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding a shared access signature.

Examples:

- `AZURE_SAS_TOKEN`
- `{"secret": "azure-sas-token","version": 1}`

`tenantId`  string default none

A service principal's tenant. Set `tenantId`, `clientId` and `clientSecret` together, or none of them.

Examples:

- `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`
- `acme.onmicrosoft.com`

`clientId`  string default none

A service principal's client id.

Example:

- `11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111`

`clientSecret`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding a service principal's client secret.

Examples:

- `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`
- `{"secret": "azure-client-secret","version": 1}`

`managedIdentityClientId`  string default the host's managed or workload identity

The client id of the user-assigned managed identity to sign in as. Set it when the worker's host has more than one managed identity. Left out, it signs in as the host's managed identity, or an AKS pod's workload identity.

Example:

- `22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222`

`prefix`  string default `%Y/%m/%d/%H/`

What each object's key starts with, for a record with no `__destination.prefix`. `%Y`, `%m`, `%d`, `%H` and `%M` are the write time, UTC, and no other `%` is allowed. A key never starts with `/`.

Examples:

- `events/%Y/%m/%d/`
- `firewall/dt=%Y-%m-%d/hour=%H/`
- `acme/audit/`

`format`  string default `ndjson`

What each object holds.

`ndjson`

Writes one JSON document per line.

`json`

Writes one JSON array of every record.

`parquet`

Writes one Parquet file.

`avro`

Writes one Avro file.

`csv`

Writes one CSV file.

`text`

Writes one line of text per record, from `field`.

`bytes`

Writes each source record's bytes as read, before pipeline processing, one per line: `__source.bytes` unless `field` names another `bytes` field.

`field`  string default `_raw` for `text`, `__source.bytes` for `bytes`

The field each line of a `text` or `bytes` object holds. Only with format `text` or `bytes`.

Example:

- `message`

`newlines`  string default `escape`

What a `bytes` object does with a record holding a line break. Only with format `bytes`.

`escape`

Writes `\`, newline and carriage return as `\\`, `\n` and `\r`, which a source with framing `escapedLines` reverses.

`refuse`

Refuses the record.

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate.

Examples:

- `store-client`
- `corp-proxy`

sections.heading: Advanced: Endpoint and delivery
sections.text:
### Advanced: Endpoint and delivery

`endpoint`  string default the account's, in Azure's public cloud

Another address, such as Azurite's or a sovereign cloud's.

Examples:

- `http://localhost:10000/acmelogs`
- `https://acmelogs.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net`

`authEndpoint`  string default its cloud's own

Where a client secret is exchanged for a token. Only with `clientSecret`.

Examples:

- `https://login.microsoftonline.us`
- `https://login.chinacloudapi.cn`

`compression`  string default `gzip`

How it compresses each object. A `parquet` object compresses each column inside the file instead, and its key ends with `.parquet` whatever the compression. An `avro` file compresses inside the file, and its key ends with `.avro`. Its `gzip` is Avro's `deflate`. Avro has no `lz4`.

`none`

Writes it uncompressed. The key ends with the format's own extension, such as `.ndjson`.

`gzip`

Compresses it with gzip and appends `.gz` to the key, such as `.ndjson.gz`.

`snappy`

Compresses it with framed Snappy and appends `.sz` to the key, such as `.ndjson.sz`.

`lz4`

Compresses it with framed LZ4 and appends `.lz4` to the key, such as `.ndjson.lz4`.

`zstd`

Compresses it with Zstandard and appends `.zst` to the key, such as `.ndjson.zst`.

`storageClass`  string default the account's default

The access tier each blob is stored in: `Hot`, `Cool`, `Cold` or `Archive`.

Examples:

- `Cool`
- `Cold`

`inFlight`  integer default `4`

How many parts of one file upload at once. 1 to 64.

Examples:

- `8`
- `1`
- `2`

`maxObjectBytes`  size default `64 MiB`

The largest file it puts in the bucket, compressed. Set it to what the tools that read the bucket handle best. 64 KiB to 64 GiB.

Examples:

- `128 MiB`
- `2 GiB`
- `32 MB`

`bufferBytes`  size default 256 MiB

Memory it may use on each worker for records not yet in the bucket. Files are finished early when it fills, so files reach `maxObjectBytes` only when it holds that many records before compression. 4 MiB to 32 TiB.

Examples:

- `1 GiB`
- `4 GiB`

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one call to the store, or one finishing of the files, may take before it counts as stalled. 1 to 120, and at least 15 on SFTP.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

`fileIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

The longest records wait, in seconds, before they land in the bucket. A longer wait makes larger files; records are acknowledged only once they land, so a source is held open up to this long, and after a crash reads that much again. 5 to 3600.

Examples:

- `30`
- `240`

sections.heading: Fields it reads
sections.text:
## Fields it reads

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__destination.prefix` | `str` | What an S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage destination's object key starts with, taken as it is. Null means the destination's own prefix, with its time placeholders filled in. |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

The destination keeps one blob open per prefix, and for Parquet, Avro and CSV per record type of the routes feeding it, across batches, named `<prefix><random id>.<extension>`, and finishes it when it reaches `maxObjectBytes` on disk, when `fileIntervalSecs` passes, when `bufferBytes` fills on the worker, or when a 65th blob opens and this one was written least recently. A batch is acknowledged once every blob holding its records has landed. Two blobs never share a key, so records written again after a failure make new blobs.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record with a unique marker through the source, then list the container under the prefix for a new blob and look for the marker in it.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**Authorization fails**

Check that the identity has a role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor on the container, or that the SAS token allows creating and writing blobs.

sections.heading: Delta Lake
sections.text:
# Delta Lake

Writes records as Parquet files to a Delta table in S3, or a store that speaks its API, and commits them as the next entry of the table's `_delta_log`. The table is reached by its location, or by its name in Databricks Unity Catalog. Each commit is a version of the table.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Writes the table at `s3://lake/tables/access_log` with the worker host's AWS credentials, and partitions it by `host` when it creates it.

```
{
  "id": "lake-access",
  "type": "delta",
  "location": "s3://lake/tables/access_log",
  "partitionBy": [
    "host"
  ]
}
```

 ![The Delta form on the Destinations page: id lake-access, location s3://lake/tables/access_log, partition by host, the host's credentials.](/delta-destination-form-light.png) 

A Delta destination on the Destinations page. Region, endpoint and role sit under Storage.

Writes the same table in a MinIO bucket, signed with the access key in the worker-host variables `MINIO_ACCESS_KEY` and `MINIO_SECRET_KEY`.

```
{
  "id": "lake-access",
  "type": "delta",
  "location": "s3://lake/tables/access_log",
  "endpoint": "https://minio.example.com:9000",
  "accessKeyId": "MINIO_ACCESS_KEY",
  "secretAccessKey": "MINIO_SECRET_KEY"
}
```

sections.heading: Before you start
Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`location`  string default the table `unityCatalog` names

The table's root in S3, `s3://bucket/path`. A missing table is created there from the route's record. Exactly one of `location` and `unityCatalog`.

Examples:

- `s3://lake/tables/web`
- `s3://acme-logs/delta/firewall`

`unityCatalog`  object default the table at `location`

A Databricks Unity Catalog external table, in place of `location`: `workspace` is the workspace's https:// address, `table` its three-part name, `catalog.schema.table`, and `clientId` and `clientSecret` the OAuth client credentials of the service principal it signs in as. Unity Catalog gives the table's root and the credentials for its storage, so no access key or role is set beside it.

Examples:

- `{"workspace": "https://dbc-1234abcd-5678.cloud.databricks.com","table": "main.logs.web","clientId": "6f1c2a3b-0d4e-4f5a-9b8c-7d6e5f4a3b2c","clientSecret": "DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET"}`
- `{"workspace": "https://dbc-1234abcd-5678.cloud.databricks.com","table": "security.firewall.events","clientId": "6f1c2a3b-0d4e-4f5a-9b8c-7d6e5f4a3b2c","clientSecret": {"secret": "databricks-client","version": 1}}`

`partitionBy`  list of strings default none, an unpartitioned table

The top-level columns a table it creates is partitioned by. A table that exists keeps its own.

Examples:

- `host`
- `dt`
- `host`

`accessKeyId`  credential default the host's credentials

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the access key's id. Set both `accessKeyId` and `secretAccessKey`, or neither.

Examples:

- `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`
- `{"secret": "aws-access-key-id","version": 1}`

`secretAccessKey`  credential default the host's credentials

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the access key's secret.

Examples:

- `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
- `{"secret": "aws-secret-access-key","version": 1}`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects to the store under, for a private CA or a client certificate.

Examples:

- `store-client`
- `corp-proxy`

`compression`  string default `zstd`

How each Parquet file compresses its columns.

`gzip`

Compresses columns with Snappy.

`lz4`

Examples:

Memory it may use on each worker for records not yet committed. Files are committed early when it fills. 4 MiB to 32 TiB.

Examples:

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one call to the store, or one commit, may take before it counts as stalled. 1 to 120.

Examples:

- `120`

`fileIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

The longest records wait, in seconds, before they are committed to the table. Each commit is an entry of the table's log; records are acknowledged only once committed, so a source is held open up to this long. 5 to 240.

Examples:

- `240`

sections.heading: Storage permissions
Unity Catalog
sections.text:
## Unity Catalog

A Delta table registered in Databricks Unity Catalog is named by `unityCatalog`, in place of `location`. The destination signs in to the workspace as a service principal, takes the table's location and storage credentials from Unity Catalog, and renews the credentials before they expire, so it holds no AWS credentials of its own. The table is an external Delta table in S3, and it must exist. Everything after that is as for a table named by `location`.

Writes the external table `main.logs.web`, signed in to its workspace as the service principal whose OAuth secret is in the worker-host variable `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET`. The table's bucket is in `us-west-2`.

```
{
  "id": "lake-web",
  "type": "delta",
  "unityCatalog": {
    "workspace": "https://dbc-1234abcd-5678.cloud.databricks.com",
    "table": "main.logs.web",
    "clientId": "6f1c2a3b-0d4e-4f5a-9b8c-7d6e5f4a3b2c",
    "clientSecret": "DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET"
  },
  "region": "us-west-2"
}
```

sections.heading: Set up Databricks
What is refused
Columns
sections.text:
## Columns

The table's schema is the record the routes write here, its fields the table's columns, nested fields as structs and arrays as arrays. A missing table is created with that schema, as a plain Delta table, with `partitionBy` as its partition columns. A table that exists keeps its columns and its partitioning: a field it lacks, at any depth, is added as a nullable column before any file is written, and a column the record lacks reads as null in the rows written. A field that can hold no value, `null` or a list or closed struct of nothing else, has no column. Each field is written as the Delta type of its [record type](/docs/code-reference#types):

| Record type | Delta type |
| --- | --- |
| `bool` | `boolean` |
| `i64` | `long` |
| `duration` | `long`, its count of microseconds |
| `f64` | `double` |
| `str` | `string` |
| `variant` | `string`, the value as JSON |
| `datetime` | `timestamp`, in UTC |
| `bytes` | `binary` |
| `array<T>` | `array` |
| `{name: T, ...}` | `struct`; an open object's other keys go in a `string` column named `rest` |

It refuses to start when the table holds a field as another type, or has two columns of one struct whose names differ only in case. A partition column is a top-level column of a primitive type other than `bytes`.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

When it starts, the destination reads the table, or creates it, and adds the record's new columns. It writes records as Parquet files under the table's root, in a directory per partition value:

```
s3://lake/tables/access_log/
  _delta_log/
    00000000000000000000.json                 the table, created
    00000000000000000001.json                 a commit: a version of the table
    …
    00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet   the table's whole state at version 10
    _last_checkpoint
  host=web-1/
    5f0c…e1.parquet
  host=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__/
    9a42…07.parquet                           rows whose host is null or empty
```

A null or empty partition value is written as `__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__` in the path. A row whose partition values would make a file's key longer than 1024 bytes is [refused](/docs/delivery#refused).

The destination commits its files as the table's next version when `fileIntervalSecs` passes, or sooner when the records it holds near `bufferBytes`. A batch is acknowledged once the commit holding its records lands. Other writers may write the same table. A failed write is tried again until `stallAfterSecs`, and then the batches are written again. When storage's answer to a commit is lost past that point, its rows may be in the table twice.

Every `delta.checkpointInterval` commits, 10 when the table does not set it, the destination writes a checkpoint, and it deletes log entries older than `delta.logRetentionDuration`, 30 days when the table does not set it, unless `delta.enableExpiredLogCleanup` is `false`.

The destination only appends. Compact small files, and vacuum the files no version needs, with the table's own maintenance. Large files go up as multipart uploads, and a worker that stops without shutting down can leave one unfinished. Give the bucket a [lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpu-abort-incomplete-mpu-lifecycle-config.html) after a day.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record with a unique marker through the source. After `fileIntervalSecs`, look for a new commit under `_delta_log/`, or a new version in the table's history, and query the table for the marker with any engine that reads Delta.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**the routes writing here write different records, and a table has one schema**

Two routes feeding the destination write records of different types. Make them write the same record, or give each table a destination of its own.

**… is … in the table, and the record writes … there as …**

The table holds a column as another type than the record's field. Rename the field in the pipeline or the column in the table.

**the table's column … is not nullable …**

Every column the destination writes is nullable. Make the column nullable in the table, or send the records to a table of their own.

**the table needs writer version …**, **reader version …**, or **the writer feature …**

The table's protocol asks for more than this writer does. Write to a table whose protocol [Before you start](#before-you-start) lists.

**the table maps columns by id, which this writer does not**

Write to a table that maps columns by name, or not at all.

**the table has the check constraint …**

The destination does not check constraints. Drop the constraint, or write another table.

**the table's column … carries …, which this writer cannot honour**

The column is generated, an identity, has a default or carries an invariant, which the destination does not compute or check. Write to a table without such a column.

**the table is partitioned by …, a … column …**

The partition column is of a type the destination writes no partition value of. Partition by another column.

**the row's partition values make a key of … bytes …**

The row's partition values make the file's key too long. Partition by a shorter value, or shorten it in the pipeline.

**another writer dropped a column the record writes**, **changed the table's partitioning**, or **another table replaced the one at its location**

The table changed under the destination, and its files no longer fit it. Commits wait until they do. Restore the column or the partitioning, or the destination takes the table as it then is when it next starts.

**commit lost to another writer 8 times over**

Other writers took every version the destination tried. Lower how often they commit, or raise `fileIntervalSecs`.

**Access denied writing to storage**

Check that whatever signs for storage has every permission [Storage permissions](#permissions) lists, under the table's location.

**names both a location and a unityCatalog table**, or **names no table**

Name the table's root in S3 as `location`, or its `unityCatalog` table.

**names no region beside a unityCatalog table**

Name the region of the table's bucket as `region`.

**names … beside a unityCatalog table**

The destination takes its storage credentials from Unity Catalog. Take the access key, the role or the auth endpoint out.

**… /oidc/v1/token refused the sign-in (…): …**

The workspace refused the service principal's client id or secret. Check `clientId` and the secret `clientSecret` names.

**the delta destination takes its client secret from …, which this worker does not have**

The worker cannot read the [credential](/docs/secrets) `clientSecret` names. Set the variable on the worker host, or store the secret.

**Unity Catalog refused the table … (…): …**

Unity Catalog answered with the status and the error the message names. On 403, check the service principal's access to the table: see [Set up Databricks](#unity-catalog-databricks). On 404, check `table`.

**the table is …, not Delta**

The table is in another format. Name a Delta table.

**the table is …; only an external table is written**

The table is managed, or of another type. Name an external Delta table.

**Unity Catalog refused credentials for the table's storage (…): …**

Check the service principal's access to write the table. See [Set up Databricks](#unity-catalog-databricks).

**Unity Catalog vended no AWS credentials, or no expiry, for the table's storage; the table must be in S3**

The destination writes only tables in S3.

sections.heading: Elasticsearch
sections.text:
# Elasticsearch

Writes each record as a JSON document through Elasticsearch's Bulk API, many documents to a request.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Authorizes with the worker-host variable `ELASTIC_AUTH`, which holds the API key. Replace the URL and index.

```
{
  "id": "search-out",
  "type": "elasticsearch",
  "url": "https://elasticsearch.example.com:9200",
  "defaultIndex": "smeltr-events",
  "auth": "ELASTIC_AUTH"
}
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Prepare the target index or data stream and its mappings, or let the account create them.
-   Give an account permission to write there, and put its API key in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
-   Select a [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) for a private CA or a client certificate.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`url`  string required

The cluster's base address.

Examples:

- `https://elasticsearch.example.com:9200`
- `https://10.20.0.5:9200`

`defaultIndex`  string required

The index for a record with no `__destination.index`.

Examples:

- `orders`
- `logs-firewall-default`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate.

Examples:

- `elastic-client`
- `elastic-mtls`

`auth`  credential default no Authorization header

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the API key.

Examples:

- `ELASTIC_AUTH`
- `{"secret": "elastic-auth","version": 1}`

`username`  string default none

The user it signs in as, in place of an API key. Set with `password`.

Example:

- `smeltr_writer`

`password`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the user's password.

Examples:

- `ELASTIC_PASSWORD`
- `{"secret": "elastic-password","version": 1}`

`docId`  string default `auto`

Who chooses each document's id. See [Duplicate documents](/docs/destinations/elasticsearch#duplicate-documents).

`auto`

Lets Elasticsearch choose each document's id.

`dedupe`

Keeps the first document written under an id.

`overwrite`

Replaces the document written under an id.

`idField`  string default `__destination.id`

The field holding a document's id under `dedupe` or `overwrite`.

Examples:

- `event.id`
- `request_id`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`inFlight`  integer default `4`

How many bulk requests it sends at once to start with. 1 to 64.

Examples:

- `8`
- `1`
- `16`

`maxBulkBytes`  size default `5 MiB`

The most one bulk request carries. A record larger than this still goes as a single record. 64 KiB to 100 MiB.

Examples:

- `10 MiB`
- `512 KiB`
- `15MB`

`bufferBytes`  size default 64 MiB, or one bulk request if that is larger

The most one worker holds for this destination, queued or sent and not yet acknowledged. It holds what the connection to it can carry, up to this. 4 MiB to 1 GiB, and at least one bulk request.

Examples:

- `256 MiB`
- `128 MiB`
- `1 GiB`

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one batch may take to deliver, every retry included, before it counts as stalled. 1 to 120.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

`zoneUrls`  map default none

An address per zone. A worker in a listed [zone](/docs/reference#settings) sends there instead of `url`.

Examples:

- `us-east-1a = https://es-a.example.com:9200`
- `us-east-1a = https://es-a.example.com:9200`
- `us-east-1b = https://es-b.example.com:9200`

`sniff`  bool default `false`

Learns the cluster's nodes from `url` and spreads requests across them, preferring the worker's [zone](/docs/reference#settings). Every node must be reachable from the workers, and the credential needs the `monitor` cluster privilege.

`zoneAttribute`  string default `zone`

The node attribute that names a node's zone, set on each node as `node.attr.<name>`. Requires `sniff` enabled.

Examples:

- `rack`
- `availability_zone`

sections.heading: Fields it reads
sections.text:
## Fields it reads

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__destination.index` | `str` | The index an Elasticsearch or Splunk HEC destination files the record under. Null means the destination's default index. A Splunk HEC destination on the `raw` endpoint refuses a record naming an index other than its own. |
| `__destination.id` | `str` | The Elasticsearch document ID, used when the destination's document ID setting is `dedupe` or `overwrite`. When it is null, the destination's id field names the field that gives it, and with neither the document is sent with no ID. |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: ## How it works

sections.heading: Duplicate documents
sections.text:
### Duplicate documents

| Policy | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| auto (default) | Sends no document ID. A record resent after a crash can create a second document. |
| dedupe | Use a stable ID and keep the first document written with that ID. |
| overwrite | Replace the document with that ID. Concurrent requests can arrive out of order. This policy cannot write to a data stream. |

For dedupe or overwrite, set `idField` to a stable field such as `event.id`, or have the pipeline set `__destination.id`. Keep auto when records have no stable ID.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record with a unique marker through the source, then search the index for it after a refresh. Check the document's fields and the worker's delivery errors.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**401 or 403**

Check the API key, that each worker has the secret, and permissions on the target index.

**Documents are refused**

Read the per-record error. Check mappings, field types, document ids and the refused-record answer before retrying.

sections.heading: Azure Event Hubs
sections.text:
# Azure Event Hubs

Writes each record to the Event Hubs namespace through its Kafka endpoint only.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Writes to the event hub `alerts` in the namespace `acme-logs`, with the connection string from the worker-host variable `EVENT_HUBS_CONNECTION_STRING`.

```
{
  "id": "alerts-out",
  "type": "eventHubs",
  "namespace": "acme-logs",
  "defaultEventHub": "alerts",
  "connectionString": "EVENT_HUBS_CONNECTION_STRING"
}
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Use a namespace with a [Kafka endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/event-hubs/azure-event-hubs-apache-kafka-overview). Microsoft [recommends the Standard tier](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/event-hubs/event-hubs-create) for Kafka.
-   Create each event hub it writes to.
-   Choose how the destination signs in, with exactly one of:
    
    -   a connection string: copy one from a [shared access policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/event-hubs/event-hubs-get-connection-string) on the namespace with the Send right, and put it in a [credential](/docs/secrets). Use the namespace's, not one that ends in `EntityPath=`.
    -   a service principal: set `tenantId`, `clientId` and `clientSecret`, with the secret in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
    -   a user-assigned managed identity: set `managedIdentityClientId` to its client id. Set it when the host has more than one managed identity.
    -   none: the destination signs in as the host's [managed identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview), or as an AKS pod's [workload identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/workload-identity-overview). The managed identities of App Service, Container Apps and Functions are not supported.
    
    Give a service principal or identity the [Azure Event Hubs Data Sender](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/event-hubs/authorize-access-azure-active-directory) role on the namespace.
-   Allow workers to reach the namespace on port 9093, such as `acme-logs.servicebus.windows.net:9093`.
-   Set `compression` to `gzip` only on a namespace that takes it. See Microsoft's [Kafka client settings for Event Hubs](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/event-hubs/apache-kafka-configurations).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`namespace`  string required

The Event Hubs namespace: its name in Azure's public cloud, or its host name in another cloud, such as `acme-logs.servicebus.usgovcloudapi.net`. A `host:port` names another address, such as the emulator's `localhost:9092`, which is reached without TLS when it is on this host.

Examples:

- `acme-logs`
- `acme-logs.servicebus.usgovcloudapi.net`
- `localhost:9092`

`defaultEventHub`  string required

The event hub for a record with no `__destination.topic`.

Examples:

- `alerts`
- `insights-clean`

`connectionString`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the namespace's connection string, with the Send right. Set at most one of `connectionString`, `clientSecret` and `managedIdentityClientId`; with none, the host's managed or workload identity is used.

Examples:

- `EVENTHUBS_CONNECTION_STRING`
- `{"secret": "eventhubs-connection-string","version": 1}`

`tenantId`  string default none

A service principal's tenant. Set `tenantId`, `clientId` and `clientSecret` together, or none of them.

Example:

- `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`

`clientId`  string default none

A service principal's client id.

Example:

- `11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111`

`clientSecret`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding a service principal's client secret.

Examples:

- `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`
- `{"secret": "azure-client-secret","version": 1}`

`managedIdentityClientId`  string default the host's managed or workload identity

The client id of the user-assigned managed identity to sign in as. Set it when the worker's host has more than one managed identity. Left out, it signs in as the host's managed identity, or an AKS pod's workload identity.

Example:

- `22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222`

`format`  string default `json`

What each message holds.

`json`

Writes the record as JSON.

`text`

Writes one field's text, from `field`.

`bytes`

Writes each source record's bytes as read, before pipeline processing, once per record: `__source.bytes` unless `field` names another `bytes` field.

`avro`

Writes Avro messages, registering the schema in the schema registry.

`schemaRegistry`  object default none

The schema registry the Avro schema is registered in. Set `url`. If the registry needs a sign-in, also set `username` and `password`. Needed for format `avro`.

Examples:

- `{"url": "https://registry.example.com"}`
- `{"url": "https://registry.example.com","username": "smeltr","password": {"secret": "registry","version": 1}}`

`field`  string default `_raw` for `text`, `__source.bytes` for `bytes`

The field each `text` or `bytes` record writes. Only with format `text` or `bytes`.

Example:

- `message`

sections.heading: Advanced: Delivery
sections.text:
### Advanced: Delivery

`authEndpoint`  string default its cloud's own

Where a client secret is exchanged for a token. Only with `clientSecret`.

Examples:

- `https://login.microsoftonline.us`
- `https://login.chinacloudapi.cn`

`compression`  string default `none`

How it compresses each batch of events. Use gzip only on a namespace that takes it.

`none`

Sends it uncompressed.

`gzip`

Compresses it with gzip.

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one batch may take to deliver before it counts as stalled. 1 to 120.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

`bufferBytes`  size default 64 MiB

The most one worker holds for this destination, accepted but not yet acknowledged by the brokers, half of it in the Kafka client. It holds what the connection to it can carry, up to this. 4 MiB to 1 GiB.

Examples:

- `256 MiB`
- `16 MiB`
- `1 GiB`

sections.heading: Fields it reads
sections.text:
## Fields it reads

`__destination.topic` names the event hub a record goes to.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__destination.topic` | `str` | The Kafka topic or Event Hub a destination writes the record to. Null means the default value for that destination. |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

The destination writes through the namespace's Kafka endpoint, as the [Kafka destination](/docs/destinations/kafka) does, over TLS, signed in with the connection string, the service principal or the host's identity. A batch is acknowledged once Event Hubs has every record in it. A record Event Hubs will not take is [refused](/docs/delivery#refused).

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record you can recognize through the source, then find it in the event hub.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**Authentication fails**

Check that the namespace has a Kafka endpoint. With a connection string, check that it is the namespace's and that its policy has the Send right. Otherwise, check that the service principal or identity has the Azure Event Hubs Data Sender role.

**Connecting times out**

Check that the worker host reaches port 9093 on the namespace, through its firewall and any network rules on the namespace.

**The destination stalls saying the namespace does not take gzip**

The namespace does not take gzip. Set `compression` to `none`.
