sections.text:
## See also

-   [Destinations](/docs/destinations)
-   [Azure Event Hubs source](/docs/sources/event-hubs)
-   [Handle refused records](/docs/delivery#refused)

sections.heading: Google Cloud Storage
sections.text:
# Google Cloud Storage

Writes batches of records as objects in a Cloud Storage bucket.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Reads the service account key from the worker-host variable `GCS_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY`.

```
{
  "id": "archive",
  "type": "gcs",
  "bucket": "acme-logs",
  "serviceAccountKey": "GCS_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY"
}
```

![The Google Cloud Storage form on the Destinations page: id archive, bucket acme-logs, format ndjson.](/gcs-destination-form-light.png)

A Google Cloud Storage destination on the Destinations page, signed in with the host's Application Default Credentials.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   [Create the bucket](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/creating-buckets).
-   Give the service account the destination writes as permission to create objects in the bucket, such as the Storage Object Creator role. See [Cloud Storage IAM roles](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles).
-   Choose how it signs in. With no key, it uses the worker host's [Application Default Credentials](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/application-default-credentials). Otherwise put a [service account key](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/keys-create-delete), the whole JSON file, in a [credential](/docs/secrets).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`bucket`  string required

The bucket.

Examples:

- `acme-logs`
- `acme-logs-eu`

`serviceAccountKey`  credential default the host's Application Default Credentials

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding a service account's JSON key.

Examples:

- `GCS_KEY`
- `{"secret": "gcs-key","version": 1}`

`prefix`  string default `%Y/%m/%d/%H/`

What each object's key starts with, for a record with no `__destination.prefix`. `%Y`, `%m`, `%d`, `%H` and `%M` are the write time, UTC, and no other `%` is allowed. A key never starts with `/`.

Examples:

- `events/%Y/%m/%d/`
- `firewall/dt=%Y-%m-%d/hour=%H/`
- `acme/audit/`

`format`  string default `ndjson`

What each object holds.

`ndjson`

Writes one JSON document per line.

`json`

Writes one JSON array of every record.

`parquet`

Writes one Parquet file.

`avro`

Writes one Avro file.

`csv`

Writes one CSV file.

`text`

Writes one line of text per record, from `field`.

`bytes`

Writes each source record's bytes as read, before pipeline processing, one per line: `__source.bytes` unless `field` names another `bytes` field.

`field`  string default `_raw` for `text`, `__source.bytes` for `bytes`

The field each line of a `text` or `bytes` object holds. Only with format `text` or `bytes`.

Example:

- `message`

`newlines`  string default `escape`

What a `bytes` object does with a record holding a line break. Only with format `bytes`.

`escape`

Writes `\`, newline and carriage return as `\\`, `\n` and `\r`, which a source with framing `escapedLines` reverses.

`refuse`

Refuses the record.

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate.

Examples:

- `store-client`
- `corp-proxy`

sections.heading: Advanced: Endpoint and delivery
sections.text:
### Advanced: Endpoint and delivery

`endpoint`  string default the key's own cloud

Another address, such as an emulator's.

Examples:

- `http://localhost:4443`
- `https://storage.example.com`

`compression`  string default `gzip`

How it compresses each object. A `parquet` object compresses each column inside the file instead, and its key ends with `.parquet` whatever the compression. An `avro` file compresses inside the file, and its key ends with `.avro`. Its `gzip` is Avro's `deflate`. Avro has no `lz4`.

`none`

Writes it uncompressed. The key ends with the format's own extension, such as `.ndjson`.

`gzip`

Compresses it with gzip and appends `.gz` to the key, such as `.ndjson.gz`.

`snappy`

Compresses it with framed Snappy and appends `.sz` to the key, such as `.ndjson.sz`.

`lz4`

Compresses it with framed LZ4 and appends `.lz4` to the key, such as `.ndjson.lz4`.

`zstd`

Compresses it with Zstandard and appends `.zst` to the key, such as `.ndjson.zst`.

`storageClass`  string default the bucket's own

The class each object is stored in, one of Cloud Storage's own: `STANDARD`, `NEARLINE`, `COLDLINE` or `ARCHIVE`.

Examples:

- `NEARLINE`
- `COLDLINE`

`inFlight`  integer default `4`

How many parts of one file upload at once. 1 to 64.

Examples:

- `8`
- `1`
- `2`

`maxObjectBytes`  size default `64 MiB`

The largest file it puts in the bucket, compressed. Set it to what the tools that read the bucket handle best. 64 KiB to 64 GiB.

Examples:

- `128 MiB`
- `2 GiB`
- `32 MB`

`bufferBytes`  size default 256 MiB

Memory it may use on each worker for records not yet in the bucket. Files are finished early when it fills, so files reach `maxObjectBytes` only when it holds that many records before compression. 4 MiB to 32 TiB.

Examples:

- `1 GiB`
- `4 GiB`

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one call to the store, or one finishing of the files, may take before it counts as stalled. 1 to 120, and at least 15 on SFTP.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

`fileIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

The longest records wait, in seconds, before they land in the bucket. A longer wait makes larger files; records are acknowledged only once they land, so a source is held open up to this long, and after a crash reads that much again. 5 to 3600.

Examples:

- `30`
- `240`

sections.heading: Fields it reads
sections.text:
## Fields it reads

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__destination.prefix` | `str` | What an S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage destination's object key starts with, taken as it is. Null means the destination's own prefix, with its time placeholders filled in. |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

The destination keeps one object open per prefix, and for Parquet, Avro and CSV per record type of the routes feeding it, across batches, named `<prefix><random id>.<extension>`, and finishes it when it reaches `maxObjectBytes` on disk, when `fileIntervalSecs` passes, when `bufferBytes` fills on the worker, or when a 65th object opens and this one was written least recently. A batch is acknowledged once every object holding its records has landed. Two objects never share a key, so records written again after a failure make new objects.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record with a unique marker through the source, then list the bucket under the prefix for a new object and look for the marker in it.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**Permission denied**

Check that the service account may create objects in the bucket.

sections.text:
## See also

-   [Destinations](/docs/destinations)
-   [Amazon S3 destination](/docs/destinations/s3)
-   [Azure Blob Storage destination](/docs/destinations/azure-blob)
-   [Secrets & credentials](/docs/secrets)

sections.heading: HTTP
sections.text:
# HTTP

POSTs records to any HTTP service, batched as NDJSON, a JSON array or text lines, or one record per request.

sections.heading: Example
Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Find the URL the service takes records at, and the body it expects.
-   Allow workers to reach the service.
-   Put each secret header's whole value in a [credential](/docs/secrets). For `Authorization`, the credential holds `Bearer <token>`, prefix included.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`url`  string required

The whole address the destination POSTs each request to, `http://` or `https://`. It sends a credential only over `https://`, or to this host.

Examples:

- `https://intake.example.com/v1/logs`
- `https://logs.example.com:8443/ingest?tenant=acme`

`body`  string default `lines`

How records become requests.

`lines`

Batches many records into a request, one per line.

`jsonArray`

Batches many records into a request, as one JSON array.

`single`

Sends each record as a request of its own.

`format`  string default `json`

What it sends each record as. See [Bodies](/docs/destinations/http#bodies).

`json`

Writes the record as JSON: NDJSON under body `lines`, or a JSON array under `jsonArray`.

`text`

Writes one field's text, from `field`. Under body `lines` it writes each line break in the text as `\n`; under `jsonArray` it writes each as a JSON string.

`bytes`

Writes one field's bytes, `__source.bytes` unless `field` names another `bytes` field: each source record's bytes as read, before pipeline processing. Under body `single` it sends them as they are; under `lines` it writes each as a base64 line, and under `jsonArray` as a base64 string.

`field`  string default `_raw` for `text`, `__source.bytes` for `bytes`

The field each `text` or `bytes` record writes. Only with format `text` or `bytes`.

Example:

- `message`

`headers`  map default none

Headers it sends on every request, each name to its value. Smeltr sets `Content-Type`, `Content-Encoding`, `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Host` and `Cookie` itself.

Examples:

- `X-Source = smeltr`
- `X-Source = smeltr`
- `X-Tenant = acme`

`credentials`  map default none

Headers whose values are secret, each name to the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding its whole value, such as `Bearer <token>`.

Examples:

- `Authorization = INTAKE_TOKEN`
- `X-Api-Key = INTAKE_API_KEY`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate. Only on an `https://` URL.

Examples:

- `intake-client`
- `intake-mtls`

`compression`  string default `none`

How it compresses each request body.

`none`

Sends it uncompressed.

`gzip`

Compresses each body and sends it with `Content-Encoding: gzip`.

`inFlight`  integer default `4`

How many requests it sends at once to start with. 1 to 64.

Examples:

- `8`
- `1`
- `16`

`maxRequestBytes`  size default `1 MiB`

The most one request carries, before compression. A record larger than this still goes as a single record. 4 KiB to 100 MiB.

Examples:

- `4 MiB`
- `256 KiB`
- `10 MB`

`bufferBytes`  size default 64 MiB, or one request if that is larger

The most one worker holds for this destination, queued or sent and not yet acknowledged. It holds what the connection to it can carry, up to this. 4 MiB to 1 GiB, and at least one request.

Examples:

- `256 MiB`
- `64 MiB`
- `1 GiB`

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one batch may take to deliver, every retry included, before the destination reports it stalled. 1 to 120.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

`zoneUrls`  map default none

An address per zone. A worker in a listed [zone](/docs/reference#settings) sends there instead of `url`.

Examples:

- `us-east-1a = https://intake-a.example.com/v1/logs`
- `us-east-1a = https://intake-a.example.com/v1/logs`
- `us-east-1b = https://intake-b.example.com/v1/logs`

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

The destination sends every record to the one URL. It reads no `__destination` field.

sections.heading: Bodies
sections.text:
### Bodies

Choose a `body` and a `format` from these nine pairs. A batch takes `lines` or `jsonArray`; one record per request takes `single`.

| body | format | What the service receives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| lines (default) | json (default) | NDJSON: one record per line, as `application/x-ndjson`. |
| jsonArray | json | One JSON array of records, as `application/json`. |
| lines | text | One field's text per line, as `text/plain`. The destination writes a line break inside the text as `\n` and a carriage return as `\r`, so each record stays one line. |
| jsonArray | text | One JSON array of one field's text, a string per record, as `application/json`. |
| lines | bytes | One field's bytes per line in base64, as `text/plain`. The field defaults to `__source.bytes`, each record's original bytes. |
| jsonArray | bytes | One JSON array of one field's bytes, a base64 string per record, as `application/json`. |
| single | json | One record per request, as `application/json`. |
| single | text | One field's text per request, as `text/plain`. |
| single | bytes | One field's bytes per request, as `application/octet-stream`. The field defaults to `__source.bytes`, each record's original bytes. |

The destination writes bytes in a batch as base64, because bytes may hold line breaks and are not JSON text.

sections.heading: Answers
sections.text:
### Answers

| The service answers | The destination |
| --- | --- |
| 2xx | counts every record the request carried as delivered. |
| 408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 | backs off and sends the request again. |
| 400, 413, 422 | splits the request in halves and sends each. Halves the service takes land; a record it still refuses on its own, the destination refuses alone. [Choose what happens to it →](/docs/delivery#refused) |
| 401, 403 | stalls, and reports that the service refused its credentials. |
| anything else, a redirect included | stalls, and reports the status and the start of the answer. It never follows a redirect. |

A batch counts as delivered once every request carrying it gets a 2xx. A record resent after a failure can arrive twice. Under `single`, the destination sends a batch's records one after another. If a request stalls the destination, it sends the whole batch again.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record with a unique marker through the source, then find it in the service. If the destination stalls, the Status page flags it, and the worker's [log](/docs/logs-metrics#gui) names the status the service answered.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**The service answers 401 or 403**

Check that the credential holds the header's whole value, prefix included, such as `Bearer <token>`.

**The service answers 404 or 405**

Give the service's intake URL, path included, not its base address.

**The service answers a redirect**

Give the URL the service redirects to.

**The destination refuses to start, naming a credential**

The credential's value holds a line break or another control character, often a trailing newline pasted from a file. Store it again without one.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text:
## See also

-   [Destinations](/docs/destinations)
-   [Handle refused records](/docs/delivery#refused)
-   [Secrets & credentials](/docs/secrets)

sections.heading: Apache Iceberg
sections.text:
# Apache Iceberg

Writes records as Parquet files to an Iceberg table in S3, or a store that speaks its API, and commits them to the table through its REST catalog. Each commit is a snapshot of the table.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Signs in to a Polaris catalog with OAuth client credentials, the client's secret in the worker-host variable `CATALOG_CLIENT_SECRET`, and writes the table `analytics.web.access_log`, partitioned by the day of `ts` and 16 buckets of `user.id` when it creates it. Storage is signed with what the catalog vends.

```
{
  "id": "access-log",
  "type": "iceberg",
  "catalog": "https://polaris.example.com/api/catalog",
  "warehouse": "analytics",
  "namespace": "analytics.web",
  "table": "access_log",
  "partitionBy": [
    "day(ts)",
    "bucket(16, user.id)"
  ],
  "clientId": "smeltr",
  "clientSecret": "CATALOG_CLIENT_SECRET",
  "scope": "PRINCIPAL_ROLE:ALL"
}
```

 ![The Apache Iceberg form on the Destinations page: catalog https://polaris.example.com/api/catalog, namespace analytics.web, table access_log, partition by day(ts) and bucket(16, user.id), catalog sign-in OAuth client credentials, client id smeltr.](/iceberg-destination-form-light.png) 

An Iceberg destination on the Destinations page. Choose the catalog sign-in, and its fields follow. Warehouse and scope sit under Catalog and storage.

Signs in to AWS Glue's Iceberg endpoint with AWS signatures, as the worker host's AWS credentials, in the region the address names. Set the warehouse to the account's id, and the namespace to a Glue database.

```
{
  "id": "access-log",
  "type": "iceberg",
  "catalog": "https://glue.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/iceberg",
  "warehouse": "111122223333",
  "namespace": "web",
  "table": "access_log",
  "signingName": "glue"
}
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Have an Iceberg REST catalog the worker hosts can reach, such as [Apache Polaris](https://polaris.apache.org/), [AWS Glue's Iceberg endpoint](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/iceberg-rest-endpoint.html), or [S3 Tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/s3-tables-integrating-open-source.html). The table's files are in S3 or a store that speaks its API.
-   Create the namespace in the catalog. The destination creates a missing table in it, but not the namespace.
-   A table that exists is of [format version](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/#format-versioning) 2 and not encrypted. A table the destination creates is of version 2.
-   Give the principal the destination signs in to the catalog as permission to load and update the table, and to create it when it is missing. [Signing in](#sign-in) lists the ways.
-   Give whatever signs for storage permission to write and delete objects under the table's data location, and to read and write objects under its metadata location: the credentials the catalog vends, the access key or role the destination names, or the worker host's own. The destination deletes no metadata.
-   Keep the table's location, its `write.data.path` and its `write.metadata.path` in one bucket. The destination refuses to start on a table whose paths are in another bucket than its location.
-   Send this destination records of one type: the routes writing to it write the same record, which is the table's schema. See [Columns](#columns).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`catalog`  string required

The REST catalog's base address, before `/v1`.

Examples:

- `https://polaris.example.com/api/catalog`
- `https://catalog.example.com:8181`

`namespace`  string required

The table's namespace, its levels joined by dots.

Examples:

- `logs`
- `analytics.web`

`table`  string required

The table it writes. A missing table is created from the route's record.

Examples:

- `firewall`
- `access_log`

`partitionBy`  list of strings default none, an unpartitioned table

How a table it creates is partitioned: a column, or `year`, `month`, `day` or `hour` of one, or `bucket(n, column)` or `truncate(width, column)`. A table that exists keeps its own.

Examples:

- `day(ts)`
- `host`
- `bucket(16, user.id)`
- `truncate(4, name)`
- `hour(ts)`

`token`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding a bearer token for the catalog. Not with `clientId`.

Examples:

- `CATALOG_TOKEN`
- `{"secret": "catalog-token","version": 1}`

`clientId`  string default none

The OAuth client it signs in to the catalog as, with `clientSecret`.

Examples:

- `smeltr`
- `0oa1b2c3d4`

`clientSecret`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the OAuth client's secret. Only with `clientId`.

Examples:

- `CATALOG_CLIENT_SECRET`
- `{"secret": "catalog-client","version": 1}`

`signingName`  string default no AWS signature

Signs every catalog call with AWS Signature Version 4 for this service, with the AWS credentials storage names, else the host's, in the region the catalog's AWS address names, else its `region`: `glue` for Glue's Iceberg endpoint, `s3tables` for S3 Tables. Needs `region` when the address names none. Not with `token` or `clientId`.

Examples:

- `glue`
- `s3tables`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects to the catalog and the store under, for a private CA or a client certificate.

Examples:

- `catalog-client`
- `lake-ca`

sections.text:
### Advanced: Catalog and storage

`warehouse`  string default the catalog's default

The warehouse the catalog serves the table from.

Examples:

- `analytics`
- `s3://lake/warehouse`

`tokenUrl`  string default the catalog's own `/v1/oauth/tokens`

Where the client's token is obtained. Only with `clientId`.

Example:

- `https://auth.example.com/oauth2/token`

`scope`  string default none

The scope the client's token is asked for. Use the scope your catalog takes. Only with `clientId`.

Examples:

- `PRINCIPAL_ROLE:ALL`
- `catalog`

`accessKeyId`  credential default what the catalog vends, else the host's credentials

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the access key's id. Set both `accessKeyId` and `secretAccessKey`, or neither.

Examples:

- `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`
- `{"secret": "aws-access-key-id","version": 1}`

`secretAccessKey`  credential default what the catalog vends, else the host's credentials

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the access key's secret.

Examples:

- `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
- `{"secret": "aws-secret-access-key","version": 1}`

`region`  string default the region the catalog gives the table, else the one the catalog's AWS address names, else the host's, else `us-east-1`

The bucket's region.

Examples:

- `us-east-2`
- `eu-west-1`
- `ap-southeast-2`

`endpoint`  string default the one the catalog gives the table, else the host's, else AWS

An S3-compatible service's address. Without an access key, the worker host's AWS settings, such as `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`, come after the catalog's.

Examples:

- `https://minio.example.com:9000`
- `https://10.0.8.20:9000`

`roleArn`  string default none

A role to assume, for a bucket in another account.

Examples:

- `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/smeltr-writer`
- `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/service-role/smeltr-writer`

`externalId`  string default none

The external id the role requires. Only with `roleArn`.

Examples:

- `smeltr`
- `acme-7f3c2a`

`authEndpoint`  string default the region's own

Where the role in `roleArn` is assumed. Only with `roleArn`.

Examples:

- `https://sts-fips.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`

sections.heading: Advanced: Delivery
sections.text:
### Advanced: Delivery

`compression`  string default `zstd`

How each Parquet file compresses its columns.

`none`

Writes columns uncompressed.

`gzip`

Compresses columns with gzip.

`snappy`

Compresses columns with Snappy.

`lz4`

Compresses columns with LZ4.

`zstd`

Compresses columns with Zstandard.

`inFlight`  integer default `4`

How many parts of one file upload at once. 1 to 64.

Examples:

- `8`
- `1`
- `2`

`maxObjectBytes`  size default `64 MiB`

The largest data file it writes, compressed. 64 KiB to 64 GiB.

Examples:

- `256 MiB`
- `512 MiB`

`bufferBytes`  size default 256 MiB

Memory it may use on each worker for records not yet committed. Files are committed early when it fills. 4 MiB to 32 TiB.

Examples:

- `1 GiB`
- `4 GiB`

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one call to the store or the catalog, or one commit, may take before it counts as stalled. 1 to 120.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

`fileIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

The longest records wait, in seconds, before they are committed to the table. Each commit is a snapshot the table keeps until it is expired; records are acknowledged only once committed, so a source is held open up to this long. 5 to 240.

Examples:

- `30`
- `240`

sections.heading: Signing in
sections.text:
## Signing in

The destination signs in to the catalog one way, and to the table's storage another. The GUI form's catalog sign-in chooses the first.

| Catalog sign-in | Settings | What it sends |
| --- | --- | --- |
| none | none of these | Calls with no sign-in, until the catalog gives a token of the table's own when it loads it. |
| A bearer token | `token` | The token from the credential on every call, until the catalog gives a token of the table's own when it loads it. |
| OAuth client credentials | `clientId`, `clientSecret`, and `tokenUrl` and `scope` when the catalog needs them | A token it obtains from the token URL with the client's id and secret, replaced before it expires, and again when the catalog refuses it. |
| AWS signatures | `signingName` | Every call signed with AWS Signature Version 4 for the service it names: `glue` for Glue's Iceberg endpoint, `s3tables` for S3 Tables. It signs with the access key or role the destination names for storage, else the worker host's AWS credentials, for the region the catalog's AWS address names, else `region`. When the address names no region, `region` is required. |

Storage is signed with the first of these the destination has:

1.  The access key in `accessKeyId` and `secretAccessKey`, or the role in `roleArn`.
2.  The credentials the catalog vends for the table. The destination asks for them when it loads the table, and asks again five minutes before they expire.
3.  The worker host's own AWS credentials, such as an instance role.

The table's bucket is in `region`, else the region the catalog gives the table, else the one the catalog's AWS address names, else the worker host's, else `us-east-1`. It is reached at `endpoint`, else the endpoint the catalog gives the table, else, with no access key named, the one the worker host's AWS settings name, else AWS's own address for the region.

sections.heading: Columns
sections.text:
## Columns

The table's schema is the record the routes write here, its fields the table's columns, nested fields as structs and arrays as lists. A missing table is created with that schema and with `partitionBy` as its partition spec. A table that exists keeps its columns and its spec: a field it lacks, at any depth, is added as an optional column before any file is written, and a column the record lacks reads as null in the rows written. A field that can hold no value, `null` or a list or closed struct of nothing else, has no column. Each field is written as the Iceberg type of its [record type](/docs/code-reference#types):

| Record type | Iceberg type |
| --- | --- |
| `bool` | `boolean` |
| `i64` | `long` |
| `duration` | `long`, its count of microseconds |
| `f64` | `double` |
| `str` | `string` |
| `variant` | `string`, the value as JSON |
| `datetime` | `timestamptz` |
| `bytes` | `binary` |
| `array<T>` | `list` |
| `{name: T, ...}` | `struct`; an open object's other keys go in a `string` column named `rest` |

Every column the destination writes is optional. It refuses to start when the table holds a field as another type, or has a required column the record may leave null or does not write.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

When it starts, the destination loads the table from the catalog, or creates it, and adds the record's new columns. It then writes each batch's records into Parquet files under the table's data location, `write.data.path` when the table sets it, partitioned by the table's own spec: identity, `year`, `month`, `day`, `hour`, `bucket` and `truncate`. Each file carries the table's column ids. A file stays open across batches, one per partition, at most 64 at once; a 65th closes the one written least recently. A file also closes at `maxObjectBytes`.

The destination commits when `fileIntervalSecs` passes, when the records it holds near `bufferBytes`, and whenever the worker waits for its destinations to acknowledge everything they hold. A commit closes every open file, writes a manifest of the new files and a manifest list under the table's metadata location, merging the parent's small manifests as the table's `commit.manifest.*` properties say, and asks the catalog to append them as the table's next snapshot on top of the one it read. A batch is acknowledged once the commit holding its records lands.

A commit another writer beat to the table is made again at once on top of the new snapshot, up to 8 times. A failed call is tried again with backoff until `stallAfterSecs`. When the catalog's answer to a commit is lost, the destination looks for that commit in the table before it tries again, so it does not make it twice. Past `stallAfterSecs` the destination aborts its open uploads and writes the batches again. It deletes the files it finished unless a lost answer may have committed them; then they stay, and their rows may be in the table twice. A file storage keeps after a failure is an orphan for the table's own cleanup.

Each commit is a snapshot the table keeps until it is expired. Expire snapshots and compact small files with the table's own maintenance.

A file larger than 8 MiB goes up as a multipart upload, which the destination completes when the file closes and aborts when it fails. Two things leave one unfinished: the worker stops without shutting down (it is killed, it crashes, or its host is lost) while the file is open, or storage does not answer the abort within `stallAfterSecs`. A file stays open at most `fileIntervalSecs`, so give the bucket a [lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpu-abort-incomplete-mpu-lifecycle-config.html) after a day: longer than any file stays open.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record with a unique marker through the source. After `fileIntervalSecs`, look for a new snapshot in the table's history, and query the table for the marker with any engine that reads Iceberg.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**the catalog refused …**

The catalog answered with the status the message names. On 401 or 403, check the sign-in: the token, the client's id, secret and scope, or the AWS credentials and the signing name. On 404, check `catalog`, `warehouse` and that the namespace exists.

**the routes writing here write different records, and a table has one schema**

Two routes feeding the destination write records of different types. Make them write the same record, or give each table a destination of its own.

**… is … in the table, and the record writes … there as …**

The table holds a column as another type than the record's field. Rename the field in the pipeline or the column in the table.

**the table's column … is required …**

Every column the destination writes is optional. Make the column optional in the table, or send the records to a table of their own.

**it is of format version …, and only version 2 is written**

Write to a table of format version 2.

**it is encrypted, and an encrypted table is not written**

Write to a table that is not encrypted.

**the catalog vended no single credential for both the table's data location …**

The catalog's credentials cover one of the table's locations and not the other. Name an access key or a role for storage, or have the catalog vend one credential for both.

**the catalog places the table's storage at …, plain HTTP off this host**

The catalog gives the table an `http://` endpoint on another host. Name an `https://` `endpoint`.

**Access denied writing to storage**

Check that whatever signs for storage may write and delete objects under the table's data location, and read and write objects under its metadata location.

sections.heading: Kafka
sections.text:
# Kafka

Writes each record to a Kafka topic.

Smeltr manages the producer, including its protection against duplicates caused by producer retries.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Writes to a plaintext test broker. Replace its address with one reachable from the worker, and keep input and output topics separate unless you mean to build a feedback path.

```
{
  "id": "events-out",
  "type": "kafka",
  "brokers": "localhost:9092",
  "defaultTopic": "smeltr-events-out"
}
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Create the output topic.
-   Allow workers to reach every broker address Kafka advertises.
-   Give the Kafka account permission to write to the topic.
-   For an authenticated broker, configure [Kafka security](/docs/secrets#kafka). Select a [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) for a private CA or a client certificate.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`brokers`  string required

The brokers a worker first connects to, `host:port`, separated by commas.

Examples:

- `kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092`
- `broker.example.com:9093`

`defaultTopic`  string required

The topic for a record with no `__destination.topic`.

Examples:

- `orders-clean`
- `security.firewall.v1`

`format`  string default `json`

What each message holds.

`json`

Writes the record as JSON.

`text`

Writes one field's text, from `field`.

`bytes`

Writes each source record's bytes as read, before pipeline processing, once per record: `__source.bytes` unless `field` names another `bytes` field.

`avro`

Writes Avro messages, registering the schema in the schema registry.

`schemaRegistry`  object default none

The schema registry the Avro schema is registered in. Set `url`. If the registry needs a sign-in, also set `username` and `password`. Needed for format `avro`.

Examples:

- `{"url": "https://registry.example.com"}`
- `{"url": "https://registry.example.com","username": "smeltr","password": {"secret": "registry","version": 1}}`

`field`  string default `_raw` for `text`, `__source.bytes` for `bytes`

The field each `text` or `bytes` record writes. Only with format `text` or `bytes`.

Example:

- `message`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate. Without one, no certificate is offered and the public roots, Mozilla's and the host's, are trusted.

Examples:

- `kafka-client`
- `kafka-mtls`

sections.heading: Advanced: Delivery and client properties
sections.text:
### Advanced: Delivery and client properties

`compression`  string default `none`

How it compresses each batch of messages.

`none`

Sends it uncompressed.

`gzip`

Compresses it with gzip.

`snappy`

Compresses it with Snappy.

`lz4`

Compresses it with LZ4.

`zstd`

Compresses it with Zstandard.

`acks`  string default `all`

How many replicas must hold each batch before it counts as delivered.

`none`

Counts a batch delivered once it is sent, without waiting for a replica.

`one`

Waits for the partition's leader replica to write it.

`all`

Waits for every in-sync replica to write it. Recommended.

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one batch may take to deliver before it counts as stalled. 1 to 120.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

`bufferBytes`  size default 64 MiB

The most one worker holds for this destination, accepted but not yet acknowledged by the brokers, half of it in the Kafka client. It holds what the connection to it can carry, up to this. 4 MiB to 1 GiB.

Examples:

- `256 MiB`
- `16 MiB`
- `1 GiB`

`properties`  map default none

Other Kafka client properties, each name to its value. See [Kafka security](/docs/secrets#kafka). A property Smeltr sets itself, such as `bootstrap.servers`, is refused, and a secret one belongs in `credentials`.

Examples:

- `security.protocol = SASL_SSL`
- `security.protocol = SASL_SSL`
- `sasl.mechanism = SCRAM-SHA-512`
- `sasl.username = smeltr`

`credentials`  map default none

Kafka client properties whose values are secret, each name to the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding its value.

Examples:

- `sasl.password = KAFKA_PASSWORD`
- `sasl.oauthbearer.client.secret = KAFKA_CLIENT_SECRET`

sections.text:
## Fields it reads

| --- | --- | --- |
| `__destination.topic` | `str` | The Kafka topic or Event Hub a destination writes the record to. Null means the default value for that destination. |

sections.text:

Check advertised addresses, that the topic exists, write permissions and [Kafka security](/docs/secrets#kafka).

sections.heading: Log Analytics workspace
sections.text:
# Log Analytics workspace

Sends each record to a Log Analytics table, through a data collection rule.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Sends to the stream `Custom-Events_CL` of a data collection rule, signed in as the host's managed identity.

```
{
  "id": "events-out",
  "type": "logAnalytics",
  "endpoint": "https://acme-logs-a1b2.eastus-1.ingest.monitor.azure.com",
  "ruleId": "dcr-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef",
  "stream": "Custom-Events_CL"
}
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Create the table and a data collection rule with a stream that sends to it. See Microsoft's [Logs Ingestion API tutorial](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/logs/tutorial-logs-ingestion-portal).
-   Choose how the destination signs in, with exactly one of:
    
    -   a service principal: set `tenantId`, `clientId` and `clientSecret`, with the secret in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
    -   a user-assigned managed identity: set `managedIdentityClientId` to its client id. Set it when the host has more than one managed identity.
    -   none: the destination signs in as the host's [managed identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview), or as an AKS pod's [workload identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/workload-identity-overview). The managed identities of App Service, Container Apps and Functions are not supported.
    
    See Microsoft's [Logs Ingestion API docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/logs/logs-ingestion-api-overview) for the role it needs.
-   Allow workers to reach the endpoint on port 443.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`endpoint`  string required

The data collection rule's logs ingestion endpoint, or the data collection endpoint it is linked to.

Examples:

- `https://acme-logs-a1b2.eastus-1.ingest.monitor.azure.com`
- `https://acme-dce-x9y8.eastus-1.ingest.monitor.azure.us`

`ruleId`  string required

The data collection rule's immutable id.

Example:

- `dcr-00000000000000000000000000000000`

`stream`  string required

The rule's input stream the records are sent to.

Examples:

- `Custom-Events_CL`
- `Custom-Firewall`

`tenantId`  string default none

A service principal's tenant. Set `tenantId`, `clientId` and `clientSecret` together, or none of them.

Example:

- `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000`

`clientId`  string default none

A service principal's client id.

Example:

- `11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111`

`clientSecret`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding a service principal's client secret.

Examples:

- `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`
- `{"secret": "azure-client-secret","version": 1}`

`managedIdentityClientId`  string default the host's managed or workload identity

The client id of the user-assigned managed identity to sign in as. Set it when the worker's host has more than one managed identity. Left out, it signs in as the host's managed identity, or an AKS pod's workload identity.

Example:

- `22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`authEndpoint`  string default its cloud's own

Where a client secret is exchanged for a token. Only with `clientSecret`.

Examples:

- `https://login.microsoftonline.us`
- `https://login.chinacloudapi.cn`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate. Only on an `https://` URL.

Examples:

- `intake-client`
- `intake-mtls`

`inFlight`  integer default `4`

How many requests it sends at once to start with. 1 to 64.

Examples:

- `8`
- `1`
- `16`

`maxRequestBytes`  size default `1 MiB`

The most one request carries, before compression. A record larger than this still goes as a single record. 4 KiB to 1 MiB.

Examples:

- `512 KiB`
- `256 KiB`

`bufferBytes`  size default 64 MiB, or one request if that is larger

The most one worker holds for this destination, queued or sent and not yet acknowledged. It holds what the connection to it can carry, up to this. 4 MiB to 1 GiB, and at least one request.

Examples:

- `256 MiB`
- `64 MiB`
- `1 GiB`

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one batch may take to deliver, every retry included, before the destination reports it stalled. 1 to 120.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

The destination sends each batch as one gzipped JSON array to the rule's stream, signed in through Entra ID. It reads no `__destination` field. It handles each answer as the [HTTP destination](/docs/destinations/http#answers) does.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record you can recognize through the source, then query its table in the workspace.

sections.text:

**The destination stalls, saying its credentials were refused**

Check that the identity it signs in as has the role the rule needs.

**The destination stalls on a 404**

Check the rule id, the stream, and that the endpoint is the rule's.

sections.heading: Prometheus remote\_write
sections.text:
# Prometheus remote\_write

Sends each record as a sample over remote\_write 1.0 or 2.0 to any store that takes it.

sections.heading: Example
Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Find the store's remote\_write URL, path included:
    -   [Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/api/#remote-write-receiver)
    -   [Mimir](https://grafana.com/docs/mimir/latest/references/http-api/#remote-write)
    -   [Cortex](https://cortexmetrics.io/docs/api/#remote-write)
    -   [Thanos Receive](https://thanos.io/tip/components/receive.md/)
    -   [VictoriaMetrics](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/integrations/prometheus/), or for a cluster its [URL format](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/cluster-victoriametrics/#url-format)
-   To send native histograms, make sure the store takes them. See its docs.
-   To send remote\_write 2.0, make sure the store takes it. See its docs. 1.0 is the default.
-   To keep exemplars, make sure the store keeps them. See its docs.
-   Allow workers to reach the store.
-   Put each secret header's whole value in a [credential](/docs/secrets). For `Authorization`, the credential holds `Bearer <token>`, prefix included.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`url`  string required

The store's remote\_write endpoint, `http://` or `https://`. It sends a credential only over `https://`, or to this host.

Examples:

- `https://prometheus.example.com/api/v1/write`
- `https://mimir.example.com/api/v1/push`

`version`  string default `1.0`

The version of remote\_write it sends.

`1.0`

The default.

`2.0`

Each series carries its family's latest metadata and its start time. A store that does not take it stalls the destination until this is set back to 1.0.

`headers`  map default none

Headers it sends on every request, each name to its value. Smeltr sets `Content-Type`, `Content-Encoding`, `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Host`, `Cookie` and `X-Prometheus-Remote-Write-Version` itself.

Example:

- `X-Scope-OrgID = tenant-1`

`credentials`  map default none

Headers whose values are secret, each name to the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding its whole value, such as `Bearer <token>`.

Example:

- `Authorization = PROMETHEUS_TOKEN`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate. Only on an `https://` URL.

Example:

- `prometheus-client`

`maxRequestBytes`  size default `1 MiB`

The most one request carries, before compression. A record larger than this still goes as a single record. 4 KiB to 100 MiB.

Examples:

- `4 MiB`
- `256 KiB`
- `10 MB`

`bufferBytes`  size default 64 MiB, or one request if that is larger

The most one worker holds for this destination, queued or sent and not yet acknowledged. It holds what the connection to it can carry, up to this. 4 MiB to 1 GiB, and at least one request.

Examples:

- `256 MiB`
- `64 MiB`
- `1 GiB`

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one batch may take to deliver, every retry included, before the destination reports it stalled. 1 to 120.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

sections.heading: Records it sends
sections.text:
## Records it sends

Each record is one sample, a float or a native histogram, in the shape the [Prometheus receiver](/docs/sources/prometheus-receiver#records) gives, so its records pass through unchanged. An OTLP receiver's metric points have the same shape. A float sample:

```
{
  "time": "2026-10-11T18:00:00.123Z",
  "name": "http_requests_total",
  "value": 1027,
  "attributes": {
    "job": "api",
    "instance": "api-1:9100",
    "code": "200"
  }
}
```

`name`

A non-empty string: the series' metric name, sent as its `__name__` label.

`value`

A number.

`time`

A datetime, sent as its milliseconds.

`attributes`

An object of the series' other labels. A number or a boolean is sent as its text. A label that is null or empty is none, and a record with no labels but its name may leave `attributes` out or null.

`type`

Absent, null, `gauge` or `sum` for a float sample. `exponentialHistogram` for a native histogram, or `histogram` for a histogram of explicit bounds. Neither needs `value`. A `summary` is refused.

A histogram also needs these, as the Prometheus receiver gives them:

`count`, `sum`

Numbers.

`aggregationTemporality`

2 for a counter's histogram; absent or null for a gauge histogram. A delta, 1, is refused.

`scale`, `zeroCount`, `zeroThreshold`, `positive`, `negative`

An exponential histogram's.

`bucketCounts`, `explicitBounds`

A `histogram`'s, sent as a [classic histogram](https://prometheus.io/docs/concepts/metric_types/#histogram): its `_bucket`, `_sum` and `_count` series.

`resetHint`

`yes` or `no`, sent as an exponential histogram's reset hint. Left out, the hint sent is unknown.

Any record may also carry exemplars, as either receiver gives them:

`exemplars`

An array of objects, each a `value`, a `time` or none for the record's, `traceId`, `spanId` and `filteredAttributes`. An exemplar the store would not keep is left out, and its record still sent.

A record with no `time` and no `value` is a family's metadata, as the Prometheus receiver gives it: its `description`, `unit` and `type` go as the family's. A point's `description` or `unit`, as an OTLP point has them, goes as its family's too.

Over remote\_write 2.0, each series carries its family's latest metadata. A record's `startTime` goes as its series' start time.

The destination refuses a record that is no sample, and names why. [Choose what happens to it →](/docs/delivery#refused) A value that was NaN or an infinity arrives with none, because JSON holds neither, so such a record is refused. Staleness markers are not sent.

sections.heading: Requests
sections.text:
## Requests

A request is remote\_write 1.0, or 2.0 with `version` set to it. A series' records in a request go oldest first.

The destination sends one request at a time, and each lands before the next is sent, so a series' samples arrive in order.

sections.heading: Answers
sections.text:
## Answers

| The store answers | The destination |
| --- | --- |
| 2xx | counts every record the request carried as delivered. |
| 429, 5xx | backs off and sends the request again. |
| 400, 409, 413, 422 to 2.0, saying it wrote some of the request | counts the request as delivered, and what the store did not write in `smeltr_destination_unwritten_total`. |
| 400, 409, 413, 422 | splits the request in halves and sends each. Halves the store takes land; a sample it still refuses on its own, the destination refuses alone. |
| 415, or a success that stored nothing, to 2.0 | stalls, and reports that the store takes only remote\_write 1.0. |
| 401, 403 | stalls, and reports that the store refused its credentials. |
| anything else, a redirect included | stalls, and reports the status. It never follows a redirect. |

A batch counts as delivered once every request carrying it gets a 2xx. A sample sent again after a failure may already be in the store.

sections.heading: Stores it sends to
sections.text:
## Stores it sends to

A store may refuse a sample older than the last it holds for that series, such as one from a second worker or another writer. Each store's out-of-order docs:

-   [Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/configuration/configuration/#tsdb)
-   [Mimir](https://grafana.com/docs/mimir/latest/configure/configure-out-of-order-samples-ingestion/)
-   [Cortex](https://cortexmetrics.io/docs/configuration/configuration-file/#limits_config)
-   [Thanos Receive](https://thanos.io/tip/components/receive.md/)

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a sample through the source, then query its series in the store. If the destination stalls, the Status page flags it, and the worker's [log](/docs/logs-metrics#gui) names the status the store answered.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**Every record is refused**

The refusal names the field at fault. A float sample needs `name`, `value` and `time`; a histogram needs `count`, `sum` and its buckets in place of `value`. A pipeline renames a record's own fields to them.

**The store answers 404 or 405**

Give the remote\_write URL, path included, and check that the store's remote\_write receiver is on.

**The store answers 415, or a success that stored nothing**

The store does not take remote\_write 2.0. Set `version` to `1.0`.

**The store answers 401 or 403**

Check that the credential holds the header's whole value, prefix included, such as `Bearer <token>`, and that the store needs no other header, such as a tenant's.

**Samples are refused as out of order**

A record arrived older than one of its series already sent, from the source itself, from another writer, or from a second worker sending the same series. Send each series from one worker, in time order, or turn on the store's out-of-order window.

sections.heading: Amazon S3
sections.text:
# Amazon S3

Writes batches of records as objects in an S3 bucket, or a bucket in an S3-compatible store.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Writes with the worker host's AWS credentials.

```
{
  "id": "archive",
  "type": "s3",
  "bucket": "acme-logs",
  "region": "us-east-2"
}
```

![The Amazon S3 form on the Destinations page: id archive, bucket acme-logs, format ndjson.](/s3-destination-form-light.png)

The same destination on the Destinations page. Region sits under Endpoint and delivery.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   [Create the bucket](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/create-bucket-overview.html).
-   Give the identity the destination writes as permission to put objects in the bucket (`s3:PutObject`). See [S3 policy examples](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/example-policies-s3.html). With `kmsKeyId`, it also needs to use that key; see [SSE-KMS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingKMSEncryption.html).
-   Choose how it signs in. With no access key, it uses the worker host's own AWS credentials, such as an instance role; see [AWS credential providers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/standardized-credentials.html). Otherwise put the access key's id and secret in [credentials](/docs/secrets).
-   For a bucket in another account, give a role to assume in `roleArn`, and its external id if it requires one. See [cross-account roles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_aws-accounts.html).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`bucket`  string required

The bucket.

Examples:

- `acme-logs`
- `acme-logs-111122223333`

`accessKeyId`  credential default the host's credentials

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the access key's id. Set both `accessKeyId` and `secretAccessKey`, or neither.

Examples:

- `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`
- `{"secret": "aws-access-key-id","version": 1}`

`secretAccessKey`  credential default the host's credentials

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the access key's secret.

Examples:

- `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
- `{"secret": "aws-secret-access-key","version": 1}`

`prefix`  string default `%Y/%m/%d/%H/`

What each object's key starts with, for a record with no `__destination.prefix`. `%Y`, `%m`, `%d`, `%H` and `%M` are the write time, UTC, and no other `%` is allowed. A key never starts with `/`.

Examples:

- `events/%Y/%m/%d/`
- `firewall/dt=%Y-%m-%d/hour=%H/`
- `acme/audit/`

`format`  string default `ndjson`

What each object holds.

`ndjson`

Writes one JSON document per line.

`json`

Writes one JSON array of every record.

`parquet`

Writes one Parquet file.

`avro`

Writes one Avro file.

`csv`

Writes one CSV file.

`text`

Writes one line of text per record, from `field`.

`bytes`

Writes each source record's bytes as read, before pipeline processing, one per line: `__source.bytes` unless `field` names another `bytes` field.

`field`  string default `_raw` for `text`, `__source.bytes` for `bytes`

The field each line of a `text` or `bytes` object holds. Only with format `text` or `bytes`.

Example:

- `message`

`newlines`  string default `escape`

What a `bytes` object does with a record holding a line break. Only with format `bytes`.

`escape`

Writes `\`, newline and carriage return as `\\`, `\n` and `\r`, which a source with framing `escapedLines` reverses.

`refuse`

Refuses the record.

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate.

Examples:

- `store-client`
- `corp-proxy`

sections.heading: Advanced: Endpoint and delivery
sections.text:
### Advanced: Endpoint and delivery

`region`  string default the host's, else `us-east-1`

The bucket's region.

Examples:

- `us-east-2`
- `eu-west-1`
- `ap-southeast-2`

`endpoint`  string default the host's, else AWS

An S3-compatible service's address. Without an access key, the worker host's AWS settings, such as `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL`, come first.

Examples:

- `https://minio.example.com:9000`
- `https://10.0.8.20:9000`

`roleArn`  string default none

A role to assume, for a bucket in another account.

Examples:

- `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/smeltr-writer`
- `arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/service-role/smeltr-writer`

`externalId`  string default none

The external id the role requires. Only with `roleArn`.

Examples:

- `smeltr`
- `acme-7f3c2a`

`authEndpoint`  string default the region's own

Where the role in `roleArn` is assumed. Only with `roleArn`.

Examples:

- `https://sts.us-east-2.amazonaws.com`
- `https://sts-fips.us-east-1.amazonaws.com`

`kmsKeyId`  string default none

The KMS key each object is encrypted under.

Examples:

- `arn:aws:kms:us-east-2:111122223333:key/1234abcd-12ab-34cd-56ef-1234567890ab`
- `arn:aws:kms:us-east-2:111122223333:alias/smeltr-logs`

`compression`  string default `gzip`

How it compresses each object. A `parquet` object compresses each column inside the file instead, and its key ends with `.parquet` whatever the compression. An `avro` file compresses inside the file, and its key ends with `.avro`. Its `gzip` is Avro's `deflate`. Avro has no `lz4`.

`none`

Writes it uncompressed. The key ends with the format's own extension, such as `.ndjson`.

`gzip`

Compresses it with gzip and appends `.gz` to the key, such as `.ndjson.gz`.

`snappy`

Compresses it with framed Snappy and appends `.sz` to the key, such as `.ndjson.sz`.

`lz4`

Compresses it with framed LZ4 and appends `.lz4` to the key, such as `.ndjson.lz4`.

`zstd`

Compresses it with Zstandard and appends `.zst` to the key, such as `.ndjson.zst`.

`storageClass`  string default the bucket's own

The class each object is stored in, one of S3's own: `STANDARD`, `REDUCED_REDUNDANCY`, `STANDARD_IA`, `ONEZONE_IA`, `INTELLIGENT_TIERING`, `GLACIER`, `GLACIER_IR`, `DEEP_ARCHIVE` or `SNOW`.

Examples:

- `STANDARD_IA`
- `INTELLIGENT_TIERING`
- `GLACIER_IR`

`inFlight`  integer default `4`

How many parts of one file upload at once. 1 to 64.

Examples:

- `8`
- `1`
- `2`

`maxObjectBytes`  size default `64 MiB`

The largest file it puts in the bucket, compressed. Set it to what the tools that read the bucket handle best. 64 KiB to 64 GiB.

Examples:

- `128 MiB`
- `2 GiB`
- `32 MB`

`bufferBytes`  size default 256 MiB

Memory it may use on each worker for records not yet in the bucket. Files are finished early when it fills, so files reach `maxObjectBytes` only when it holds that many records before compression. 4 MiB to 32 TiB.

Examples:

- `1 GiB`
- `4 GiB`

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one call to the store, or one finishing of the files, may take before it counts as stalled. 1 to 120, and at least 15 on SFTP.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

`fileIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

The longest records wait, in seconds, before they land in the bucket. A longer wait makes larger files; records are acknowledged only once they land, so a source is held open up to this long, and after a crash reads that much again. 5 to 3600.

Examples:

- `30`
- `240`

sections.heading: Fields it reads
sections.text:
## Fields it reads

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__destination.prefix` | `str` | What an S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage destination's object key starts with, taken as it is. Null means the destination's own prefix, with its time placeholders filled in. |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

The destination keeps one object open per prefix, and for Parquet, Avro and CSV per record type of the routes feeding it, across batches, named `<prefix><random id>.<extension>`, and finishes it when it reaches `maxObjectBytes` on disk, when `fileIntervalSecs` passes, when `bufferBytes` fills on the worker, or when a 65th object opens and this one was written least recently. A batch is acknowledged once every object holding its records has landed. Two objects never share a key, so records written again after a failure make new objects.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record with a unique marker through the source, then list the bucket under the prefix for a new object and look for the marker in it.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**Access denied**

Check that the identity may put objects in the bucket, and may use the KMS key when `kmsKeyId` is set.

sections.heading: SFTP
sections.text:
# SFTP

Writes batches of records as files in a directory on an SFTP server. A reader of the directory never sees part of a file.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Signs in as `smeltr` with the private key in the worker-host variable `SFTP_PRIVATE_KEY`, and connects only to the server holding the pinned host key.

```
{
  "id": "partner-inbox",
  "type": "sftp",
  "host": "sftp.example.com",
  "username": "smeltr",
  "privateKey": "SFTP_PRIVATE_KEY",
  "hostKey": "ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAID3o82ivVxzYDbjz/HQTXSvCvoEb7fBpGzXPVbqK+q63",
  "directory": "/srv/inbox"
}
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Create the directory on the server. It must exist, as a bucket must; the destination makes the folders a prefix names under it as needed.
-   Have an account on the server that may create files and folders in the directory and rename files there.
-   Get the server's host key: a line such as `ssh-ed25519 AAAA…`. Copy it from the server's `/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub`, or run `ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 sftp.example.com` and drop the host name the line starts with. `ssh-keyscan` trusts the network it asks over, so check its answer against the server's file.
-   Put the account's password, or its private key, in a [credential](/docs/secrets). The private key is an unencrypted RSA, ed25519 or ECDSA key in OpenSSH's format.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`host`  string required

The server's host name or address.

Examples:

- `sftp.example.com`
- `203.0.113.10`

`port`  integer default `22`

The server's SSH port.

Examples:

- `2222`
- `8022`

`username`  string required

The user it signs in as, who needs write access to `directory`.

Examples:

- `smeltr`
- `logship`

`password`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the user's password. Set exactly one of `password` and `privateKey`.

Examples:

- `SFTP_PASSWORD`
- `{"secret": "sftp-password","version": 1}`

`privateKey`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the user's private key: an unencrypted RSA, ed25519 or ECDSA key in OpenSSH's format.

Examples:

- `SFTP_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `{"secret": "sftp-private-key","version": 1}`

`hostKey`  string required

The server's public key as OpenSSH writes it, `ssh-ed25519 AAAA…`, without a host name: it connects to that server and no other. Copy it from the server's `/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub`, or from `ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 sftp.example.com`, dropping the host name it starts with; keyscan trusts the network it asks over, so check its answer against the server's file.

Example:

- `ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAID3o82ivVxzYDbjz/HQTXSvCvoEb7fBpGzXPVbqK+q63`

The directory it writes into: absolute, or under the user's home directory. Empty is the home directory. It must exist, as a bucket must; the folders a prefix names under it are made as needed.

- `/srv/inbox`

Writes one Parquet file.

`avro`

Writes one Avro file.

`csv`

Writes one CSV file.

`text`

Writes one line of text per record, from `field`.

`bytes`

Writes each source record's bytes as read, before pipeline processing, one per line: `__source.bytes` unless `field` names another `bytes` field.

`field`  string default `_raw` for `text`, `__source.bytes` for `bytes`

The field each line of a `text` or `bytes` object holds. Only with format `text` or `bytes`.

Example:

- `message`

`newlines`  string default `escape`

What a `bytes` object does with a record holding a line break. Only with format `bytes`.

`escape`

Writes `\`, newline and carriage return as `\\`, `\n` and `\r`, which a source with framing `escapedLines` reverses.

`refuse`

Refuses the record.

| Field | Type | Holds |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

The destination keeps one file open per prefix, and for Parquet, Avro and CSV per record type of the routes feeding it, across batches, at `<directory>/<prefix><random id>.<extension>`. It finishes the file when it reaches `maxObjectBytes` on disk, when `fileIntervalSecs` passes, when `bufferBytes` fills on the worker, or when a 65th file opens and this one was written least recently, and acknowledges a batch once every file holding its records has landed. It makes the folders the prefix names first when they are not there.

It writes a file under a hidden temporary name in the same folder, a dot, its own name and a tag, ending in `.tmp`, such as `.3f9c…e1.ndjson.gz.4182-7-123456789.tmp`. Once it has written every byte, it renames the file to its own name, so a reader sees the whole file or none of it. An [SFTP source](/docs/sources/sftp) skips these temporary files.

Two files never share a name, so records written again after a failure make new files. On a failure the destination deletes the files it already finished, best effort; one it cannot delete holds records that land twice. When the rename fails, the destination removes the temporary file; a connection lost while writing can leave one behind, which is safe to delete.

One SSH connection carries the destination's writes. It connects only to a server that shows the pinned host key, and asks the server for that key's algorithm alone. The destination closes a connection that stops answering, and the next write opens a new one.

sections.text:

sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**the server's host key is not the one configured**

The server showed another key than `hostKey`. Check that `host` names the right server and that `hostKey` is its current key.

**the server refused the password given for user …**

With a private key, the text names it in place of the password. Check `username`, and that the credential holds that user's password, or a private key whose public half the server accepts for that user.

**no connection within 30s**

Connecting and signing in did not finish. Check that the worker host can reach `host` on `port`.

**writing … no answer within …**

The server stopped answering while the worker made a folder, wrote the named file or renamed it. With `stallAfterSecs` at 30 or less, an unreachable host shows this too, before the 30s connection limit runs out.

**Writing fails with a file not found**

Create `directory` on the server.

**Writing fails with permission denied**

Check that the user may create files and folders in `directory` and rename files there.

sections.heading: Splunk HEC
sections.text:
# Splunk HEC

Sends each record to a Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC).

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Reads the token from the worker-host variable `SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN`. The URL is the collector's base address; the destination adds the endpoint path itself.

```
{
  "id": "splunk-out",
  "type": "splunkHec",
  "url": "https://splunk.example.com:8088",
  "token": "SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN",
  "index": "smeltr_events",
  "sourcetype": "_json"
}
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Create a HEC token in Splunk and allow it to write to the target indexes.
-   Allow workers to reach the collector's port.
-   Put the token alone, without the `Splunk` prefix, in a [credential](/docs/secrets).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every destination](/docs/destinations#settings) takes.

`url`  string required

The collector's base address. The destination adds the endpoint path itself, so an address naming `/services/collector` is refused.

Examples:

- `https://splunk.example.com:8088`
- `https://http-inputs-acme.splunkcloud.com`

`token`  credential required

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the HEC token, without the `Splunk` prefix.

Examples:

- `SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN`
- `{"secret": "splunk-hec-token","version": 1}`

`endpoint`  string default `event`

Which HEC endpoint it sends to. See [Event and raw endpoints](/docs/destinations/splunk#event-and-raw-endpoints).

`event`

Sends each record as the event of its own envelope.

`raw`

Sends each record as a line of text.

`format`  string default `json`

What each event holds.

`json`

Writes the record as JSON.

`text`

Writes one field's text, from `field`.

`bytes`

Writes each source record's bytes as read, before pipeline processing, once per record: `__source.bytes` unless `field` names another `bytes` field. Only with endpoint `raw`.

`field`  string default `_raw` for `text`, `__source.bytes` for `bytes`

The field each `text` or `bytes` record writes. Only with format `text` or `bytes`.

Example:

- `message`

`index`  string default the token's default index

On the `event` endpoint, the index for a record with no `__destination.index`. On the `raw` endpoint, the index for every record: a record whose `__destination.index` names another is refused, so send it to the `event` endpoint.

Examples:

- `main`
- `firewall`

`sourcetype`  string default none

On the `event` endpoint, the sourcetype for a record with no top-level `sourcetype`. On the `raw` endpoint, the sourcetype for every record.

Examples:

- `_json`
- `pan:traffic`
- `access_combined`

`source`  string default none

On the `event` endpoint, the source for a record with no top-level `source`. On the `raw` endpoint, the source for every record.

Examples:

- `smeltr`
- `edge-gateway`

`host`  string default none

On the `event` endpoint, the host for a record with no top-level `host`. On the `raw` endpoint, the host for every record.

Examples:

- `edge-1`
- `10.0.3.7`

`acknowledgement`  string default `indexer`

When it counts a batch delivered. It must match the token's indexer acknowledgement setting.

`indexer`

Counts a batch delivered once Splunk reports it indexed.

`receipt`

Counts a batch delivered once Splunk accepts the request.

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate.

Examples:

- `splunk-client`
- `splunk-ca`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`inFlight`  integer default `4`

How many requests it sends at once to start with. 1 to 64.

Examples:

- `8`
- `1`
- `16`

`maxRequestBytes`  size default `1 MiB`

The most one request carries. A record larger than this still goes as a single record. 4 KiB to 100 MiB.

Examples:

- `4 MiB`
- `512 KiB`
- `16 MiB`

`bufferBytes`  size default 64 MiB, or one request if that is larger

The most one worker holds for this destination, queued or sent and not yet acknowledged. It holds what the connection to it can carry, up to this. 4 MiB to 1 GiB, and at least one request.

Examples:

- `256 MiB`
- `64 MiB`
- `1 GiB`

`stallAfterSecs`  integer default `30`

Seconds one batch may take to deliver, its acknowledgement included, before it counts as stalled. 1 to 120.

Examples:

- `60`
- `120`

`zoneUrls`  map default none

An address per zone. A worker in a listed [zone](/docs/reference#settings) sends there instead of `url`.

Examples:

- `us-east-1a = https://splunk-a.example.com:8088`
- `us-east-1a = https://splunk-a.example.com:8088`
- `us-east-1b = https://splunk-b.example.com:8088`

sections.heading: Fields it reads
sections.text:
## Fields it reads

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__destination.index` | `str` | The index an Elasticsearch or Splunk HEC destination files the record under. Null means the destination's default index. A Splunk HEC destination on the `raw` endpoint refuses a record naming an index other than its own. |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: ## How it works

sections.heading: Event and raw endpoints
sections.text:
### Event and raw endpoints

| endpoint | What Splunk receives |
| --- | --- |
| event (default) | Each record is the event of its own HEC envelope. A record's top-level `_time`, `host`, `source` and `sourcetype` file the event; the destination's settings fill in any it lacks. `_time` is Unix seconds or a datetime. `__destination.index` picks the index. |
| raw | Each record is sent as one line of text. Every line gets the destination's index, host, source and sourcetype. |

sections.heading: Acknowledgement
sections.text:
### Acknowledgement

| acknowledgement | When a batch counts as delivered |
| --- | --- |
| indexer (default) | Once Splunk reports the events indexed. Turn on indexer acknowledgement for the token. A record resent after a failure can arrive more than once. |
| receipt | Once Splunk accepts the request. Smeltr does not send it again. Turn indexer acknowledgement off for the token. |

If the token's acknowledgement setting does not match, the destination reports it and delivers nothing until one of them changes. If Splunk refuses one event in a request, only that event is refused. [Choose what happens to it →](/docs/delivery#refused)

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Send a record with a unique marker through the source, then search the index for it in Splunk. Check the event's time, host, source and sourcetype.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**The URL is refused**

Give the base address, such as `https://splunk.example.com:8088`, not one ending in `/services/collector`.

sections.text:
