-   [Secrets & credentials](/docs/secrets)

title: Enroll a worker on a host

sections.heading: Enroll a worker on a host
sections.text:
# Enroll a worker on a host

This guide is for a worker running separately from the leader. A [standalone deployment](/docs/install-leader/binary#first-start) enrolls its own worker automatically. To run workers in a cluster, see [Enroll workers on Kubernetes](/docs/enroll-worker/kubernetes).

Run the leader and its workers from one major release: verified binaries, or image digests from [`ghcr.io/smeltr-sh/smeltr`](/docs/install-leader/container#pull). A worker on another major keeps running what it has and takes no new deployment, and Status shows it as **On another build** with both releases. A build that is not a release matches only its own commit.

The leader trusts an enrolled worker with every group's configuration and every credential it stores. Worker groups organize processing; use separate Smeltr clusters when you must isolate hosts from one another's configuration or credentials.

sections.heading: Prepare the group and host
sections.text:
## Prepare the group and host

Install that Smeltr executable or image on the worker host. Its built-in Git client fetches configuration from the leader. For a container, mount the configuration read-only and the worker state directory read-write outside the container. Give each worker its own state directory and preserve it across restarts. Never copy an enrolled worker’s state to another machine. The host must be able to connect to the leader, sources, and destinations.

Use the default group for a first installation. For another group, open Admin → Worker groups, choose **\+ Add group**, enter Name and Id, then choose **Add**. Review and deploy that change: a Pending group is not live until you deploy it.

Group name changes also need deployment; group colors apply immediately. Deleting a group also needs deployment. Once it deploys, workers still in that group stop all their pipelines until you move them to another group or shut them down. Set `worker.group` to the group ID. Shared configuration can affect more than one group, so inspect the full change before deploying.

sections.heading: Create an enrollment code
sections.text:
## Create an enrollment code

An enrollment code is the value that lets a new worker connect to the leader and obtain its own credential.

1.  Open Admin → Workers → Enrollment codes and choose **\+ Add enrollment code**.
2.  Set Group and Workers it brings in. A Permanent enrollment code also takes Workers and Valid for (hours); defaults are one worker and 24 hours. An Ephemeral one takes neither. No enrollment code outlasts the leader's certificate authority. Then select **Mint**.
3.  Correct “The address this worker will reach the leader at” to a URL reachable from the worker. A browser's localhost URL is not suitable for a remote worker.
4.  Copy the enrollment code before dismissing it. Smeltr shows the secret once and cannot retrieve it.

The enrollment code includes a secret and tells the worker how to verify the leader's certificate. A permanent enrollment code works until it expires, you withdraw it, or it reaches its allowed number of workers. An ephemeral one works until you withdraw it, for workers an autoscaler starts and stops; see [Autoscale workers](/docs/enroll-worker/kubernetes#autoscale). Either stops working when the leader's certificate authority is replaced.

sections.heading: Configure and start
sections.text:
## Configure and start

Save this as the worker’s configuration. Replace the placeholder with the complete enrollment code you copied. This example uses the direct HTTPS leader from the installation guide:

```
[worker]
enabled = true
group = "default"
enrollment_code = "PASTE_THE_COMPLETE_ENROLLMENT_CODE_HERE"

[worker.leader]
url = "https://smeltr.example.com"

[worker.storage]
state_dir = "/var/lib/smeltr-worker"
```

```
SMELTR_CONFIG_FILE=/absolute/path/to/worker.toml /absolute/path/to/smeltr
```

A worker whose group runs a [receiver](/docs/sources#push-all-workers) listens on the receiver's port, so the host's firewall must let senders reach that port.

For a container worker, set `SMELTR_CONFIG_FILE` to its mounted configuration path and mount `/var/lib/smeltr-worker` persistently. The container needs no inbound published port unless its group runs a receiver; then publish the receiver's port, for example `-p 8088:8088`. It must be able to reach the leader and every configured source and destination.

Leave `worker.leader.ca` unset for normal enrollment. An enrollment code can verify the leader’s CA fingerprint and save the matching certificate. The worker also trusts the public roots, Mozilla’s and the host’s own, unless `worker.leader.trust_public` is false. If you set a CA file yourself, you must maintain it when the authority changes; automatic updates no longer apply. Keep certificate verification enabled.

After enrollment, the state directory contains worker\_id, credential.token, the configuration clone and trust material. Protect it. After enrollment, the worker uses its saved credential. Remove a permanent enrollment code from configuration, restart the worker, and confirm it reconnects. A fresh host or lost state needs a new enrollment.

sections.heading: Verify and handle failures
sections.text:
## Verify and handle failures

On Status, confirm the worker is Online, reports the expected group, and shows its deployment state. Enrollment alone does not prove that a pipeline is running. A new worker must complete its first check-in and fetch configuration. A running worker keeps running through a leader outage; by default it does not stop solely because the leader is unreachable. A worker that restarts runs nothing until the leader answers its first check-in. See [stop\_after\_unreachable\_secs](/docs/reference).

If enrollment fails, check the URL, the complete enrollment code, lifetime, remaining uses, group and certificate name. Withdraw an exposed enrollment code in the Enrollment codes table and mint another. Withdrawal prevents further enrollment but does not revoke workers already enrolled.

sections.heading: Revoke or replace a worker
sections.text:
## Revoke or replace a worker

Stop or isolate a compromised worker through your host-management controls, then select **Revoke** for that worker in Admin → Workers. Revocation refuses subsequent leader requests; it does not stop its running pipeline or its access to external data systems. Rotate external credentials where necessary. Enroll a rebuilt host using a new state directory and enrollment code, rather than reusing the revoked identity.

sections.heading: Enroll workers on Kubernetes
sections.text:
# Enroll workers on Kubernetes

Workers run the leader's image, named by the same digest, and connect to a leader deployed as in [Run the leader on Kubernetes](/docs/install-leader/kubernetes). Workers run either as a StatefulSet, each with its own persistent identity, or as a Deployment that an autoscaler grows and shrinks, each pod enrolling itself when it starts.

sections.heading: Deploy a worker
sections.text:
## Deploy a worker

First create and deploy the worker group in Smeltr, then mint a permanent enrollment code that brings in enough workers for the pods you are starting. Save this as `smeltr-worker.yaml` and replace the image digest, leader URL and enrollment code:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: smeltr-worker-default
data:
  smeltr.toml: |
    [worker]
    enabled = true
    group = "default"

    [worker.leader]
    url = "https://smeltr.example.com"

    [worker.storage]
    state_dir = "/var/lib/smeltr-worker"

    [worker.runtime]
    thread_limit = 2
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: smeltr-worker-default-enrollment-code
type: Opaque
stringData:
  enrollment-code: PASTE_THE_COMPLETE_ENROLLMENT_CODE_HERE
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: smeltr-worker-default
spec:
  serviceName: smeltr-worker-default
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: smeltr-worker-default
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: smeltr-worker-default
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 430
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000
      containers:
        - name: smeltr
          image: ghcr.io/smeltr-sh/smeltr@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_DIGEST
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: [ALL]
            seccompProfile:
              type: RuntimeDefault
          env:
            - name: SMELTR_CONFIG_FILE
              value: /config/smeltr.toml
            - name: SMELTR_WORKER_ENROLLMENT_CODE
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: smeltr-worker-default-enrollment-code
                  key: enrollment-code
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "2"
              memory: 2Gi
            limits:
              memory: 2Gi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
            - name: worker-state
              mountPath: /var/lib/smeltr-worker
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: smeltr-worker-default
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: worker-state
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 2Gi
```

The StatefulSet gives each numbered worker pod its own persistent volume. Never share or clone those claims: each contains one worker identity and credential. Workers require outbound access to the public leader URL and to their configured sources and destinations. They require no Service or inbound port unless their group runs a [receiver](/docs/sources#push-all-workers); see [Expose a receiver](#receiver).

`thread_limit` matches the CPU request, since a pod with no CPU limit otherwise runs a transform thread for every core on its node. Size the memory limit for what the group runs: see [Size a worker](/docs/enroll-worker/sizing).

`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` gives a stopping worker time to stop cleanly. It gives its pipeline up to 90 seconds to drain before killing it, then tells the leader it is stopping, then exits. Most stops take seconds, and the pod ends when the worker exits. Every step is bounded. The slowest stop takes about seven minutes: a pipeline the worker must kill, a stop that lands mid-deploy, and a leader slow to answer. 430 seconds covers the slowest stop. Status shows a worker that stops this way as Stopped, and it raises no warning. A shorter grace period can end a worker mid-drain: what it read since its last commit is read again by whichever worker next owns it, and the leader reports the worker silent.

After the worker appears Online, remove the `SMELTR_WORKER_ENROLLMENT_CODE` environment entry from the StatefulSet, apply the change, and confirm the restarted pod reconnects using its persisted credential. Then delete the enrollment code Secret. The worker needs it only to enroll.

sections.heading: Autoscale workers
sections.text:
## Autoscale workers

A group that grows and shrinks with load runs as a Deployment. Every pod enrolls itself with one ephemeral enrollment code, and the leader forgets each worker once it is gone. Create and deploy the group, then in Admin → Workers → Enrollment codes choose **\+ Add enrollment code**, set _Workers it brings in_ to Ephemeral and select **Mint**. An ephemeral enrollment code has no expiry and no limit on the workers it brings in: it works until you withdraw it. Save this as `smeltr-worker-ingest.yaml` and replace the image digest, leader URL and enrollment code:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: smeltr-worker-ingest
data:
  smeltr.toml: |
    [worker]
    enabled = true
    group = "ingest"

    [worker.leader]
    url = "https://smeltr.example.com"

    [worker.storage]
    state_dir = "/var/lib/smeltr-worker"

    [worker.runtime]
    thread_limit = 2
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: smeltr-worker-ingest-enrollment-code
type: Opaque
stringData:
  enrollment-code: PASTE_THE_COMPLETE_EPHEMERAL_ENROLLMENT_CODE_HERE
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: smeltr-worker-ingest
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: smeltr-worker-ingest
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: smeltr-worker-ingest
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 430
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000
      containers:
        - name: smeltr
          image: ghcr.io/smeltr-sh/smeltr@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_DIGEST
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: [ALL]
            seccompProfile:
              type: RuntimeDefault
          env:
            - name: SMELTR_CONFIG_FILE
              value: /config/smeltr.toml
            - name: SMELTR_WORKER_ENROLLMENT_CODE
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: smeltr-worker-ingest-enrollment-code
                  key: enrollment-code
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "2"
              memory: 2Gi
            limits:
              memory: 2Gi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
            - name: worker-state
              mountPath: /var/lib/smeltr-worker
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: smeltr-worker-ingest
        - name: worker-state
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: smeltr-worker-ingest
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: smeltr-worker-ingest
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 12
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
```

Keep the enrollment code Secret and its environment entry: every new pod enrolls with it. The state directory is an `emptyDir`, so a worker's identity lives and dies with its pod. A container that restarts in its pod keeps its identity; a pod that is replaced enrolls as a new worker, and clones the leader's configuration repository before it runs anything.

A worker that stops cleanly tells the leader, which forgets it at once. The leader forgets a worker that is killed without stopping cleanly once it has been silent for the time set under Admin → Workers → Ephemeral workers, ten minutes by default. A worker the leader has forgotten that comes back, such as one cut off from the leader for longer than that, enrolls again with the enrollment code as a new worker and restarts as it.

-   Keep `maxReplicas` at or below the partition count of the Kafka topics the group reads. A worker beyond that is assigned no partitions and sits idle.
-   Do not autoscale a group whose Kafka source reads a selected range, one with a start or stop position. A range read shares no work: every pod reads the whole range.
-   Set a CPU request for the HorizontalPodAutoscaler to scale on.
-   The enrollment code enrolls a worker, and an enrolled worker can receive every credential the leader stores. Restrict who can read the Secret. If it is exposed, withdraw it in the Enrollment codes table and mint another: running workers keep their credentials, and new pods need the new one.
-   Rotating the leader's certificate authority withdraws the enrollment code at cutover, and you cannot mint one while the rotation is open. Mint a new ephemeral enrollment code after cutover and update the Secret; until then new pods cannot enroll.

sections.heading: Expose a receiver
sections.text:
## Expose a receiver

A receiver is a source that senders connect to. Every worker of its group listens on the receiver's `port`, so each worker pod needs that port open, and senders need one address that reaches all of them. Add the port to the worker container, beside its `env`. This example uses port 8088:

```
          ports:
            - name: receiver
              containerPort: 8088
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: receiver
            periodSeconds: 5
```

Then add a Service that selects the worker pods:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: smeltr-worker-default-receiver
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: smeltr-worker-default
  ports:
    - name: receiver
      port: 8088
      targetPort: receiver
```

Pick a [Service type](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#publishing-services-service-types) for your balancer. For an autoscaled group, select its Deployment's pods.

`GET /health` on the receiver port answers 200 while the receiver takes requests and 503 while it is full, blocked or stopping, so the readiness probe takes a busy worker out of the Service until it can take requests again. The probe is optional.

-   A receiver served under an identity speaks TLS, so its probe adds `scheme: HTTPS`.
-   Under an identity with authorities, every connection to the receiver must present a client certificate, `/health` included. An `httpGet` probe has none, so use a `tcpSocket` probe on the receiver port there. It confirms only that the worker listens.
-   The worker runs as a non-root user without capabilities and cannot listen on a port below 1024. For syslog's 514, set the receiver's `port` to a high one, such as 5514, and give the Service `port: 514` with `targetPort: receiver`.
-   A syslog receiver over UDP needs `protocol: UDP` on its container port and on the Service's, and has no health path, so it takes no probe. Its `allowFrom` sees the address a datagram arrives from, so the Service keeps the sender's own: `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service.

sections.heading: Size a worker
sections.text:
# Size a worker

A worker's memory is a fixed columnar budget plus a ceiling for each source and destination it runs. Its CPU is one transform thread per core. Its disk is the state directory.

sections.heading: Memory
sections.text:
## Memory

Give a worker at least the sum of the parts below for the sources and destinations its group runs, plus about 150 MiB for the process itself and the size of every lookup table the group uses and its index, which a worker holds in memory whole. Each amount below is the default; a source or destination with a larger `fetchBytes` or `bufferBytes` holds that instead. Every worker in a group runs the whole group's configuration, so size each one for all of it. The warning below counts the parts and not the lookup tables.

| Part | Default | For each | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Columnar budget | 1 GiB | worker running any source | Memory every transform thread shares while it runs a batch. `SMELTR_MEMORY_BUDGET_BYTES` changes it. A batch that needs more is split and run in parts, which costs time. |
| Lanes | 4 MiB | source, and again per transform thread | One batch per slot: about 20 MiB for one source on four threads, about 80 MiB for ten sources on sixteen. |
| Fetch queue | 64 MiB | source, plus half of it per broker in the cluster | `fetchBytes`. A fetch already asked of each broker still lands once the queue is full. The warning counts only the brokers named in `brokers`. |
| Request bodies | 128 MiB | source | Twice the receiver's inbox: bodies being read, and bodies admitted. |
| Record | 64 MiB | source | The largest record it reads from an object. |
| Answer | 256 MiB | source | The largest answer it takes. A whole answer is held while it is cut into records. |
| Result | 256 MiB | source | The largest result one poll takes. A whole result is held while it is handed out; a larger one fails the poll. |
| Buffer | 64 MiB | destination | `bufferBytes`. Elasticsearch, Splunk HEC, HTTP, Log Analytics workspace and Prometheus take one request's size instead when that is larger. A Kafka destination's covers its client's own queue too. |
| Buffer and open files | 512 MiB | destination | `bufferBytes` for rows not yet in the bucket, and as much again for the open files encoding and uploading them. |

A group on four cores reading one Kafka topic from three brokers into Elasticsearch and S3 adds up to 1780 MiB:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Columnar budget | 1024 MiB |
| Lanes, 1 source and 4 threads | 20 MiB |
| Fetch queue, a cluster of 3 brokers | 160 MiB |
| Elasticsearch buffer | 64 MiB |
| S3 buffer and open files | 512 MiB |
| Total | 1780 MiB |

Each ceiling is a worst case, and they rarely all fill at once. A worker whose deployment adds up to more than its memory limit still runs, but can be killed for memory under load. It logs a warning naming each part and its share, and the warning stays on Issues while it holds. Select the worker on Status and open **Memory by part** to see which part it is. Raise the limit, or lower `fetchBytes`, `bufferBytes` or `SMELTR_MEMORY_BUDGET_BYTES`.

The limit a worker checks against is its container's memory limit, or the host's memory when it has none. Set a memory limit on every worker container, so the warning compares against what the worker may really use.

`smeltr_memory_peak_bytes` shows how much of the columnar budget batches have needed. A peak well under the budget means the budget can come down.

sections.heading: CPU
sections.text:
## CPU

Transform does most of the CPU work, and it runs one thread per core the worker may use. Readers and destinations run threads of their own that mostly wait on the network, except a receiver decompressing gzip and an object destination compressing its files. Two cores is a sensible start; add cores or workers while CPU stays high under normal load.

The cores a worker counts are its CPU limit, or the host's cores when it has none. A container with a CPU request and no limit counts every core on its node. Set `worker.runtime.thread_limit` to its request, or give it a CPU limit.

sections.heading: Disk
sections.text:
## Disk

The state directory holds the worker's credential, its clone of the configuration repository, the lookup tables that configuration names and the progress of the single-worker sources it holds. A new version of a lookup table, and the index built beside it, arrive before the old ones are removed, so leave room for each table and its index twice. Once this volume is full, the worker takes no new configuration, lookup table or source handoff.

sections.text:

sections.heading: First login
sections.text:
# First login

A new leader creates one administrator on first start. Follow these steps once, after [installing the binary](/docs/install-leader/binary), [running the container](/docs/install-leader/container) or [deploying on Kubernetes](/docs/install-leader/kubernetes).

sections.heading: Sign in with the printed credentials
sections.text:
## Sign in with the printed credentials

1.  Read the startup console of the leader you just started. A fresh account store prints a username and one-time password to the process console (stderr), not the fleet log viewer. Look for output in this form; the values below are placeholders, not credentials you can use:
    
    ```
    smeltr: this leader had no accounts, so one was created.
               username: admin
      one-time password: <generated one-time password>
    It is shown once and is not recoverable. Signing in with it requires choosing a new one.
    ```
    
2.  Open the configured public origin URL in a browser: `http://127.0.0.1:4000` for the local examples.
3.  Sign in with the printed credentials and choose your own password when prompted. Protect any service-console logs containing the temporary password.
4.  Open Admin → Accounts and create named administrators as described in [Accounts and access](/docs/accounts).
5.  For standalone mode, open Status and wait for the automatically enrolled worker in `default` to appear Online. Check that its running commit matches `main`. For a leader-only installation, [enroll a separate worker](/docs/enroll-worker/host) first.

sections.heading: Your first pipeline
sections.text:
Tutorial

# Your first pipeline

Read JSON records from one Kafka topic, uppercase each message, add a field, and send them to another topic. You'll build it all from one route and review the change before it reaches a worker.

You'll need a running Smeltr installation, administrator access, and an online worker in a group you can use for testing. If you're still setting up, start with [the setup guide](/docs/getting-started).

sections.heading: 1\. Before you start
sections.text:
## 1\. Before you start

We'll use two Kafka topics: one for incoming records and one for the result. Keeping them separate prevents the output from feeding back into the pipeline.

In a terminal with Kafka's command-line tools available, replace `localhost:9092` with your test broker's address and create the topics:

```
export BROKERS='localhost:9092'
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server "$BROKERS" --create \
  --topic smeltr-tutorial-in --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server "$BROKERS" --create \
  --topic smeltr-tutorial-out --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
```

These commands assume a single test broker with a plaintext listener. For an authenticated broker, see the [Kafka source](/docs/sources/kafka) and [Kafka destination](/docs/destinations/kafka) guides. If the topics already exist, make sure they're yours to use for this exercise.

Send three records to the input topic, so there is something to capture:

```
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"service":"checkout","message":"payment declined"}' \
  '{"service":"search","message":"query timed out"}' \
  '{"service":"checkout","message":"order placed"}' |
kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server "$BROKERS" --topic smeltr-tutorial-in
```

sections.heading: 2\. Start a route
sections.text:
## 2\. Start a route

A route takes records from a source, runs them through a pipeline, and delivers them to destinations. You'll make all three from the route itself.

In Smeltr, select your test worker group and open **Build**. It opens on Routes. Choose **\+ Add route**. The new route shows **from source**, **pipeline** and **destination**.

sections.heading: 3\. Add the source
sections.text:
## 3\. Add the source

In **from source**, choose **\+ New source…**. Choose **Pull, all workers**, then Kafka. Fill in the settings below and choose **Add**.

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| id | `tutorial-in` |
| brokers | Your broker address |
| topics | `smeltr-tutorial-in` |

Use broker addresses the worker can reach, including the addresses Kafka advertises to clients. The worker needs permission to read the input topic and write to the output topic.

Smeltr saves the source at once. The first save asks for a branch, because `main` is only changed by deploying. Call it `tutorial-first-pipeline` and choose **Edit on this branch**. Everything you save from here on goes on that branch.

sections.heading: 4\. Make the pipeline from a capture
sections.text:
## 4\. Make the pipeline from a capture

In **pipeline**, choose **\+ New pipeline…**. The pipeline `tutorial-in-parse` opens and asks for a capture of your source. A capture reads records through a worker without deploying anything.

Open **Advanced**, set **Start at** to earliest, and choose **Start**. When the three records appear, choose **Stop capture**. Enter `tutorial-message` under **Save as** and choose **Save sample**.

Smeltr reads the sample and proposes the steps. It reports that 3 of 3 records read as JSON, and adds a Parser step that declares `service` and `message`. The parsed records show beside the steps.

sections.heading: 5\. Shape the records
sections.text:
## 5\. Shape the records

After the Parser step, choose **\+ step**, then Eval. An Eval step sets fields to the values of expressions. Fill in the first row, then choose **\+ assignment** for the second:

| Target field | Expression |
| --- | --- |
| `message` | `message.toUpperCase()` |
| `event.dataset` | `"smeltr.tutorial"` |

The first row uppercases the parsed message. The second labels it as part of this tutorial. A dot in the field name puts `dataset` inside an `event` object. The output updates as you type. Its first record should have these fields, along with any it kept from the input:

```
{
  "service": "checkout",
  "message": "PAYMENT DECLINED",
  "event": {
    "dataset": "smeltr.tutorial"
  }
}
```

Choose **Save**. Smeltr saves the pipeline and takes you back to the route, with `tutorial-in-parse` picked.

sections.heading: 6\. Add the destination
sections.text:
## 6\. Add the destination

Under **destination**, choose **\+ destination**, then **\+ New destination…**, then Kafka. Fill in the settings below and choose **Add**. If the route already sends to another destination, choose its ✕ to stop sending there.

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| id | `tutorial-out` |
| brokers | The same broker |
| default topic | `smeltr-tutorial-out` |

The route now reads `tutorial-in` → `tutorial-in-parse` → `tutorial-out`. Choose **Save** to save the route.

sections.heading: 7\. Check where records go
sections.text:
## 7\. Check where records go

Open the **Route a sample** tab. Select `tutorial-message` and choose **Run**. Smeltr runs the sample through your routes. Nothing is delivered.

All three records should reach `tutorial-out`, with none unrouted or dropped. Choose the `tutorial-out` count to see the documents as they would be sent.

sections.heading: 8\. Review and deploy
sections.text:
## 8\. Review and deploy

Nothing you've saved runs until it's deployed. In the branch bar, choose **Open for review**. Smeltr fills in the title from what changed. Give it a description and choose **Open for review**.

On the review page, read through **Saves** and make sure it holds only your tutorial changes.

If someone has changed `main` while you were working, choose **Bring current** and check the saves again. Then choose **Approve & deploy** and confirm. Smeltr opens Status, where you can watch your workers pick up the change. If a worker reports a deployment failure, resolve it before sending a record.

sections.heading: 9\. Send a real record
sections.text:
## 9\. Send a real record

Back in the same terminal, send a fresh message to the input topic. The timestamp in it will help you tell it apart from earlier attempts.

```
export RUN_ID="smeltr-tutorial-$(date +%s)"
printf '{"service":"checkout","message":"%s"}\n' "$RUN_ID" | kafka-console-producer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server "$BROKERS" --topic smeltr-tutorial-in
```

Read the output topic into a file, then open it. The command stops after 30 seconds without another record.

```
kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server "$BROKERS" \
  --topic smeltr-tutorial-out --from-beginning \
  --timeout-ms 30000 > delivered.jsonl
cat delivered.jsonl
```

Look for the message you just sent, now in uppercase, with `event.dataset` set to `smeltr.tutorial`. The three records you sent first are there too: the source starts at the earliest record. Open **Map** to see your route with records flowing through it.

Check the result with a script

This Python 3 snippet finds the record from your latest attempt and checks both fields. Run it in the same terminal so it can read `RUN_ID`.

```
python3 - <<'PY'
import json, os
expected = os.environ["RUN_ID"].upper()
with open("delivered.jsonl") as records:
    found = any(
        row.get("message") == expected
        and row.get("event", {}).get("dataset") == "smeltr.tutorial"
        for line in records if line.strip()
        for row in [json.loads(line)]
    )
assert found, f"Expected record not delivered: {expected}"
print(f"Verified delivery: {expected}")
PY
```

It prints `Verified delivery:` followed by your uppercase message when it finds a match.

| If you don't see the result | What to try |
| --- | --- |
| The file is empty | Check for an error from the producer. Then look at Status → Issues and Logs for connection, permission, or deployment errors. |
| The message isn't uppercase or has the wrong dataset | Check the saved Eval expressions, and make sure you're looking at the right worker group and running commit. |
| You only see older messages | Check for a backlog or worker errors, then read the topic again. If you're using the script, keep the same terminal so `RUN_ID` still identifies the message you sent. |

When you're finished, remove the tutorial route, pipeline, sample, source and destination in a new reviewed change. Once the workers are running that change, you can remove the two Kafka topics too.

sections.heading: Try filtering rows and fields
sections.text:
## Try filtering rows and fields

Use a separate pipeline to try this example. Keep order and error events, drop routine health checks, and remove the debug field. Copy each input below into its own saved sample.

1.  Add a JSON Parser step with `_raw` as its input. Declare `event_type`, `message`, and `debug` as `str` fields.
2.  Add a Drop step with condition `event_type == "health_check"`. A true condition removes the whole record.
3.  Add an Eval step with the assignments below. Setting these fields to `null` leaves them out of the delivered JSON. `_raw` is the original input text.

| Target field | Expression |
| --- | --- |
| `debug` | `null` |
| `_raw` | `null` |

3 records in · 2 records out · debug fields removed

Input 1

```
{
  "event_type": "order",
  "message": "Order placed",
  "debug": "trace-101"
}
```

Kept

```
{
  "event_type": "order",
  "message": "Order placed"
}
```

Keep the order event; remove the debug field.

Input 2

```
{
  "event_type": "health_check",
  "message": "Service is healthy",
  "debug": "trace-102"
}
```

Dropped

No record sent to the destination.

Drop the whole record because event\_type is health\_check.

Input 3

```
{
  "event_type": "error",
  "message": "Payment timed out",
  "debug": "trace-103"
}
```

Kept

```
{
  "event_type": "error",
  "message": "Payment timed out"
}
```

Keep the error event; remove the debug field.

Run each sample and check the result shown above.

sections.heading: Try your own data
sections.text:
## Try your own data

Pick a few records from your source and remove sensitive values before saving them as samples. Work on a branch and check which routes use the pipeline; an edit to shared logic can affect other worker groups. Add one step at a time and inspect the fields and types in the preview.

Include records that are awkward to handle. If your next pipeline converts a status code to a number, try these cases:

| Input | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| `"200"` | The result is a number. |
| `"unknown"` | The pipeline handles an invalid value as you intend. |
| A missing field | The pipeline handles an absent value as you intend. |

Test filtering in both directions too. For a Drop step, save one record the step should drop and another that should pass through. When removing fields, check that unwanted columns are absent and the fields you need are still present.

The preview checks your transformation; send a real record to check destination access too.

Use the [expression reference](/docs/code-reference) as you build, then follow the [review checklist](/docs/review#check) before deploying.

title: Set up a small Smeltr deployment.

sections.heading: Set up a small Smeltr deployment.
sections.text:
Getting started

# Set up a small Smeltr deployment.

Use the leader's browser interface to build, test, and deploy configuration. Workers run that configuration and move records from sources to destinations.

sections.heading: How Smeltr fits together
sections.text:
## How Smeltr fits together

*Diagram: How Smeltr fits together. An administrator edits and reviews configuration on the leader. The leader stores it in Git. Workers fetch main and report their status to the leader. Source records flow through workers to destinations. The stacked worker cards represent one or more workers.*

The leader provides the editing and review screens and stores configuration in Git. Workers fetch main and report their status. Workers also connect directly to sources and destinations, where they read, filter, and deliver records. Dashed arrows show workers fetching configuration and reporting status. The stack represents one or more workers.

A **worker group** is a set of workers that run the same group configuration. Groups let you manage different environments separately while sharing reusable pipelines. [Read how workers follow main →](/docs/git/configuration)

sections.heading: What you need
sections.text:
## What you need

-   A Smeltr binary, or the [container image](/docs/install-leader/container#pull) from `ghcr.io/smeltr-sh/smeltr`, with its version and checksum or digest.
-   One host for a standalone install, or a leader host and separate worker hosts for a distributed deployment.
-   Each separate worker can reach the leader over the network.
-   Git installed on the leader host to serve the configuration repository. Workers use a built-in Git client. See [Repository hosting](/docs/git/external-host#hosting).
-   Access to the sources and destinations your configuration will use.

**Start small.** One leader and one worker group suit an evaluation or small deployment. Add groups to organize workloads and deployment policies.

The leader trusts every enrolled worker with the whole cluster's configuration and leader-stored credentials. Groups do not restrict that access. Use separate clusters when workloads require separate trust boundaries.

sections.heading: Connect your data systems
sections.text:
## Connect your data systems

Choose a source to read, a pipeline to shape the records, and a destination to receive them. Workers make these connections, so check network access and credentials from the worker hosts. Use the connector options and release notes supplied with your version.

-   [Sources](/docs/sources) — input types, read positions, authentication, and setup.
-   [Destinations](/docs/destinations) — output types, delivery settings, and verification.
-   [Secrets & credentials](/docs/secrets) — shared credentials and connection identities.

sections.heading: Choose where to run Smeltr
sections.text: ## Choose where to run Smeltr

sections.heading: Standalone: one host
sections.text:
### Standalone: one host

Run the leader and one worker as one Smeltr service, from one configuration file. Enable both `leader.enabled` and `worker.enabled`. For a local test, bind to `127.0.0.1` so only that machine can connect.

*Diagram: Standalone: leader and worker on one host. An administrator connects to the leader. One Smeltr service runs the leader and one worker together, shown as joined cards. Sources send records through the worker to destinations.*

One binary, one service: the leader and one worker run together. The administrator uses the leader; the worker reads from sources, filters records, and delivers them to destinations.

sections.heading: Distributed: separate machines
sections.text:
### Distributed: separate machines

Run the leader on its own machine and place workers near their sources and destinations. Workers connect to the leader; the leader does not need inbound access to worker hosts.

The leader stores configuration history, accounts, and other installation state on its host. Preserve its data directory across restarts and upgrades, and back it up.

sections.heading: Quick start
sections.text:
## Quick start

1.  Choose your setup: [standalone with one built-in worker](/docs/install-leader/binary#first-start), or [a leader with separate workers](/docs/https#direct). Prepare the account, files and directories in the installation guide before starting.
2.  Sign in with the initial credentials, choose a password, and confirm the default worker group exists.
3.  For standalone mode, the worker enrolls automatically. For separate workers, [create an enrollment code and enroll each worker](/docs/enroll-worker/host).
4.  Open Status. Wait for the worker to appear Online and compare its running commit with `main`. An online worker has contacted the leader; its running commit confirms which configuration it loaded.
5.  Use [Your first pipeline](/docs/first-pipeline) to build, test, review and deploy a change, then verify a real record at the destination.

sections.heading: Check the installation
sections.text:
## Check the installation

Before handing a network deployment over, check each result. The local HTTP evaluation can defer HTTPS until you make it reachable over the network:

-   **Trusted HTTPS.** Open the leader at its configured address. The browser accepts its certificate. [Set up trust](/docs/certificates#model).
-   **Named administrator access.** Sign in with your own account and complete any first-login password change. [Create an account](/docs/accounts#accounts).
-   **An online worker.** Status shows the expected group and a recent heartbeat. [Check worker status](/docs/enroll-worker/host#verify).
-   **The intended configuration is running.** Each worker in the test group reports the deployed commit. [Check deployment](/docs/first-pipeline#deploy).
-   **A record arrives at the destination.** Send a fresh record and check its transformed fields where Smeltr delivers it. [Verify the data path](/docs/first-pipeline#verify).
-   **A recoverable backup.** Take a consistent leader backup, keep the matching [secrets encryption key](/docs/secrets#encryption-key), and test a restore in isolation. [Follow the backup procedure](/docs/backup-recovery#backup).

sections.heading: Next steps
sections.text:
## Next steps

Use the [operations guide](/docs/operations) to check workers, deploy changes, and recover from failures. If a check fails, use [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) to work through the connection, certificate, or deployment error.

sections.heading: How Git is used
sections.text:
# How Git is used

Git is Smeltr's configuration control plane: it stores the versions that workers run. Your edits live on a draft branch until you deploy them to `main`. Workers follow `main` and report the commit they are running. A commit identifies a saved version of the configuration.

[See the leader, workers, and data connections in one diagram →](/docs/getting-started#overview)

sections.heading: What Git holds
sections.text:
## What Git holds

Sources, destinations, routes, pipelines, saved samples, tests, and supporting resource files are versioned together. Each worker group has its own configuration under `groups/<group-id>/`. Reusable configuration lives under `shared/`. A worker loads its group's configuration together with the shared content at the same commit.

Configuration refers to credentials by name and version. You manage secret values through [Secrets](/docs/secrets) or the worker environment. Host startup settings, accounts, and worker state have their own storage. To recover an installation, follow the [leader backup procedure](/docs/backup-recovery); a copy of the Git repository alone does not contain all of that state.

Workers clone the whole configuration repository, including other groups. The leader also trusts an enrolled worker with every credential it stores. A group selects what a worker runs; it does not restrict what that worker can access. Use separate clusters for workloads that require this isolation.

sections.heading: From a branch to main
sections.text:
## From a branch to main

*Diagram: From a draft to running workers. Draft changes go to review. Review can send them back for revision. Approval and deployment publish a commit on main. Each worker fetches main and reports its running commit.*

Review the diff and test results before approval. Each worker fetches main independently; check its running commit to confirm adoption.

Work on a branch in the Smeltr UI. Save your changes, run the tests, and open the change for review. Review the diff and the pipelines and routes it reaches. Bring the branch current if `main` has moved, then review the result again.

Approval and deployment publish the change as a commit on `main`. That commit becomes the configuration workers follow. Saving a draft branch leaves the deployed configuration in place. See [Review and deploy](/docs/review) for the procedure.

To return to an earlier configuration, use Branches → History → **Roll back to here**. Review its effect across worker groups and check that its secret versions are still available. Then check the workers’ running commits and destination output, just as you would for any other deployment.

A rollback writes no commit. It deploys the earlier commit and holds the fleet there: the leader does not deploy commits that reach `main` afterwards. History shows the hold, who made it, and how many commits wait, and Status reports **Deploy held** for as long as it lasts. **Release** deploys `main`'s head and ends the hold. A change approved during the hold merges to `main` and waits there for **Release**.

sections.heading: How workers follow main
sections.text:
## How workers follow main

1.  An enrolled worker completes its initial check-in with the leader.
2.  It periodically fetches the deployed commit into its local Git repository: `main`'s head, or the commit a rollback holds. The worker discovers it itself; its heartbeat reports deployment state back to the leader.
3.  It prepares the configuration for its worker group and the shared resources at that commit. If preparation fails, it can keep running its previous configuration and report the failure.
4.  It reports the commit it is running. When a change leaves its group and shared content unchanged, the worker can adopt the new commit without restarting its pipeline runtime.

Each worker finds and loads changes independently. Publishing a commit does not switch the whole fleet at once. If a fetch fails, a worker keeps its current configuration and retries. A running worker keeps running through a leader outage; a worker that restarts runs nothing until the leader answers its first check-in. Check its [setting for stopping when the leader cannot be reached](/docs/operations#outages).

sections.heading: Check the running version
sections.text:
## Check the running version

Record the deployed commit on `main`, then open Status for each intended worker.

In the selected worker's details, compare **Commit** with the deployed main commit. This is the version the worker reports running. Check its last-seen time and active issues if it differs or the worker is offline.

Once the intended workers report the deployed commit, send a fresh record and verify its output at the destination.

sections.heading: External Git host
sections.text: # External Git host

sections.heading: Repository hosting
sections.text:
## Repository hosting

The leader manages one Git repository for the fleet at `<data-dir>/repos/config.git`. Workers fetch it over the leader's HTTPS endpoint using their enrolled credentials and configured TLS trust. The worker endpoint serves reads; configuration changes go through the Smeltr UI.

Install Git on the leader host: it uses `git http-backend` to serve the repository. Workers use a built-in Git client and do not need a separate Git installation. Preserve each worker's state directory so its local repository and cached configuration survive restarts. See [leader installation](/docs/install-leader/binary) and [worker enrollment](/docs/enroll-worker/host).

sections.heading: Follow a Git host
sections.text:
## Follow a Git host

The leader can follow a repository on a Git host. The host's `main` is then what the fleet runs, and review and merge happen on the host. The leader keeps its own repository and goes on serving workers from it; workers never reach the host and never hold its token.

*Diagram: Follow a Git host. A save in the Smeltr UI is a branch on the leader, which the leader pushes to the Git host. The host reviews and merges it to main. The leader fetches main, loads every worker group at it and deploys it only if all of them load. Workers fetch the deployed commit from the leader.*

Branches go out to the host and main comes back. Workers only ever talk to the leader.

1.  **Saves go out.** A save in the Smeltr UI is a commit on the leader at once, which the leader then pushes to the host's branch of the same name. Branches shows each branch's push state.
2.  **Main comes in.** The leader fetches the host on a timer and on **Sync now**. When the host's `main` moves, the leader loads every worker group at the new commit and deploys it only if all of them load. A commit that does not load leaves the fleet on the last one that did, and Status reports **Remote not followed** with the reason until a later sync succeeds.

sections.heading: Connect a host
sections.text:
### Connect a host

Set the remote under Admin → System → **Git remote**:

![The Git remote tab under Admin, System: URL, User, Token, Fetch every minutes, and Approve: pushes to main.](/git-remote-settings-light.png)

The Git remote settings, with a GitHub repository's clone URL.

| Setting | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| URL | The repository's HTTP or HTTPS clone URL. The leader does not support SSH. |
| User | The name the leader sends the token with. Use the name your host takes with a token. |
| Token | An access token that can read the repository and push branches to it, Git LFS included. The leader stores it encrypted, never shows it again, and forgets it when the URL changes. |
| Fetch | How often the leader fetches the host, every 1 to 1440 minutes. Off, it fetches only on Sync now. |
| Approve | Its _pushes to main_ box, off by default. See [Approve with a remote](#remote-approve). |

Connected to an empty repository, the leader pushes its own `main` there first. The leader follows a repository that already has a `main` from then on.

sections.heading: Branches and refused pushes
sections.text:
### Branches and refused pushes

Branches go from the leader to the host, never back: edit a Smeltr branch in the UI, not on the host. A save waits for nothing on the host; while the host cannot be reached, its branch shows **not pushed** and the leader pushes it when the host answers. If someone else pushed to that branch on the host, the push is refused rather than dropping their commits. Branches then shows both tips, and **Overwrite remote** puts the leader's branch there anyway.

sections.heading: Approve with a remote
sections.text:
### Approve with a remote

With **pushes to main** clear, Smeltr does not offer Approve: merge the branch on the host, and the leader deploys the result once it follows it. Checked, Approve squashes the change, pushes it to the host's `main`, and deploys it once the host takes it. A host that protects `main`, or whose `main` moved since the last sync, refuses the push; nothing moves, and Approve shows the host's reason.

sections.heading: Lookup files
sections.text:
### Lookup files

Lookup files travel by Git LFS. Pushing a branch uploads its lookup files to the host's LFS server first, so a clone with git-lfs has every file. When a commit from the host names a lookup the leader lacks, the leader downloads it from that server and checks it against its pointer before it loads it. Commit lookup files on the host with git-lfs, or upload them through Smeltr: the leader refuses a lookup committed as a plain file.

sections.heading: HTTPS
sections.text:
# HTTPS

Remote browsers and workers reach the leader over HTTPS: the leader serves it on port 443, or a reverse proxy in front of it does.

sections.heading: Direct HTTPS
sections.text:
## Direct HTTPS

For a network deployment, configure DNS to reach this host, permit TCP 443 only from intended clients, and save this as `smeltr.toml`:

```
[leader]
enabled = true

[leader.http]
bind = "0.0.0.0"
public_origin = "https://smeltr.example.com"

[leader.tls]
enabled = true

[leader.storage]
data_dir = "/var/lib/smeltr"

[leader.secrets]
key = "/etc/smeltr/secrets/sealing.key"
```

Port 443 is the default, so you need no `port` line. On Linux, grant the service `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` to listen on a port below 1024 (see [capabilities](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html)). Keep the leader under a dedicated, non-root service account. Provision these directories for the service account. Back up the secrets encryption key as [Encryption key](/docs/secrets#encryption-key) describes. The hostname and port must match the URL users actually open. Trust the generated public CA through your organization's browser/OS trust procedure before signing in; see [Certificates](/docs/certificates). Setting public\_origin does not create DNS, open a firewall, or configure a proxy.

To run it as a service, follow [Run as a systemd service](/docs/install-leader/binary#service), which grants that capability. Then confirm `https://smeltr.example.com` is reachable and trusted from a client.

sections.heading: HTTPS reverse proxy
sections.text:
## HTTPS reverse proxy

When a proxy on the same host terminates HTTPS for a host-installed binary, set `leader.http.bind = "127.0.0.1"`, `leader.tls.enabled = false`, and set `leader.http.public_origin = "https://smeltr.example.com"`. Set `leader.http.port = 4000` (or another unprivileged port) so the process needs no extra capability, and configure the proxy separately to forward that origin to `http://127.0.0.1:4000`. Serve a certificate clients trust. Keep the upstream listener private and preserve the browser Origin header.

For a container, the Smeltr process normally listens on `0.0.0.0` inside its network namespace. Restrict the published host port instead, for example with `-p 127.0.0.1:4000:4000`, and point the same-host proxy at that address. In Kubernetes, expose Smeltr with a ClusterIP Service and keep the workload private behind the ingress.

Set workers to use the proxy’s externally reachable HTTPS URL. In this setup, enrollment codes tell workers to verify the proxy certificate using the operating system’s trusted certificates. Install your private CA there if needed. Test both browser login and worker enrollment before opening general access.

sections.heading: Install the binary
sections.text:
# Install the binary

[Download](/get#download) the Linux archive or the Windows zip.

sections.heading: Verify the executable
sections.text:
## Verify the executable

Compare the archive's SHA-256 checksum with the one shown beside it on the release page, and stop if it differs:

```
sha256sum smeltr-linux.tar.gz
```

On Windows use `Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 smeltr-windows.zip`. The archive holds the executable, the cryptography library it loads, the license and the third-party notices.

sections.heading: Install the binary
sections.text:
## Install the binary

The following commands target Linux with `useradd`. Create a dedicated service account once. If it already exists, use it. Keep the supplied executable name, version and checksum with your installation records.

```
sudo useradd --system --user-group --home-dir /var/lib/smeltr --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin smeltr
sudo install -d -o root -g root -m 0755 /opt/smeltr
tar -xzf smeltr-linux.tar.gz
sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 smeltr /opt/smeltr/smeltr
sudo install -d -o root -g smeltr -m 0750 /etc/smeltr
sudo install -d -o smeltr -g smeltr -m 0700 /var/lib/smeltr /etc/smeltr/secrets
```

Install Git using your operating system's package manager and confirm `git --version` succeeds. The leader uses `git http-backend` to serve configuration; workers have a built-in Git client. The executable includes the browser UI.

The **secrets encryption key** encrypts secrets the leader stores. On a fresh installation, leave `/etc/smeltr/secrets/sealing.key` absent so Smeltr creates it. Back it up and keep the matching copies for recovery; [Encryption key](/docs/secrets#encryption-key) says where to keep that backup.

sections.heading: Standalone: first local start
sections.text:
## Standalone: first local start

Save this complete configuration as `smeltr.toml` in your current directory. It runs the leader and one worker as one service, with the browser interface restricted to this machine.

```
[leader]
enabled = true

[leader.http]
bind = "127.0.0.1"
port = 4000
public_origin = "http://127.0.0.1:4000"

[leader.tls]
enabled = false

[leader.storage]
data_dir = "/var/lib/smeltr"

[leader.secrets]
key = "/etc/smeltr/secrets/sealing.key"

[worker]
enabled = true
group = "default"
```

The worker enrolls automatically and uses the local leader. Leave its enrollment code and leader URL unset. It stores its identity, credential and cached configuration in `/var/lib/smeltr/worker`. This HTTP setup is for local evaluation; use [HTTPS](/docs/https) for network access.

Install the configuration, then start Smeltr in the foreground as its service account:

```
sudo install -o root -g smeltr -m 0640 ./smeltr.toml /etc/smeltr/smeltr.toml
sudo -u smeltr env SMELTR_CONFIG_FILE=/etc/smeltr/smeltr.toml /opt/smeltr/smeltr
```

Keep this process running while you [sign in](/docs/first-login). Stopping it stops both the leader and worker. The absolute configuration and storage paths make startup independent of your working directory.

sections.heading: Run as a systemd service
sections.text:
## Run as a systemd service

Stop any foreground evaluation process before starting the service. Install the configuration it runs: the local one above, or a network one from [HTTPS](/docs/https).

```
sudo install -o root -g smeltr -m 0640 ./smeltr.toml /etc/smeltr/smeltr.toml
```

The HTTPS configuration runs the leader only. To keep standalone mode, add the `[worker]` settings from the local example before installing it. Save this unit as `/etc/systemd/system/smeltr-leader.service`:

```
[Unit]
Description=Smeltr leader
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=smeltr
Group=smeltr
StateDirectory=smeltr
StateDirectoryMode=0700
WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/smeltr
Environment=SMELTR_CONFIG_FILE=/etc/smeltr/smeltr.toml
ExecStart=/opt/smeltr/smeltr
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=true
UMask=0077
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

The service can bind port 443 while running as `smeltr`.

```
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now smeltr-leader
sudo journalctl -u smeltr-leader -b
```

On first start, read the one-time administrator credentials in the service journal and complete the [first login](/docs/first-login). Restrict access to that journal as you would other credential-bearing console logs.

For another service manager, set the executable, absolute configuration path, working directory, service account and restart policy explicitly. Preserve the data, key and configuration across replacing the executable. Do not start a second leader against the same data.

sections.heading: Run the container image
sections.text:
# Run the container image

Smeltr publishes its image at `ghcr.io/smeltr-sh/smeltr`, tagged by release. For a cluster, use [Kubernetes](/docs/install-leader/kubernetes).

sections.heading: Pull and verify the image
sections.text:
## Pull and verify the image

The release workflow signs each image and attaches its package list (a CycloneDX SBOM). A tag can move to a newer image, so pull it, then check and run that exact digest:

```
docker pull ghcr.io/smeltr-sh/smeltr:<version>
image=$(docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' ghcr.io/smeltr-sh/smeltr:<version>)
```

Both checks fail unless that workflow, run for a release tag, made the image:

```
cosign verify "$image" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/smeltr-sh/smeltr/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v'
cosign verify-attestation --type cyclonedx "$image" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/smeltr-sh/smeltr/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v'
```

Name the verified digest the way the commands below expect:

```
docker tag "$image" smeltr:<version>
```

sections.heading: Why not `latest`
sections.text:
### Why not `latest`

A tag names the image it was last pushed to. `latest`, `1` and `1.2` move to each newer release they cover, which makes them a way to find the newest release. A container keeps the image it was created from, but a new one, such as a worker added on another host or a new Kubernetes pod, may pull whatever the tag names at that moment. After a release those run the new build while the rest stay on the old one.

A worker takes deployments only from a leader of its own major release: 1.2 and 1.3 work together, 2.0 does not. A worker on an older release of that major refuses a configuration that uses something newer, and keeps running what it has. A leader that starts on a newer build upgrades its data without the backup an [upgrade](/docs/upgrade) begins with. Name the image by its digest, and change the digest only as an upgrade.

sections.heading: Load an image archive
sections.text:
## Load an image archive

A host that cannot reach ghcr.io loads the image from the archive in the release's extras. Compare the extras zip's SHA-256 checksum with the one shown beside it on the release page, and stop if it differs. Then unzip the image archive, load it and check its name, tag and runtime user:

```
sha256sum smeltr-extras.zip
unzip smeltr-extras.zip smeltr-image.tar.gz
docker load --input smeltr-image.tar.gz
docker image inspect smeltr:<version> --format '{{.Id}} user={{.Config.User}}'
```

sections.heading: Run the container
sections.text:
## Run the container

The image runs as UID/GID 1000. Prepare persistent host directories before starting it:

```
sudo install -d -o root -g 1000 -m 0750 /srv/smeltr
sudo install -d -o 1000 -g 1000 -m 0700 /srv/smeltr/leader-data /srv/smeltr/leader-secrets
```

Save this leader-only configuration as `container-smeltr.toml` in your current directory. HTTP listens on port 4000 inside the container; the run command below restricts the published port to the host.

```
[leader]
enabled = true

[leader.http]
bind = "0.0.0.0"
port = 4000
public_origin = "http://127.0.0.1:4000"

[leader.tls]
enabled = false

[leader.storage]
data_dir = "/var/lib/smeltr"

[leader.secrets]
key = "/run/secrets/smeltr/sealing.key"
```

For a standalone container, append `[worker]` with `enabled = true` and `group = "default"`. Its worker state stays within the leader-data mount. Leave the secrets encryption key file absent on a fresh installation.

```
sudo install -o root -g 1000 -m 0640 ./container-smeltr.toml /srv/smeltr/smeltr.toml
docker run --name smeltr-leader \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  -p 127.0.0.1:4000:4000 \
  -e SMELTR_CONFIG_FILE=/etc/smeltr/smeltr.toml \
  --mount type=bind,src=/srv/smeltr/smeltr.toml,dst=/etc/smeltr/smeltr.toml,readonly \
  --mount type=bind,src=/srv/smeltr/leader-data,dst=/var/lib/smeltr \
  --mount type=bind,src=/srv/smeltr/leader-secrets,dst=/run/secrets/smeltr \
  smeltr:<version>
```

Read the first-login credentials from the container output, then follow [First login](/docs/first-login). The bind mounts preserve state when you replace the container. The local `smeltr:<version>` tag above names the verified image; use the verified digest when deploying on other hosts. Smeltr writes only to those mounts, so the run command makes the root filesystem read-only, drops every Linux capability, and lets no process gain privileges. Use the [HTTPS proxy setup](/docs/https#proxy) before allowing remote browsers or workers to connect. A remote worker cannot reach this loopback-only example.

sections.heading: Run the leader on Kubernetes
sections.text:
# Run the leader on Kubernetes

This deployment runs the leader as one persistent replica. Smeltr does not provide a multi-replica or active/standby leader in this release. To run workers in the cluster, see [Enroll workers on Kubernetes](/docs/enroll-worker/kubernetes); to upgrade, see [Upgrade Smeltr](/docs/upgrade#kubernetes).

*Diagram: Smeltr on Kubernetes. An administrator reaches the ingress over HTTPS. The ingress forwards through a private ClusterIP Service to one leader pod. Workers fetch main and report status through the ingress and connect directly to sources and destinations. The leader and each worker have persistent storage.*

Dashed arrows show workers fetching main and reporting status through the ingress HTTPS address. The ingress forwards to the leader through a private ClusterIP Service. Dotted lines connect processes to persistent volumes: keep leader data and its secrets encryption key on separate volumes, and give each worker its own state volume. Back up the volumes. Sources and destinations may be inside or outside the cluster.

sections.heading: Requirements and image
sections.text:
## Requirements and image

Before deploying, provide:

-   A Kubernetes cluster with a default or explicitly selected StorageClass that supports ReadWriteOnce persistent volumes.
-   An ingress controller, DNS name and a TLS certificate that browsers and workers trust.
-   Nodes that can pull from `ghcr.io`, or a registry your organization mirrors the image into.

Pull the release's image, [verify its signature](/docs/install-leader/container#pull), and name it by that digest in the manifests: [a tag can move to a newer image](/docs/install-leader/container#latest), a digest cannot. Keep the digest and the release notes with the deployment. If you mirror the image, replace the whole image reference, registry and digest, in every manifest, the workers' included.

sections.heading: Deploy the leader
sections.text:
## Deploy the leader

Save the following as `smeltr-leader.yaml`. Replace the public hostname, image digest and storage requests for your environment. TLS terminates at the ingress, so Smeltr serves HTTP only inside the cluster.

The port default is 443, which is privileged, and the pod runs as user 1000 -- so `leader.http.port` names an unprivileged port instead. Set it in the file rather than the environment: the file only backfills variables that are unset, so an environment variable wins over it. `fsGroup` matches the image's group, without which the process cannot write a freshly provisioned volume.

The container's own `securityContext` meets the Kubernetes "restricted" Pod Security Standard: no privilege escalation, no capabilities, the runtime's default seccomp profile, and a read-only root filesystem. Smeltr writes only to its volumes, so nothing else needs to be writable.

The leader makes its data directory and the secrets encryption key's directory private to itself, and only a directory's owner can do that. A volume's root belongs to root whatever `fsGroup` says, so `data_dir` and `key` name directories inside their volumes, which the leader creates on first start.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: smeltr-leader
data:
  smeltr.toml: |
    [leader]
    enabled = true

    [leader.http]
    bind = "0.0.0.0"
    port = 4000
    public_origin = "https://smeltr.example.com"

    [leader.tls]
    enabled = false

    [leader.storage]
    data_dir = "/var/lib/smeltr/data"

    [leader.secrets]
    key = "/var/lib/smeltr-secrets/key/sealing.key"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: smeltr-leader
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: smeltr-leader
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 4000
      targetPort: http
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: smeltr-leader
spec:
  serviceName: smeltr-leader
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: smeltr-leader
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: smeltr-leader
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000
      containers:
        - name: smeltr
          image: ghcr.io/smeltr-sh/smeltr@sha256:REPLACE_WITH_DIGEST
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: [ALL]
            seccompProfile:
              type: RuntimeDefault
          env:
            - name: SMELTR_CONFIG_FILE
              value: /config/smeltr.toml
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 4000
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
            - name: leader-data
              mountPath: /var/lib/smeltr
            - name: leader-secrets
              mountPath: /var/lib/smeltr-secrets
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: smeltr-leader
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: leader-data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi
    - metadata:
        name: leader-secrets
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 1Gi
```

Apply it in the intended namespace, wait for `smeltr-leader-0`, and inspect its console for startup errors:

```
kubectl apply -f smeltr-leader.yaml
kubectl rollout status statefulset/smeltr-leader
kubectl logs smeltr-leader-0
```

A new leader prints the initial administrator username and one-time password to stderr. Treat the pod log as sensitive until you change that password. The data and sealing-key claims are deliberately separate; back them up as one matched recovery set.

sections.heading: Expose the leader
sections.text:
## Expose the leader

Create an Ingress using the same hostname as `leader.http.public_origin`. Controller annotations and certificate provisioning are cluster-specific:

```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: smeltr
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - smeltr.example.com
      secretName: smeltr-ingress-tls
  rules:
    - host: smeltr.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: smeltr-leader
                port:
                  name: http
```

Keep the Service as ClusterIP; only the ingress should be externally reachable. Configure the ingress to preserve the browser `Origin` header. Open the configured public origin URL, change the initial password, and create named administrator accounts. Because TLS terminates before Smeltr, workers use platform trust for the ingress certificate.

sections.heading: Logs & metrics
sections.text:
# Logs & metrics

Every Smeltr process keeps two accounts of itself: logs, which are timed, structured events, and metrics, which are counters and gauges. A worker's heartbeat carries both to the leader, and a bundle can route either through a pipeline to any destination.

sections.heading: Where logs and metrics go
sections.text:
## Where logs and metrics go

| Goes to | Logs | Metrics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The console | Every process writes one line per event to stderr. | — |
| The leader | Each worker sends its logs with its heartbeat. The leader keeps the newest 100,000 rows for the fleet. | Each worker sends its metrics with its heartbeat. The leader keeps them for 30 days, in coarser buckets as they age. |
| A destination | Through a [Smeltr logs source](/docs/sources/logs). | Through a [Smeltr metrics source](/docs/sources/metrics). |

The leader's copy is its operational view. Send logs and metrics you need to keep or search elsewhere to a destination.

sections.heading: Read them in the GUI
sections.text:
## Read them in the GUI

-   **Status → Logs** shows the fleet's logs, newest first. Choose severities, a worker, a group, a site, or text in the message, then choose **Search**. A severity is not a minimum: choose `error` and `warn` to see both. Select a row's fields to open them. The filters are in the page's address, so you can share a view as a link.
-   **Status** shows Rows in and out, Errors and Furthest from normal, from the metrics the heartbeat carries. Choose the window of Rows in and out: 15m, 60m, 24h, 7d or 30d. A gap in a line is missing history, not zero.

The leader cuts a log's site, message and each text field to 1,000 characters, and keeps its first 16 fields. A search cannot find what the leader cut. A worker out of contact with the leader holds the oldest 4,096 of its own events and the newest 2,048 from the process running its pipelines.

sections.heading: Send them to a destination
sections.text:
## Send them to a destination

1.  Select the worker group and work on a branch.
2.  Open Build → Sources, choose **\+ Add source**, choose **Local, each worker**, and then **smeltr logs** or **smeltr metrics**. Its settings are on the [Smeltr logs](/docs/sources/logs#settings) and [Smeltr metrics](/docs/sources/metrics#settings) pages.
3.  Connect it to a route, which sends its records through a pipeline to a [destination](/docs/destinations). [Follow the routing example](/docs/first-pipeline#route).
4.  [Review and deploy](/docs/review).

Each source gives the logs or metrics of the worker it runs on, covering both of that worker's processes: the `supervisor`, which talks to the leader, and the `runtime`, which runs its pipelines. Add one to every worker group you want to watch. Its records carry `__source.topic` `__smeltr_logs` or `__smeltr_metrics`.

sections.heading: What metrics exist
sections.text:
## What metrics exist

Smeltr has 74 metrics, grouped by what they measure: sources, processing, pipeline steps, destinations, memory, the worker and its logs. Each is a counter or a gauge with labels naming its subject. The [Smeltr metrics source](/docs/sources/metrics#how-it-works) lists every one, with its labels and what it measures, and shows the record each one makes.

sections.heading: Check for lost logs
sections.text:
## Check for lost logs

Writing a log never waits. A process with no room for an event drops it and counts it. These metrics carry a `process` label naming the process that wrote them.

| Metric | Measures |
| --- | --- |
| `smeltr_logs_written_total` | Log events written since the process started, by the `site` that wrote them. |
| `smeltr_logs_dropped_total` | Log events dropped for want of room since the process started. |
| `smeltr_logs_unread_total` | Log events a full logs reader's queue refused since the process started, one count per reader. |
| `smeltr_logs_undelivered_total` | Log events refused while the leader was out of contact, since the process started. |
| `smeltr_logs_unwritable_total` | Log events the console would not take since the process started. |

sections.heading: Change log verbosity
sections.text:
## Change log verbosity

A process collects logs at or above its log level, `info` unless you set it. The console, the leader and every Smeltr logs source get only what the process collects. To change it, see [Change log verbosity](/docs/operations#logs).

sections.heading: Operate and recover the fleet
sections.text: # Operate and recover the fleet

sections.heading: Read the running state
sections.text:
## Read the running state

1.  Open Status and check Online, Silent, Never heartbeated and Stopped workers, plus active warnings. A Stopped worker said it was stopping and raises no warning. An ephemeral worker leaves the list once it is gone.
2.  Select an affected worker and compare its reported Commit with the deployed main commit. Check its active issues and last-seen time. A heartbeat shows the worker recently contacted the leader. Check the running commit to see whether deployment succeeded.
3.  Trace the affected source, pipeline and destination in the map. Inspect throughput and owned partitions before changing thread limits. A source warns when its rows in the last 30 minutes fall outside its expected range, learned from the same time of day over the last week. Set how wide that range is in Admin → System → General.
4.  Use Logs to narrow by severity, worker, group, message and time. Preserve timestamps, commit IDs and error text for an incident report; omit secrets and sensitive sample records.

[How to compare the deployed and running commits →](/docs/git/configuration#verify)

sections.heading: Delivery and recovery
sections.text:
## Delivery and recovery

For a stalled destination, distinguish connection failures from refused records. Check the destination's errors, its action for refused records, and any destinations chosen to keep those records. Check how many records are waiting and how long the source will keep them. Fix the cause before replaying or changing policy.

Delivery covers [holding and retrying delivery](/docs/delivery#hold), [failures while saving refused records](/docs/delivery#dlq), and [recovering and replaying records](/docs/delivery#recovery).

sections.heading: Change log verbosity
sections.text:
## Change log verbosity

Set the top-level `log_level` before any TOML section header, or set SMELTR\_LOG\_LEVEL in the process environment, and restart the affected leader or worker:

```
log_level = "debug"

[leader]
enabled = true
```

Levels: error, warn, info (default), debug and trace. Use debug or trace briefly, then restore info. Do not share logs containing credentials or sensitive records.

sections.heading: Deploy and roll back configuration
sections.text:
## Deploy and roll back configuration

Save, test, review, then deploy. Deployment publishes configuration to `main`.

1.  For rollback, open Branches → History and identify the earlier known-good commit.
2.  Review its affected files and secret-version requirements. Rollback can affect the whole fleet, not only the group selected in the UI.
3.  Select **Roll back to here** and confirm **Deploy**. The fleet stays on that commit until **Release** on the same page.
4.  Check data flow in Status.

Do not rewrite the worker's local configuration manually. A configuration rollback is different from [downgrading the executable](/docs/upgrade#executable).

sections.heading: Leader outages and revoked workers
sections.text:
## Leader outages and revoked workers

These outage rules apply to workers running separately from the leader. In standalone mode, stopping or restarting the process affects both roles. New workers need a successful initial check-in before they start following main. Once initialized, workers keep running while the leader is unavailable. A worker that restarts runs nothing until the leader answers its first check-in. The default unreachable policy has no automatic stop; an explicit worker.heartbeat.stop\_after\_unreachable\_secs changes this behavior.

Ephemeral workers run on through a leader outage and stay enrolled: the leader counts a worker's silence only while it is up. One that stops during the outage keeps trying to say so while it stops. If it never gets through, the leader reports it silent, then forgets it once the leader has been back for longer than the Ephemeral workers setting.

Revoking a worker blocks leader access but does not stop its pipeline. To stop it immediately, stop or isolate the host and revoke its external credentials.

sections.heading: Startup configuration reference
sections.text:
