sections.heading: Google Cloud Storage
sections.text:
# Google Cloud Storage

Lists a prefix of one Cloud Storage bucket every poll interval, reads each new or changed object it finds, and splits it into records. Only one worker of each group reads this source at a time.

Use it for a bucket that cannot send Pub/Sub notifications, or one you may not configure. When the bucket can notify, use [Google Cloud Storage via Pub/Sub](/docs/sources/gcs-pubsub): every worker of the group reads, and nothing lists the bucket.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Reads each object under `app/` one line per record, signed in with the worker host's Application Default Credentials, and moves each object under `done/` once Smeltr delivers every record.

```
{
  "id": "bucket-export",
  "type": "gcsList",
  "bucket": "acme-logs",
  "prefix": "app/",
  "framing": "lines",
  "afterCommit": "move",
  "movePrefix": "done/"
}
```

![The GCS listing form on the Sources page: id bucket-export, bucket acme-logs, prefix app/, after commit move to done/, framing lines.](/gcs-list-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog, as it is added.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Choose what happens to an object once Smeltr delivers it, `afterCommit`. `keep` leaves the bucket as it is. `delete` and `move` drain it, so each listing finds only what is still to read.
-   Give the service account it reads as a role on the bucket. `keep` needs to list and read objects: Storage Object Viewer. `delete` also needs to delete them, and `move` to create them as well, since a move copies the object and then deletes it: Storage Object User covers both. See [Cloud Storage IAM roles](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles).
-   Choose how it signs in. With no key, it uses the worker host's [Application Default Credentials](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/application-default-credentials). Otherwise put a [service account key](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/keys-create-delete), the whole JSON file, in a [credential](/docs/secrets).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`bucket`  string required

The bucket's name, alone.

Examples:

- `acme-logs`
- `acme-audit-logs-prod`
- `logs.acme.example`

`prefix`  string default

Only objects whose name starts with it. It does not start with `/`. Empty is the whole bucket.

Examples:

- `app/`
- `cloudaudit.googleapis.com/activity/`
- `logs/2026/`

`serviceAccountKey`  credential default the host's Application Default Credentials

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding a service account's JSON key. The account needs to list and read the bucket, and to delete or create objects in it for `delete` and `move`.

Examples:

- `GCS_KEY`
- `{"secret": "gcs-key","version": 1}`

`format`  string default each payload is text, in `_raw`

How each payload becomes the record.

`avro`

Reads Avro files. Fields you don't declare are kept.

`fields`  list of fields default none

The Avro fields to read, each with a `name` and a `type` such as `i64` or `str`. Name a nested field with dots, such as `user.id`. Top-level fields you don't list are kept. Only with format `avro`.

Example:

- `[{"name": "user_id","type": "i64"},{"name": "user.name","type": "str"}]`

`framing`  string default `lines`

How an object becomes records.

`lines`

Gives one record per line, or per piece `lineBreaker` cuts.

`object`

Gives the whole object as one record, for a JSON document such as CloudTrail's that a pipeline unrolls.

`escapedLines`

Gives one record per line, unescaped as a `bytes` object destination wrote it.

`lineBreaker`  string default a record per line

With `lines` framing, and only then: where a record ends. Its first capture group is the break and is dropped: the bytes before it end a record, line ends and all, and the bytes after it start the next. What follows the group is kept, so the pattern can say how a record starts: `([\r\n]+)\d{4}-` keeps a stack trace with the line that logged it, and `</event>(\s*)` cuts XML events with no line ends between them. It needs a capture group and must not match the empty string.

Examples:

- `([\r\n]+)\d{4}-`
- `</event>(\s*)`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate.

Examples:

- `gcp-proxy`
- `corp-proxy`

`afterCommit`  string default `keep`

What it does with an object once every record is delivered.

`keep`

Leaves it and records it as read. Needs only read access, and costs a full listing per poll.

`delete`

Deletes it.

`move`

Copies it under `movePrefix` in place of `prefix`, then deletes it.

`movePrefix`  string default none

Where `move` puts an object, in place of `prefix`. Only with `move`, and outside `prefix`. It does not start with `/`, and ends in `/` when `prefix` does or is empty, and only then.

Examples:

- `done/`
- `archive/2026/`
- `processed/app/`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`start`  string default `everything`

What it reads first.

`everything`

Reads everything its first listing finds.

`new`

Reads only what arrives after its first listing. Needs `afterCommit` `keep`.

`pollIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

Seconds from the start of one listing to the start of the next. At least 1.

Examples:

- `300`
- `30`
- `3600`

`endpoint`  string default the key's own cloud

Cloud Storage's address, such as an emulator's.

Examples:

- `http://localhost:4443`
- `https://storage-acme.p.googleapis.com`

`encoding`  string default `auto`

How a record's bytes become `_raw`'s text: `auto`, `none`, or a WHATWG encoding label other than the replacement ones, such as `utf-8`, `utf-16le` or `shift_jis`.

`auto`

Detects each record's encoding.

`utf-8`

Decodes every record as UTF-8, as any other label decodes as its own encoding. Bytes that do not decode become U+FFFD.

`none`

Decodes nothing: the record has no `_raw`, and its payload is `__source.bytes` alone. A pipeline reads it as text with `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)`.

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.bucket` | `str` | The bucket, or Azure container, the record's object is in. |
| `__source.key` | `str` | The key, or Azure blob name, of the object the record was read from. |
| `__source.offset` | `i64` | The record's offset in its Kafka or Event Hubs partition, or its record number in its object, from 0. |
| `__source.bytes` | `bytes` | The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text. |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

Every `pollIntervalSecs`, counted from the start of the last listing, the source lists the objects whose names start with `prefix`. It reads each object the listing finds new, or changed since it last read it, and reads a changed object again whole. An empty object holds no record, and the source does not read it. The source decompresses a gzip, zstd, framed snappy or framed lz4 object first and reads any other as it is.

One worker of the group holds the source and reads it; every other worker running it reads nothing. The leader chooses the holder from the workers' heartbeats. The leader gives the hold to another worker after three heartbeat intervals without hearing from the holder, the holder's interval or the leader's, whichever is longer, and that worker resumes from the last progress the leader kept. That worker delivers again what the previous holder delivered after that progress.

With `afterCommit` `keep`, the progress is a **ledger**: each object read, by name and version. The holder records an object in it once Smeltr delivers every record of the object and reports it to the leader on its heartbeats, so the next holder reads only what is not in it. An object that leaves the bucket leaves the ledger. Every listing walks the whole prefix, so a large prefix costs a full listing each poll.

With `delete` or `move`, the bucket itself says what is still to read and there is no ledger. Once Smeltr delivers every record of an object, the source deletes it, or copies it to `movePrefix` in place of `prefix` and deletes the original. An object overwritten since the source read it stays in place, and the source reads it again. It deletes or moves an empty object unread.

`start` `everything` reads every object the first listing finds. `new` records the first listing as read and reads only what arrives or changes after it, so it needs `keep`.

The source's progress belongs to its name and to its bucket and prefix. Renamed, or pointed at another bucket or prefix, it starts afresh.

Once you remove the source and deploy, the leader forgets its progress, so a rollback that brings the source back starts it afresh.

An object handed out five times and never delivered is no longer offered until it changes. With `keep` it is recorded in the ledger as read; with `delete` or `move` it stays in the bucket. The worker log names it. With `delete` or `move` only the holder remembers it, so a restart or a new holder hands it out again.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Upload an object with a line you can recognize under the prefix, then find that line at the destination after the next listing. On the **Sources** page, the source's **worker** column names the worker holding it, and with `keep` how many objects its ledger holds. With `delete` or `move`, the object leaves the prefix once it is delivered.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**Nothing arrives**

Check that the object's name starts with `prefix`, and that the poll interval has passed. With `start` `new`, the source does not read what was there at the first listing until it changes. The worker log of the holder says why a listing failed, such as a missing role.

**The worker column is empty**

No worker holds the source: check that a worker of its group runs the deployment that has it.

**The holder was last heard some time ago**

The leader has not heard from that worker. It gives the hold to another worker after three heartbeat intervals without hearing from the holder, the holder's interval or the leader's, whichever is longer.

**An object stays under the prefix**

The source could not read it or could not delete it: check the role on the bucket and the worker log for the reason.

sections.heading: Google Cloud Storage via Pub/Sub
sections.text:
# Google Cloud Storage via Pub/Sub

Reads each object Cloud Storage announces on a Pub/Sub subscription, splits it into records, and acknowledges the message once Smeltr delivers every record.

A bucket's **Pub/Sub notifications** publish a message to a topic for each change to its objects. The source pulls those messages from a subscription on the topic and reads the objects they name, from whichever bucket each one names.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Reads each announced object one line per record, with the service account key from the worker-host variable `GCS_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY`.

```
{
  "id": "bucket-logs",
  "type": "gcsPubSub",
  "subscription": "projects/acme/subscriptions/gcs-events",
  "serviceAccountKey": "GCS_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY",
  "framing": "lines"
}
```

![The Google Cloud Storage via Pub/Sub form on the Sources page: id bucket-logs, its subscription, framing lines.](/gcs-pubsub-source-form-light.png)

A Google Cloud Storage via Pub/Sub source on the Sources page, signed in with the host's Application Default Credentials.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   [Configure Pub/Sub notifications](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/reporting-changes) for the bucket to a topic. Either payload format works, and you may limit the event type to `OBJECT_FINALIZE`.
-   [Create a pull subscription](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/create-subscription) on the topic, and give it a [dead-letter topic](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/handling-failures), so a message the source cannot use stops returning: one whose object it cannot read, or one that is not a Cloud Storage notification at all. Exactly-once delivery may be on or off.
-   Give the service account it reads as the Pub/Sub Subscriber role on the subscription and the Storage Object Viewer role on the buckets. See [Cloud Storage IAM roles](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-roles).
-   Choose how it signs in. With no key, it uses the worker host's [Application Default Credentials](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/application-default-credentials). Otherwise put a [service account key](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/keys-create-delete), the whole JSON file, in a [credential](/docs/secrets).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`subscription`  string required

The Pub/Sub subscription on the topic a bucket's notifications go to, named in full. Only `OBJECT_FINALIZE` notifications are read, at the generation they announce. Give the subscription a dead-letter policy: a message whose object cannot be read, such as an overwritten generation in a bucket without versioning, ends only through it.

Examples:

- `projects/acme/subscriptions/gcs-events`
- `projects/acme-logging-prod/subscriptions/smeltr-audit`

`serviceAccountKey`  credential default the host's Application Default Credentials

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding a service account's JSON key. The account needs to read the buckets and to consume the subscription.

Examples:

- `GCS_KEY`
- `{"secret": "gcs-key","version": 1}`

`format`  string default each payload is text, in `_raw`

How each payload becomes the record.

`avro`

Reads Avro files. Fields you don't declare are kept.

`fields`  list of fields default none

The Avro fields to read, each with a `name` and a `type` such as `i64` or `str`. Name a nested field with dots, such as `user.id`. Top-level fields you don't list are kept. Only with format `avro`.

Example:

- `[{"name": "user_id","type": "i64"},{"name": "user.name","type": "str"}]`

`framing`  string default `lines`

How an object becomes records.

`lines`

Gives one record per line, or per piece `lineBreaker` cuts.

`object`

Gives the whole object as one record, for a JSON document such as CloudTrail's that a pipeline unrolls.

`escapedLines`

Gives one record per line, unescaped as a `bytes` object destination wrote it.

`lineBreaker`  string default a record per line

With `lines` framing, and only then: where a record ends. Its first capture group is the break and is dropped: the bytes before it end a record, line ends and all, and the bytes after it start the next. What follows the group is kept, so the pattern can say how a record starts: `([\r\n]+)\d{4}-` keeps a stack trace with the line that logged it, and `</event>(\s*)` cuts XML events with no line ends between them. It needs a capture group and must not match the empty string.

Examples:

- `([\r\n]+)\d{4}-`
- `</event>(\s*)`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate.

Examples:

- `gcp-proxy`
- `corp-proxy`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`pubsubEndpoint`  string default the key's own cloud

Pub/Sub's address, such as an emulator's.

Examples:

- `http://localhost:8085`
- `https://pubsub-acme.p.googleapis.com`

`endpoint`  string default the key's own cloud

Cloud Storage's address, such as an emulator's.

Examples:

- `http://localhost:4443`
- `https://storage-acme.p.googleapis.com`

`encoding`  string default `auto`

How a record's bytes become `_raw`'s text: `auto`, `none`, or a WHATWG encoding label other than the replacement ones, such as `utf-8`, `utf-16le` or `shift_jis`.

`auto`

Detects each record's encoding.

`utf-8`

Decodes every record as UTF-8, as any other label decodes as its own encoding. Bytes that do not decode become U+FFFD.

`none`

Decodes nothing: the record has no `_raw`, and its payload is `__source.bytes` alone. A pipeline reads it as text with `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)`.

`visibilitySecs`  integer default `60`

Seconds a received message is held from other readers, its ack deadline. The source extends it while it reads the message's objects. 1 to 600.

Examples:

- `300`
- `30`
- `600`

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.bucket` | `str` | The bucket, or Azure container, the record's object is in. |
| `__source.key` | `str` | The key, or Azure blob name, of the object the record was read from. |
| `__source.offset` | `i64` | The record's offset in its Kafka or Event Hubs partition, or its record number in its object, from 0. |
| `__source.bytes` | `bytes` | The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text. |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

The source reads a notification from its message's attributes, so both payload formats read the same. It reads the object generation an `OBJECT_FINALIZE` notification names. The source acknowledges a notification of any other event, such as a deleted object, without reading anything. A message that is not a Cloud Storage notification stays on the subscription, like one whose object the source cannot read.

The source decompresses a gzip, zstd, framed snappy or framed lz4 object first and reads any other as it is.

The source extends a message's ack deadline while it reads the message's objects and Smeltr delivers them, and acknowledges the message once Smeltr commits every record of every object it names. It never acknowledges a message whose object it cannot read.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Upload an object with a line you can recognize to the bucket, then find that line at the destination. The subscription's unacknowledged message count returns to zero once Smeltr delivers it.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**Nothing arrives**

Check that the bucket has a notification configuration for this topic, that Cloud Storage's service agent may publish to the topic, and that the subscription is on the same topic.

**The same object is read again and again**

The source cannot read the object at the generation announced: check Storage Object Viewer on its bucket and the worker log for the reason. A dead-letter topic stops the repeats.

sections.heading: HEC receiver
sections.text:
# HEC receiver

Takes what Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC) clients send to its port, at Splunk's paths. It answers each request once every destination has its events.

OpenTelemetry Collectors, Fluent Bit, Vector, logging libraries and Splunk forwarders' `httpout` send to it. Every worker in the group listens on its port, and the sender, or a balancer in front of the workers, picks a worker for each request. Add workers to take more.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Takes HEC events on port 8088, over TLS with the [identity](/docs/secrets#identities) `receiver-tls`. Senders present the token held in the worker-host variable `HEC_TOKEN`.

```
{
  "id": "otel-logs",
  "type": "hecReceiver",
  "port": 8088,
  "tokens": {
    "otel": {
      "token": "HEC_TOKEN"
    }
  },
  "identity": "receiver-tls"
}
```

![The HEC receiver form on the Sources page: id otel-logs, port 8088, no tokens yet.](/hec-receiver-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog, before you add its token and identity.

A sender posts an event like this:

```
curl -H "Authorization: Splunk $HEC_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"event":"hello","host":"web-1","sourcetype":"demo"}' \
  https://workers.example.com:8088/services/collector/event
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Pick a port no other receiver in the group uses.
-   Decide how senders prove who they are: a token, a client certificate, or both. See [Tokens and certificates](#senders).
-   Put each token in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
-   Open the port on every worker, and give senders one address that reaches them all. See [Open its port](#port).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`port`  integer required

The port it listens on. Every worker of the group binds it, so no two receivers share one.

Examples:

- `8088`
- `8089`

`tokens`  map default none

Each token's name to its `token`, the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding it, and `acknowledgement`. A sender presents a token as `Authorization: Splunk <token>`, and any other request is refused with code `2`, `3` or `4`. With `acknowledgement` true, as Splunk's `useACK`, its senders name a channel and are answered at once with an `ackId`, and one that names none is refused code `10`; without it, a request is held until delivered and `/services/collector/ack` answers code `14`. A receiver with no token needs an `identity` with authorities, and holds every request.

Examples:

- `{"forwarders": {"token": "HEC_TOKEN"}}`
- `{"otel": {"token": "OTEL_HEC_TOKEN"},"vector": {"token": "VECTOR_HEC_TOKEN","acknowledgement": true}}`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`identity`  identity default plain HTTP

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it serves TLS under: its certificate and key. With authorities, a sender must present a certificate that chains to one of them.

Example:

- `receiver-tls`

`sourcetypes`  map default a record per line for every sourcetype

Maps each sourcetype to a lineBreaker, which splits text into multiple events. Its first capture group is the break and is dropped: the bytes before it end an event, line ends and all, and the bytes after it start the next. It needs a capture group and must not match the empty string. A raw request of a sourcetype not named, or named with no `lineBreaker` or with `([\r\n]+)`, is a record per line. The event endpoint's envelopes are not broken.

Example:

- `{"app:xml": {"lineBreaker": "</event>(\\s*)"}}`

`maxRequestBytes`  integer default `10485760`

The largest request body it reads, between 1024 and 67108864. A larger one is refused `413`. A body sent as gzip is held to it as it inflates.

Examples:

- `1048576`
- `67108864`

sections.heading: Paths it serves
sections.text:
## Paths it serves

**POST** `/services/collector`, `/services/collector/event`, `/services/collector/event/1.0`

The body holds HEC envelopes back to back, such as `{"event":"hello","host":"web-1"}`, with or without whitespace between them. Each envelope becomes one record: a string `event` becomes the record's text, and any other `event` its JSON. The envelope's `host`, `source`, `sourcetype`, `index`, `time` and `fields` become [`__source` fields](#fields-it-gives).

**POST** `/services/collector/raw`, `/services/collector/raw/1.0`

The body is text, one record per line. The query's `host`, `source`, `sourcetype`, `index` and `time` apply to every line, as in `/services/collector/raw?sourcetype=syslog`. Matching sourcetypes apply their linebreaker to replace the default of `([\r\n]+)`.

**POST** `/services/collector/s2s`

What a Splunk forwarder's `httpout` posts: S2S, as its `tcpout` sends to an [S2S receiver](/docs/sources/s2s-receiver), compressed. Each request is whole: its channels' events are broken by sourcetype as on the raw path, and the request ends each channel's last event. A record carries what the forwarder parsed, as an S2S receiver's does. See [Senders it takes](#clients).

**GET** `/services/collector/health`, `/services/collector/health/1.0`

Says whether the receiver takes requests. See [Health check](#health).

**POST** `/services/collector/ack`, `/services/collector/ack/1.0`

For a sender whose token has `acknowledgement`: takes `{"acks":[0,1]}` on a channel and answers `{"acks":{"0":true,"1":false}}`. See [Indexer acknowledgement](#acks).

`time` is Unix seconds, as a number or as text, and `fields` is a JSON object. The receiver inflates a body sent with `Content-Encoding: gzip`.

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

A field the sender did not set is null. `__source.remote` holds the IP address the request came from: the balancer's, when one is in front of the workers.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.remote` | `str` | The address of the sender that delivered the record to a receiver. |
| `__source.host` | `str` | The host a HEC sender filed the event under, or null where it named none. |
| `__source.source` | `str` | The source a HEC sender filed the event under, or null where it named none. |
| `__source.sourcetype` | `str` | The sourcetype a HEC sender filed the event under, or null where it named none. |
| `__source.index` | `str` | The index a HEC sender filed the event under, or an Elasticsearch client's bulk action named for its document; null where it named none. |
| `__source.time` | `datetime` | The time a sender gave the event, null otherwise. |
| `__source.fields` | `variant` | The indexed fields a HEC sender gave the event, or null where it gave none. Read one as text with `__source.fields.env as str`. |
| `__source.bytes` | `bytes` | The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text. |

sections.heading: Tokens and certificates
sections.text:
## Tokens and certificates

Anyone a receiver admits can put records into the group's pipelines, so a receiver needs `tokens`, an `identity` with authorities, or both. The leader refuses a receiver with neither.

-   **Tokens:** a sender presents one as `Authorization: Splunk <token>`, as HEC clients do. The receiver refuses any other request before reading its body. Without an identity, the token crosses the network in the clear, so use a token alone only behind a balancer that terminates TLS.
-   **Client certificates:** with an [identity](/docs/secrets#identities), the receiver serves TLS with the identity's certificate and key. If the identity has authorities, every connection, health checks included, must present a certificate that chains to one of them.

With both, a sender presents a certificate and a token.

sections.heading: What it answers
sections.text:
## What it answers

The receiver answers in HEC's JSON, `{"text": ..., "code": ...}`. The receiver answers success only once every destination has the request's events, so a sender that retries an unanswered request loses nothing.

**200**, code `0`

`{"text":"Success","code":0}`: every destination has the request's events.

**503**, code `9`, with `Retry-After`

The receiver is full, [blocked](/docs/delivery#hold) or stopping. It refuses a new request at once, and a stopping receiver answers every request it holds. A sender may send it again.

**401**, code `2` or `3`

The request has no token (`2`), or gives one other than as `Splunk <token>` (`3`).

**403**, code `4`

The receiver does not hold the token.

**400**, code `5`, `6`, `12`, `13` or `15`

The body is empty (`5`), is not HEC envelopes, or at `/services/collector/s2s` not whole S2S (`6`), has an envelope without an `event` (`12`) or with an empty one (`13`), or has `fields` that are not an object (`15`). `invalid-event-number` names the faulty envelope, counting from 0. The receiver refuses the whole body and takes none of its events.

**400**, code `10`, `11` or `14`

A sender whose token has `acknowledgement` named no channel (`10`), a channel is not 1 to 128 letters, digits, `-` and `_` (`11`), or a sender whose token lacks `acknowledgement` asked after an `ackId` (`14`, ACK is disabled).

**413**

The body, or what it inflates to, is larger than `maxRequestBytes`, or a forwarder's `httpout` request holds more than the receiver holds at once.

**408**

The sender took more than 30 seconds to send the whole body.

**415**

The body uses a `Content-Encoding` other than `gzip` or `identity`.

sections.heading: Indexer acknowledgement
Health check
sections.text:
## Health check

`GET /services/collector/health` answers 200 with code `17`, `HEC is healthy`, while the receiver takes requests, and 503 with code `18` while it is full, blocked or stopping. It needs no token. Point a balancer's health check or a readiness probe at it, so a busy worker gets no requests until it can take them. With an identity that has authorities, it needs a client certificate like any other request.

sections.heading: Senders it takes
sections.text:
## Senders it takes

Any sender that speaks HEC over HTTP works:

-   The OpenTelemetry Collector's `splunk_hec` exporter.
-   Fluent Bit's `splunk` output.
-   Vector's `splunk_hec_logs` sink. With indexer acknowledgements on, set [`acknowledgement`](#acks) on its token.
-   Logging libraries that send to HEC.

A Splunk universal or heavy forwarder's `httpout` posts S2S to `/services/collector/s2s`, presenting one of the receiver's tokens. The receiver holds each request until delivered, whatever its token's `acknowledgement`. A forwarder sending with `tcpout` needs an [S2S receiver](/docs/sources/s2s-receiver) instead.

```
# outputs.conf on the forwarder
[httpout]
httpEventCollectorToken = <a token of the receiver>
uri = https://workers.example.com:8088
```

This OpenTelemetry Collector configuration sends logs to the receiver, with `HEC_TOKEN` set in the collector's environment:

```
exporters:
  splunk_hec:
    token: ${env:HEC_TOKEN}
    endpoint: https://workers.example.com:8088/services/collector
    source: otel
    sourcetype: otel

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [splunk_hec]
```

sections.heading: Open its port
sections.text:
## Open its port

Every worker in the group listens on the receiver's `port`. Open that port to senders on each worker, and give senders one address that reaches them all, such as a balancer's. On a Unix host, a request sent while a worker deploys a new configuration waits, and the new configuration answers it.

-   On Kubernetes, add the port to the worker pods and put a Service in front of them: [Expose a receiver](/docs/enroll-worker/kubernetes#receiver).
-   On a host or in a container, open the host's firewall or publish the container's port: [Enroll a worker on a host](/docs/enroll-worker/host).

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

POST an event you can recognize, as in the [example](#example). The receiver answers `{"text":"Success","code":0}` once every destination has it. Then find it at the destination.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**The sender cannot connect**

Check that the port is open on every worker and that the sender's address reaches them. An identity with authorities refuses a connection without a certificate that chains to one of them.

**Every request gets code 2, 3 or 4**

Check that the sender presents `Authorization: Splunk <token>`, with a token one of the receiver's credentials holds.

**Every request gets code 9**

Check the source's status. A blocked receiver takes nothing until its destinations take records again. A full one takes more with more workers.

**Acks never read true, and the sender sends everything again**

The ack queries reach a different worker from the one that took the request. Keep each sender's connections on one worker at the balancer, or turn indexer acknowledgement off in both the sender and its token.

**The sender reports code 10 or 14**

The sender and its token disagree on indexer acknowledgement. Set `acknowledgement: true` on the token when the sender has it on, and leave it out when not.

**A Splunk forwarder cannot send to it**

A forwarder sending with `tcpout` needs an [S2S receiver](/docs/sources/s2s-receiver). Point it at one, or switch it to `httpout`, which this receiver takes at `/services/collector/s2s`.

**The same events arrive twice**

A sender that hears no answer may send the request again. Give the sender a timeout longer than its destinations take to deliver.

sections.heading: HTTP API
sections.text:
# HTTP API

Asks one address with a GET, or a POST of a fixed JSON body, every poll interval and reads what it answers as records.

Many services list their events or alerts at an address that answers a GET with JSON or lines of text, and some, such as Starlink's telemetry stream, answer a POST of what to send. This source polls such an address. A service that needs more than one request and its pages, such as Okta's System Log, has a source of its own.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Asks `api.example.com` for its events every minute. The source sends the `Authorization` header from the worker-host variable `API_TOKEN`, reads each element of the array at `/data` as one record, and follows the API's next links. It asks only for what happened since its last poll, through the `since` query parameter.

```
{
  "id": "events",
  "type": "httpApi",
  "url": "https://api.example.com/v1/events?limit=500",
  "credentials": {
    "Authorization": "API_TOKEN"
  },
  "records": "array",
  "recordsAt": "/data",
  "followLinks": true,
  "sinceParam": "since"
}
```

![The HTTP API form on the Sources page: id events, the URL, records array at /data, pages follow next links, since parameter since.](/http-api-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog, before you add its credential.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Find the address that lists what you want, and check that a GET to it, or a POST of the body it asks for, answers with JSON or lines of text. If the answer is a JSON object, note the [JSON pointer](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6901) to the array that holds the records, such as `/data`.
-   Find out how the API pages. This source follows a `Link: rel="next"` header. An API that pages another way gives one page per poll.
-   Find the query parameter that asks for what happened since a time, if the API has one. Without it, every poll reads everything again.
-   Put each secret header's whole value, such as `Bearer <token>`, in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
-   Allow workers to reach the address.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`url`  string required

The whole address it asks, `http://` or `https://`, with any fixed query parameters. It sends a credential only over `https://`, or to this host.

Examples:

- `https://api.example.com/v1/events?limit=500`
- `https://siem.example.com:8443/api/alerts`

`method`  string default `GET`

How it asks.

`GET`

Asks with a GET.

`POST`

POSTs `body` on every request, for an API that is asked by what it is sent.

`body`  json default a POST of nothing

The JSON every POST carries, sent as `application/json` unless `headers` names a `Content-Type`. Only with `method` `POST`.

Examples:

- `{"batchSize": 1000,"maxLingerMs": 15000}`
- `{"query": "status:open","limit": 500}`

`credentials`  map default none

Headers whose values are secret, each name to the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding its whole value, such as `Bearer <token>`.

Examples:

- `Authorization = API_TOKEN`
- `X-Api-Key = VENDOR_API_KEY`

`clientId`  string default none

The OAuth client it signs in as, with `clientSecret` or `privateKey`.

Examples:

- `smeltr`
- `0oa1b2c3d4`

`clientSecret`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the OAuth client's secret. Only with `clientId`.

Examples:

- `API_CLIENT_SECRET`
- `{"secret": "api-client","version": 1}`

`privateKey`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the client's RSA private key, PEM PKCS#8. Replaces `clientSecret`.

Examples:

- `API_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `{"secret": "api-key","version": 1}`

`tokenUrl`  string default none

Where the client's token is obtained. Replaces `issuer`.

Example:

- `https://auth.example.com/oauth2/token`

`issuer`  string default none

The OpenID issuer, exactly as the provider writes it. Replaces `tokenUrl`.

Example:

- `https://login.example.com/realms/acme`

`records`  string default `body`

Where an answer's records are.

`body`

Gives the whole answer as one record.

`lines`

Gives one record per line.

`array`

Gives one record per element of the JSON array at `recordsAt`.

`recordsAt`  string default the answer is the array

The [JSON pointer](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6901) to the array `array` reads, such as `/data` or `/result/items`. An answer with nothing there, or `null`, holds no records. Only with `records` `array`.

Examples:

- `/data`
- `/result/items`

`followLinks`  bool default `false`

Follows each answer's `Link: rel="next"` to the next page, within the same poll. A link to another host is refused, since the credentials go with every request.

`sinceParam`  string default every poll reads everything

The query parameter that asks for what happened since a time. Each poll sends it the start of the last poll whose records every destination took, in RFC 3339 UTC, such as `2026-10-10T13:00:00.000Z`.

Examples:

- `since`
- `start_time`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`headers`  map default none

Headers it sends on every request, each name to its value. Smeltr sets `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding` and `Host` itself.

Examples:

- `Accept = application/json`
- `Accept = application/json`
- `X-Tenant = acme`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate. Only on an `https://` URL.

Examples:

- `api-client`
- `corp-proxy`

`keyId`  string default none

The `kid` naming `privateKey`, for a client with several keys.

Example:

- `k1`

`scope`  string default none

The scope the client's token is asked for. Only with `clientId`.

Example:

- `read:events`

`start`  string default `everything`

What its first poll asks for.

`everything`

Asks without `sinceParam`, for everything the API gives.

`new`

Asks from the first poll's start. Needs `sinceParam`.

`sinceOverlapSecs`  integer default `0`

Seconds before the last poll's start that `sinceParam` asks from, for an API that records events late. What falls in the overlap is read twice. Only with `sinceParam`.

Examples:

- `30`
- `300`

`pollIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

Seconds from the start of one poll to the start of the next. At least 1.

Examples:

- `300`
- `60`

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

Each record holds its text exactly as the API wrote it. `__source.url` holds the address of the page the source read it from.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.url` | `str` | The address of the page an API source read the record from. |
| `__source.bytes` | `bytes` | The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text. |

sections.heading: Where it starts
sections.text:
## Where it starts

Without `sinceParam`, every poll asks for everything the API lists, so the source delivers the same records again on every poll. Leave the `sinceParam` parameter out of `url`; the source adds it whenever a poll asks from a time. A `start` of `new` needs `sinceParam`.

With `sinceParam`, the first poll asks for everything, or with `start` set to `new`, for what happens from the first poll onward. Every later poll asks from the start of the last poll every destination took, less `sinceOverlapSecs`. A restarted worker resumes there, so it skips nothing. An API that records events late needs an overlap, and the events in the overlap arrive twice.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

One worker of the group holds the source, and the leader keeps how far it got. Each poll sends a GET, or a POST of `body`, to `url` with the committed headers and the credential headers. With `followLinks`, the source follows each answer's next link within the same poll, but only to the same scheme, host and port, because the credentials go with every request. A page that holds no records, or a link back to a page the poll already asked, ends the poll.

The source holds each answer whole, up to 256 MiB, and asks for the next page only once every record of the last one is handed on. It follows no redirects. Each request has 120 seconds to connect and read its whole answer. A request that runs longer, or an answer larger than 256 MiB, fails.

When the API answers 429 or 503, the source waits as long as its `Retry-After` asks, up to an hour. After any other failure it asks the same page again, waiting one second at first and up to five minutes.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Find a record you know the API lists at the destination within a poll interval. On the Sources page, the **worker** column names the worker that holds the source.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

The worker log shows what the API answered.

**Refused the credentials (401 or 403)**

Check that the credential holds the header's whole value, such as `Bearer <token>`, and that the token may read the address.

**Answered 301 or 302, give the address it leads to**

Set `url` to the address the log names.

**The same records arrive on every poll**

Set `sinceParam` to the API's query parameter for a start time, or accept that each poll reads everything.

**Nothing arrives**

Check that `records` matches the answer, and with `array` that `recordsAt` points at the array. An answer with nothing at the pointer holds no records.

sections.text:

sections.heading: HTTP receiver
sections.text:
# HTTP receiver

Takes what senders POST to a path on its port, and answers each request once every destination has its records.

A webhook, a log shipper or a script sends to it. Every worker of the group listens on the receiver's port, and the sender, or a balancer in front of the workers, picks one worker for each request. More workers take more.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Takes what a CI system POSTs to `/hooks/ci` on port 8088, one record per line, over TLS with the [identity](/docs/secrets#identities) `receiver-tls`. Senders present the token held in the worker-host variable `HOOK_TOKEN`.

```
{
  "id": "ci-hooks",
  "type": "httpReceiver",
  "port": 8088,
  "path": "/hooks/ci",
  "tokens": {
    "ci": "HOOK_TOKEN"
  },
  "identity": "receiver-tls",
  "records": "lines"
}
```

![The HTTP receiver form on the Sources page: id ci-hooks, port 8088, path /hooks/ci, records one per line, no tokens yet.](/http-receiver-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog, before you add its token and identity.

A sender posts a file of lines like this:

```
curl --data-binary @build.log \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $HOOK_TOKEN" \
  https://workers.example.com:8088/hooks/ci
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Pick a port no other receiver of the group listens on.
-   Decide how senders prove who they are: a token, a client certificate, or both. See [Tokens and certificates](#senders).
-   Put each token in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
-   Open the port on every worker of the group, and give senders one address that reaches them. See [Open its port](#port).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`port`  integer required

The port it listens on. Every worker of the group binds it, so no two receivers share one.

Examples:

- `8088`
- `9880`

`path`  string default `/`

The path senders POST to. It starts with `/` and holds no `?`, `#`, `:`, `*` or space. Not `/health`, where it answers health checks.

Examples:

- `/hooks/github`
- `/ingest`

`tokens`  map default none

Each token's name to the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding it. A sender presents one as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, and any other request is refused `401`. A receiver with no token needs an `identity` with authorities.

Examples:

- `ci = HOOK_TOKEN`
- `github = GITHUB_HOOK_TOKEN`
- `jenkins = JENKINS_HOOK_TOKEN`

`records`  string default `body`

Where a request body's records are.

`body`

Gives the whole body as one record.

`lines`

Gives one record per line.

`array`

Gives one record per element of the JSON array at `recordsAt`.

`recordsAt`  string default the body is the array

The [JSON pointer](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6901) to the array `array` reads. A body with no array there is refused `400`. Only with `records` `array`.

Examples:

- `/events`
- `/records`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`identity`  identity default plain HTTP

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it serves TLS under: its certificate and key. With authorities, a sender must present a certificate that chains to one of them.

Example:

- `receiver-tls`

`maxRequestBytes`  integer default `10485760`

The largest request body it reads, between 1024 and 67108864. A larger one is refused `413`. A body sent as gzip is held to it as it inflates.

Examples:

- `1048576`
- `67108864`

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

Each record holds its text exactly as the sender wrote it. `__source.remote` holds the IP address the request came from: the balancer's, when one is in front of the workers.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.remote` | `str` | The address of the sender that delivered the record to a receiver. |
| `__source.bytes` | `bytes` | The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text. |

sections.heading: Tokens and certificates
sections.text:
## Tokens and certificates

Whoever a receiver admits puts records into the group's pipelines, so a receiver needs `tokens`, an `identity` with authorities, or both. A receiver with neither is refused at load.

-   **Tokens:** a sender presents one as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Any other request is refused 401 before any of its body is read. Without an identity, the token crosses the network in the clear, which suits a receiver behind a balancer that ends TLS for it.
-   **Client certificates:** under an [identity](/docs/secrets#identities), the receiver serves TLS with the identity's certificate and key. When the identity has authorities, every connection must present a certificate that chains to one of them, health checks included.

With both, a sender presents a certificate and a token.

sections.heading: What it answers
sections.text:
## What it answers

The receiver answers 200 only once every destination has the request's records, so a sender that retries an unanswered request loses nothing.

**200**

Every destination has the request's records.

**503** with `Retry-After`

The receiver is full, [blocked](/docs/delivery#hold), or stopping. It answers a new request at once, and a stopping receiver answers every request it holds. A sender may send it again.

**401**

The request presents none of the receiver's tokens.

**400**

The body does not read as `records` says, such as one with no array at `recordsAt`. It is refused whole: none of its records is taken.

**413**

The body, or what it inflates to, is larger than `maxRequestBytes`.

**415**

The body uses a `Content-Encoding` other than `gzip` or `identity`. The receiver inflates a gzip body itself.

**408**

The sender did not send the whole body within 30 seconds.

sections.heading: Health check
sections.text:
## Health check

`GET /health` on the receiver's port answers 200 while the receiver takes requests and 503 while it is full, blocked or stopping. It needs no token, and says only whether the receiver takes requests. Point a balancer's health check or a readiness probe at it, so a busy worker gets no requests until it can take them. Under an identity with authorities it needs a client certificate like any other request.

sections.heading: Open its port
sections.text:
## Open its port

Every worker of the group listens on the receiver's `port`. Open that port to senders on each worker, and give senders one address that reaches all of them, such as a balancer's. On a Unix host, a request sent while a worker deploys a new configuration waits for it and is answered by the new one.

-   On Kubernetes, add the port to the worker pods and a Service in front of them: [Expose a receiver](/docs/enroll-worker/kubernetes#receiver).
-   On a host or in a container, open the host's firewall or publish the container's port: [Enroll a worker on a host](/docs/enroll-worker/host).

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

POST a record you can recognize, as in the [example](#example). The receiver answers 200 once every destination has it. Find it at the destination.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**The sender cannot connect**

Check that the port is open on every worker and that the sender's address reaches them. An identity with authorities refuses a connection with no certificate that chains to them.

**Every request is answered 401**

Check that the sender presents `Authorization: Bearer <token>` with a token one of the receiver's credentials holds.

**Every request is answered 503**

Check the source's status. A blocked receiver takes nothing until its destinations take records again. A full one takes more with more workers.

**The same records arrive twice**

A sender that hears no answer may send the request again. Give the sender a timeout longer than its destinations take to deliver.

sections.text:
## See also

-   [Sources](/docs/sources)
-   [HTTP API source](/docs/sources/http-api)
-   [Credentials](/docs/secrets)
-   [Delivery](/docs/delivery)

sections.heading: Kafka
sections.text:
# Kafka

Reads records from Kafka topics, as they arrive or as a range of existing records.

Workers reading in one **consumer group** share the work, and a source in a different group reads the same records independently.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Reads UTF-8 records from a plaintext test broker. Replace `localhost:9092` with an address reachable from the worker; localhost means the worker's own host.

```
{
  "id": "events-in",
  "type": "kafka",
  "brokers": "localhost:9092",
  "topics": [
    "smeltr-events-in"
  ],
  "encoding": "utf-8"
}
```

![The Kafka form on the Sources page: id events-in, broker localhost:9092, topic smeltr-events-in.](/kafka-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog.

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Create the input topic.
-   Leave the group id blank unless this source needs offsets of its own. Blank reads as its worker group's consumer group, `smeltr.<worker group>`, so every worker group reads every record and rebalances only among its own workers. The leader refuses two sources that read one topic in one consumer group on the same brokers.
-   Allow workers to reach the initial broker addresses you enter and every broker address Kafka returns when they connect.
-   Give the Kafka account permission to read the topics and use the consumer group.
-   For an authenticated broker, configure [Kafka security](/docs/secrets#kafka). Select a [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) for a private CA or a client certificate.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`brokers`  string required

The brokers a worker first connects to, `host:port`, separated by commas.

Examples:

- `kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092`
- `kafka.example.com:9093`
- `10.0.1.15:9092,10.0.2.15:9092,10.0.3.15:9092`

`topics`  list of strings required

The topics to read. One that starts with `^` is a [regular expression](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/#syntax): it reads every topic whose whole name matches it, including topics created later, which are read within 30 seconds. A matching topic that another source already reads in the same group is left to that source.

Examples:

- `orders`
- `orders`
- `payments`
- `refunds`
- `^orders-.*`

`start`  position default `{"type": "earliest"}`

Where this source reads from. Changing it will move offsets to the new position.

`earliest`

Reads from the oldest record each partition holds.

`latest`

Reads only what is written after it starts.

`timestamp`

Reads from the first record at or after `millis`, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

`stop`  position default never

When to stop reading. Absent, never stops.

`timestamp`

Stops at the first record at or after `millis`, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

`format`  string default each payload is text, in `_raw`

How each payload becomes the record.

`avro`

Reads Avro messages using the schema registry. Fields you don't declare are kept.

`schemaRegistry`  object default none

The schema registry that holds your Avro schemas. Set `url`. If the registry needs a sign-in, also set `username` and `password`. Needed for format `avro`.

Examples:

- `{"url": "https://registry.example.com"}`
- `{"url": "https://registry.example.com","username": "smeltr","password": {"secret": "registry","version": 1}}`

`fields`  list of fields default none

The Avro fields to read, each with a `name` and a `type` such as `i64` or `str`. Name a nested field with dots, such as `user.id`. Top-level fields you don't list are kept. Only with format `avro`.

Example:

- `[{"name": "user_id","type": "i64"},{"name": "user.name","type": "str"}]`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a private CA or a client certificate. Without one, no certificate is offered and the public roots, Mozilla's and the host's, are trusted.

Examples:

- `kafka-client`
- `kafka-mtls`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`groupId`  string default smeltr.<worker group>

The consumer group. Readers in one group share the work and resume from the group's saved positions. Set one only when this source needs positions of its own. The leader refuses two sources that read one topic in one consumer group on the same brokers.

Example:

- `smeltr-replay`

`fetchBytes`  size default 64 MiB

How much fetched input may wait in memory before it is processed. 4 MiB to 512 MiB.

Examples:

- `128 MiB`
- `16 MiB`
- `256 MB`

`encoding`  string default `auto`

How a record's bytes become `_raw`'s text: `auto`, `none`, or a WHATWG encoding label other than the replacement ones, such as `utf-8`, `utf-16le` or `shift_jis`.

`auto`

Detects each record's encoding.

`utf-8`

Decodes every record as UTF-8, as any other label decodes as its own encoding. Bytes that do not decode become U+FFFD.

`none`

Decodes nothing: the record has no `_raw`, and its payload is `__source.bytes` alone. A pipeline reads it as text with `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)`.

`properties`  map default none

Other Kafka client properties, each name to its value. See [Kafka security](/docs/secrets#kafka). A property Smeltr sets itself, such as `bootstrap.servers`, is refused, and a secret one belongs in `credentials`.

Examples:

- `security.protocol = SASL_SSL`
- `security.protocol = SASL_SSL`
- `sasl.mechanism = SCRAM-SHA-512`
- `sasl.username = smeltr`

`credentials`  map default none

Kafka client properties whose values are secret, each name to the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding its value.

Examples:

- `sasl.password = KAFKA_PASSWORD`
- `sasl.oauthbearer.client.secret = KAFKA_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.topic` | `str` | The Kafka topic, or event hub, the record came from. A metrics record carries `__smeltr_metrics` and a logs record `__smeltr_logs`. |
| `__source.partition` | `i64` | The Kafka or Event Hubs partition the record came from. |
| `__source.offset` | `i64` | The record's offset in its Kafka or Event Hubs partition, or its record number in its object, from 0. |
| `__source.time` | `datetime` | The time a sender gave the event, null otherwise. |
| `__source.headers` | `variant` | The Kafka record's headers, each key to its value as text. A key the record repeats holds its last value, and a header with no value is not there. Read one as text with `__source.headers.trace as str`. |
| `__source.bytes` | `bytes` | The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text. |

sections.heading: Where it starts and stops
sections.text:
## Where it starts and stops

`start` and `stop` apply to each partition of every topic the source reads. The group's workers share the partitions, whatever the start and the stop.

-   **Start.** Where the source reads from: beginning, end, or a specific time.
-   **Stop.** When to stop reading: never, or a specific time. Once every partition has reached it, the source waits, idle, until it is changed.
-   Progress is saved and restarted sources continue from where they left off.

To read the topics as a stream, leave both out. To read between 4 and 8 AM yesterday, start at 4 AM and stop at 8 AM.

sections.heading: Moving a source
sections.text:
### Moving a source

To reread or skip records, change `start` and deploy. Each partition moves there once, then reads on.

-   Setting the same `start` again moves nothing.
-   Rolling back a deploy does not move the source back.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

Smeltr manages the consumer's commits. The extra properties refuse Kafka settings Smeltr sets itself, such as auto-commit.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Produce a record you can recognize to the input topic, then find it at the destination. The [tutorial's delivery check](/docs/first-pipeline#verify) shows the commands.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**Kafka connects, then times out**

Check the brokers' advertised addresses from the worker host, plus DNS, firewall rules and TLS names.

**Authentication or authorization fails**

Check the security protocol, mechanism, secret availability, and topic and group permissions. See [Kafka security](/docs/secrets#kafka).

**Old records do not replay**

Check the group's saved positions and the topic's retention. To read old records again, [move](#move) the source.

# Smeltr logs

sections.text:
# Smeltr metrics

Gives the worker's own metrics as records, one per series every bucket. It reads locally and needs no credentials.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Gives a record per series every 10 seconds. A shorter bucket gives records more often.

```
{
  "id": "worker-metrics",
  "type": "metrics",
  "bucketSeconds": 10
}
```

![The smeltr metrics form on the Sources page: id worker-metrics, bucket seconds 10.](/metrics-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog, as it is added.

sections.text:

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`bucketSeconds`  integer required

Seconds per bucket, at least 1. The form starts at 10.

Examples:

- `10`
- `1`
- `60`

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.topic` | `str` | The Kafka topic, or event hub, the record came from. A metrics record carries `__smeltr_metrics` and a logs record `__smeltr_logs`. |
| `__source.bytes` | `bytes` | The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text. |

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

Each bucket, the source gives one record per series. `metric` holds the series' name, each label is a string field of its own, `value` holds the number, and `ts` holds the time of the bucket in Unix epoch milliseconds. Every record's `__source.topic` is `__smeltr_metrics`.

```
{
  "metric": "smeltr_rows_polled_total",
  "source": "orders-west",
  "thread": "reader-0",
  "value": 1250,
  "ts": 1791100800000
}
```

A counter's value is how much it grew since its last record, and a counter that did not grow gives no record. A gauge gives its current value every bucket. The first bucket comes at once and holds everything counted since the worker started. A bucket larger than the source's batch limits is cut, and the counts cut from it are lost.

Every record carries `thread`, the worker thread that counted it: `reader-N` for a source, `transform-N` for a pipeline thread, `egress-N` for a destination, `deploy` for the deployment as a whole, and `capture` for a sample capture. The `source`, `destination`, `route`, `pipeline` and `function` labels hold the names they have in the deployment.

| Metric | Kind | Labels | Measures |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sources |
| `smeltr_rows_polled_total` | counter | `source` | Records the source returned. |
| `smeltr_bytes_polled_total` | counter | `source` | Bytes of those records. |
| `smeltr_tick_poll_seconds_total` | counter | `source` | Seconds spent waiting on the source for records. |
| `smeltr_tick_idle_polls_total` | counter | `source` | Polls that returned no records. |
| `smeltr_commits_total` | counter | `source` | Offset commits the source accepted. |
| `smeltr_commits_dropped_total` | counter | `source` | Offset commits that failed and were let go. The next commit covers their records. |
| `smeltr_source_in_flight` | gauge | `source` | Batches read and not yet committed. |
| `smeltr_source_lag` | gauge | `source`,`topic`,`partition` | What the source has yet to finish. Kafka: records in the partition past the group's committed offset. SQS and Azure Storage Queue: messages on the queue, held ones included, as partition 0 of a topic named for the queue. |
| `smeltr_source_messages_finished_total` | counter | `source` | Queue messages the source finished with: every object they named read and committed. A queue's lag drains at this rate. |
| `smeltr_source_blocked` | gauge | `source` | 1 while the source is stopped on a record it may not pass: an exception or refusal answered `block`, or nothing could process or deliver the record. 0 once it reads again. |
| `smeltr_source_dropped_total` | counter | `source` | Records the source let go because it had no room for them. A syslog receiver over UDP counts each datagram that arrives while it is full or blocked. |
| `smeltr_source_full_total` | counter | `source` | Times a receiver had no memory left for what a sender offered: a request it answered busy, or a connection it stopped reading. Its memory, not its sender, set the pace. |
| `smeltr_source_poll_failures_total` | counter | `source` | Reads of the source that failed. The source is read again after a wait, and what it has not delivered stays uncommitted there. |
| `smeltr_source_refused_total` | counter | `source`,`reason` | Requests a receiver refused, by reason: token, unreadable, too\_large, unsupported, late, busy or other. |
| Processing |
| `smeltr_tick_batches_total` | counter | `source` | Batches run through routes and pipelines. |
| `smeltr_tick_process_seconds_total` | counter | `source` | Seconds spent running those batches. |
| `smeltr_tick_flush_seconds_total` | counter | `source` | Seconds spent handing processed batches to destinations. |
| `smeltr_batches_waiting_for_room_total` | counter | `source` | Hand-offs that waited because a destination's queue was full. |
| `smeltr_batches_poisoned_total` | counter | `source` | Batches a pipeline could not finish because it crashed on them. |
| `smeltr_batches_dlq_total` | counter | `source`,`destination` | Batches no pipeline could process, sent whole to a dead-letter destination. |
| `smeltr_route_matched_total` | counter | `source`,`route` | Records the route's condition matched. |
| `smeltr_rows_unmatched_total` | counter | `source`,`cause` | Records that met Unmatched. `cause` is `route` (no route matched) or `rule` (no delivery rule of its route took it). |
| `smeltr_rows_dropped_total` | counter | `source`,`reason` | Records let go. `reason` is `unmatched` (Unmatched answered drop), `exception` (an exception answered drop), `unprocessable` (no pipeline could process it) or `rejected` (a destination refused it for good). |
| `smeltr_rows_dlq_over_budget_total` | counter | `source` | Records sent to a dead-letter destination because one alone does not fit the memory budget. |
| Pipeline steps |
| `smeltr_function_calls_total` | counter | `pipeline`,`function` | Instructions the step ran. A step can compile to several, and one inside a loop counts on every pass. |
| `smeltr_function_seconds_total` | counter | `pipeline`,`function` | Seconds the step ran. A step inside a loop is not timed: its time goes to the loop step. |
| `smeltr_rows_dropped_total` | counter | `pipeline`,`function` | Records the step removed. |
| `smeltr_rows_errored_total` | counter | `pipeline`,`function`,`kind` | Records the step gave an exception, by its kind. |
| `smeltr_rows_in_total` | counter | `pipeline`,`function` | Records in each batch that reached a loop step, whether its condition holds for them or not. |
| `smeltr_rows_out_total` | counter | `pipeline`,`function` | Records the loop step's condition let in. |
| Destinations |
| `smeltr_rows_sent_total` | counter | `destination` | Records handed to the destination. |
| `smeltr_rows_without_doc_id_total` | counter | `destination` | Records sent to a `dedupe` or `overwrite` destination with no document ID. |
| `smeltr_rows_send_failed_total` | counter | `destination` | Records in a hand-over that failed. They are sent again. |
| `smeltr_flushes_total` | counter | `destination` | Hand-overs the destination finished. |
| `smeltr_rows_delivered_total` | counter | `destination` | Records in batches the destination acknowledged, including records it refused within them. |
| `smeltr_bytes_delivered_total` | counter | `destination` | Bytes of those records. |
| `smeltr_rows_rejected_total` | counter | `source`,`destination` | Records the destination refused for good. |
| `smeltr_rows_salvaged_total` | counter | `destination` | Refused records a dead-letter destination took. |
| `smeltr_rows_lost_total` | counter | `destination` | Refused records with nowhere left to go. |
| `smeltr_destination_healthy` | gauge | `destination` | 1 while the destination takes writes, 0 after a failed send. |
| `smeltr_destination_stalls_total` | counter | `destination` | Failed sends that marked the destination unhealthy. |
| `smeltr_destination_in_flight` | gauge | `destination` | Requests the destination may have open at once. |
| `smeltr_destination_held_rows` | gauge | `destination` | Rows the destination refused and keeps to send again. |
| `smeltr_destination_open_bytes` | gauge | `destination` | Bytes in a destination pending an upload. |
| `smeltr_destination_queue_bytes` | gauge | `destination` | Bytes waiting in the destination's queue. |
| `smeltr_destination_queue_budget_bytes` | gauge | `destination` | The most bytes the destination's queue holds. |
| `smeltr_destination_unwritten_total` | counter | `destination`,`kind` | What the store took but said it did not store as sent, in its own units: a Prometheus remote\_write 2.0 store's samples, histograms and exemplars, and documents an Elasticsearch failure store took. |
| `smeltr_destination_throttled_seconds_total` | counter | `destination` | Seconds the destination was held back because it was asked to slow down: by its brokers for Kafka, and in the backoff after a throttled answer for an HTTP destination (Elasticsearch, Splunk HEC, HTTP, Prometheus). Summed over concurrent requests. |
| `smeltr_destination_buffered_bytes` | gauge | `destination` | Bytes waiting inside the Kafka client. Kafka only. |
| `smeltr_destination_rtt_seconds` | gauge | `destination` | Mean round trip to the brokers in seconds. Kafka only. |
| Memory |
| `smeltr_memory_budget_bytes` | gauge |  | The worker's memory budget. 0 under `thread=deploy` means none. |
| `smeltr_memory_peak_bytes` | gauge |  | The most memory the worker's threads have held at once. Present only with a memory budget. |
| `smeltr_memory_splits_total` | counter | `source` | Batches split in half to fit the memory budget. |
| `smeltr_memory_abandoned_seconds_total` | counter | `source` | Seconds spent on attempts given up for memory. |
| `smeltr_destination_pool_bytes` | gauge |  | Bytes the destination queues sized to the worker's memory have borrowed above their reserves. At smeltr\_destination\_pool\_budget\_bytes, memory is what holds them back. |
| `smeltr_destination_pool_budget_bytes` | gauge |  | The most the destination queues sized to the worker's memory may borrow above their reserves, together. |
| `smeltr_receiver_pool_bytes` | gauge |  | Bytes the receivers sized to the worker's memory have borrowed from the pool they share. At smeltr\_receiver\_pool\_budget\_bytes, memory is what holds them back. |
| `smeltr_memory_allocated_bytes` | gauge |  | Bytes the worker's runtime has allocated and not freed. What its resident memory holds above this is what the allocator keeps of what was freed, and what C libraries allocate themselves. |
| `smeltr_receiver_pool_budget_bytes` | gauge |  | The most the receivers sized to the worker's memory may borrow above their reserves, together. |
| `smeltr_memory_part_bytes` | gauge | `part`,`source`,`destination` | The most one part of the deployment may hold, one sample per part: what `part` names, under the source or destination it belongs to when it belongs to one. Together they are what the worker's memory must fit. |
| `smeltr_source_held_bytes` | gauge | `source` | Bytes a source holds that its reader has not taken. |
| `smeltr_source_lane_bytes` | gauge | `source` | Bytes waiting between a source's reader and transform. |
| `smeltr_process_memory_bytes` | gauge | `process` | Bytes of memory a worker process holds: the supervisor's or the runtime's. |
| Worker |
| `smeltr_worker_threads_budget` | gauge |  | The most threads the deployment may use. |
| `smeltr_worker_slice_bytes` | gauge |  | The raw bytes of a batch a transform thread runs at once, sized to the CPU's cache. |
| `smeltr_worker_readers` | gauge |  | Reader threads, one per source. |
| `smeltr_worker_transform_threads` | gauge |  | Threads running pipelines. |
| `smeltr_worker_egress_threads` | gauge |  | Threads sending to destinations. |
| `smeltr_capture_records_total` | counter | `source` | Records a sample capture read. Its `source` label holds the source's name. |
| Logs |
| `smeltr_logs_written_total` | counter | `process`,`site` | Log events written since the process started, by the `site` that wrote them. |
| `smeltr_logs_dropped_total` | counter | `process` | Log events dropped for want of room since the process started. |
| `smeltr_logs_unread_total` | counter | `process` | Log events a full logs reader's queue refused since the process started, one count per reader. |
| `smeltr_logs_undelivered_total` | counter | `process` | Log events refused while the leader was out of contact, since the process started. |
| `smeltr_logs_unwritable_total` | counter | `process` | Log events the console would not take since the process started. |
