sections.heading: MySQL and MariaDB
sections.text:
# MySQL and MariaDB

Runs a query you write against a MySQL or MariaDB database every poll, and reads each row of its result as one record.

Use it for what an application keeps in its own tables, such as an audit table or a sign-in history. The source reads only what your query returns, and its mode decides which of those rows are new. One source kind serves both servers.

sections.heading: Example
Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Create a user that can connect from the workers' addresses and read the tables the query reads, and nothing more. See [CREATE USER](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/create-user.html) and [GRANT](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/grant.html) for MySQL, or [CREATE USER](https://mariadb.com/kb/en/create-user/) and [GRANT](https://mariadb.com/kb/en/grant/) for MariaDB.
-   Allow workers to reach the server's port.
-   With `tls` `require`, the default, the server needs encrypted connections on, with a certificate that names `host`. See [MySQL: Using encrypted connections](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/using-encrypted-connections.html) or [MariaDB: Secure connections overview](https://mariadb.com/kb/en/secure-connections-overview/). For a certificate from a private authority, give the source a [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) that trusts it.
-   Put the password in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
-   For Incrementing or Updated at, index the first field of `position`, so each poll reads only the new rows. See [CREATE INDEX](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/create-index.html).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

The form on the Sources page asks for the connection first, then the query. Its **Run** button runs the query on a worker of the group and shows the rows it read, so you choose the mode and the fields from the real result. The source also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`host`  string required

The database server's host name or address.

Examples:

- `db.internal`
- `10.4.0.12`

`database`  string required

The database the query runs in.

Examples:

- `auth`
- `shop`

`user`  string required

The user it connects as. Give it read access and nothing more: the query runs in a read-only transaction, but only the user's own grants keep a source from writing.

Example:

- `smeltr_reader`

`password`  credential default none, for a server that asks for no password

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the user's password.

Examples:

- `MYSQL_PASSWORD`
- `{"secret": "auth-db-reader","version": 1}`

`query`  string required

A `SELECT` or a `WITH`, with no `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT` of its own: the statement around it orders by the position and sets the batch. `:last.<field>` is the value that field held in the last row sent, `NULL` before the first, for a filter the statement's own cannot reach, such as one inside a `GROUP BY`. The statement still reads past the last row sent, so the filter keeps the last value (`>=`) and rows sharing it are not lost.

Examples:

- `SELECT event_id, occurred_at, user_name FROM auth.events`
- `SELECT event_id, occurred_at, user_name FROM auth.events WHERE (:last.occurred_at IS NULL OR occurred_at >= :last.occurred_at)`

`mode`  mode required

How it knows a row is due. `position` is the field rows are read in the order of, then the fields that tell apart rows with the same value in it. A position that starts with a datetime waits `settleSecs` (default 30) behind the database's clock for late commits. A source with no progress begins where `start` says: `"now"` (default) at the largest position the query returns on its first poll, `"beginning"` at every row, or `"from"` at `startFrom`, an integer or an ISO 8601 time with its offset.

`incrementing`

Each row once, by a field that only grows as rows are added: an id, or the time it was inserted. Reads only the new rows.

`updatedAt`

Each row when it is added and again each time it changes, by a datetime every insert and update sets. A deleted row is not seen.

`comparing`

Each row when its `key` is new or its values changed, by reading the whole result every poll. Up to a million rows; the leader keeps an entry for each.

`everyPoll`

The whole result every poll. Nothing is remembered.

`fields`  list of fields required

Each field of the record: the result column of the same `name`, and its `type` as a pipeline spells one, such as `i64`, `datetime`, `str`, `bytes` or `array<str>`. A column the fields do not name is not read.

Example:

- `[{"name": "event_id","type": "i64"},{"name": "occurred_at","type": "datetime"},{"name": "user_name","type": "str"}]`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`port`  integer default `3306`

The server's port.

Examples:

- `3307`
- `6033`

`tls`  string default `require`

Whether the connection is encrypted.

`require`

Encrypts, and verifies the server's certificate and its name.

`disable`

Sends everything in the clear, the password too.

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under: the authorities it trusts for the server's certificate, and a certificate to present. Only with `tls` `require`.

Examples:

- `auth-db-client`
- `corp-ca`

`pollIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

Seconds from the start of one poll to the start of the next. At least 1. A poll that reads a full batch reads the next at once.

Examples:

- `30`
- `300`

`batch`  integer default `5000`

The most rows one poll reads by a position. With no field after the first in `position`, a full poll leaves its last rows sharing one value to the next, which reads up to twice `batch` when they fill a poll; past that, the rest of the rows sharing that value are skipped with a warning. In `everyPoll`, a result with more fails the poll. Between 1 and 100000.

Examples:

- `1000`
- `20000`

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

Each record is one row. It holds a field for each entry of `fields`, read from the result column of the same name and held as the type the entry declares. A column no entry names is not read.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.database` | `str` | The database an SQL source read the record from, as `host:port/database`. |

sections.heading: How it finds new rows
sections.text:
## How it finds new rows

`mode` says which rows a poll sends. The form lists the modes cheapest first, and suggests one from the result of **Run**.

**Incrementing**

Sends each row once. `position` names a field whose value only grows as rows are added, such as an id or the time a row was inserted. Each poll reads the rows past the last row sent, in the order of `position`. A row added later with a smaller value than one already sent is never read.

**Updated at**

Sends each row when it is added and again each time it changes. `position` starts with a datetime that every insert and every update sets. A deleted row sends nothing.

**Comparing**

Sends each row whose `key` is new, or whose fields changed since the last poll. Each poll reads the whole result, up to 1,000,000 rows, and the leader keeps a hash of each row. Use it for a table with no column that grows, such as a list of accounts. A deleted row sends nothing; a row whose key comes back is sent again.

**Every poll**

Sends the whole result on every poll, and remembers nothing. Use it for a small table read as a whole, such as current settings.

In `position`, the fields after the first tell apart rows that share a value in it, such as an id after a time. When many rows share one time, add such a field. Without one, a poll that fills `batch` leaves its last rows sharing one value to the next poll, which reads up to twice `batch`. Past that, the rest of the rows sharing the value are skipped, and the worker log says so.

A position that starts with a datetime reads only rows at least `settleSecs` behind the database's clock. A transaction that commits after a later one is then still read, as long as it commits within `settleSecs`. Rows arrive that much later.

`:last.<field>` in the query is the value that field held in the last row sent, and `NULL` before the first. Use it to filter where the statement's own test cannot reach, such as inside a `GROUP BY`. Keep rows with the last value (`>=`, not `>`), because rows sharing it may not all have been sent.

sections.heading: Column types
sections.text:
## Column types

**Run** suggests each field's type from its column's type. A column of a type not listed here, such as a geometry, is read as its text.

| MySQL or MariaDB type | Field type |
| --- | --- |
| `tinyint(1)`, `boolean` | `bool` |
| `tinyint`, `smallint`, `mediumint`, `int`, `bigint`, `year`, `bit` | `i64` |
| `float`, `double` | `f64` |
| `char`, `varchar`, `text`, `decimal`, `enum`, `set` | `str` |
| `date`, `datetime`, `timestamp` | `datetime` |
| `time` | `duration` |
| `json` on MySQL | `variant` |
| `binary`, `varbinary`, `blob` | `bytes` |

A `decimal` is read as its exact decimal text. A zero date, such as `0000-00-00`, is read as null. A MariaDB `json` column reads as `str`. A `tinyint(1)` that holds other than 0 or 1 needs an `i64` field, not `bool`. An unsigned `bigint` or `bit(64)` past 9223372036854775807 is read as its decimal text, so it needs a `str` field.

sections.heading: Where it starts
sections.text:
## Where it starts

A source in Incrementing or Updated at with no progress begins where `start` says:

-   `now`, the default: at the largest position the query returns on its first poll. It sends the rows that hold that value, then the rows added after them.
-   `beginning`: every row the query returns.
-   `from`: the rows whose position is at or past `startFrom`.

Comparing sends every row on its first poll. After that, the leader keeps how far every destination has taken, and a restarted worker, or another worker that takes the source over, resumes there. It may send a row twice and never skips one. Changing the connection's host, port or database, the query, the mode, or the fields of `position` or `key` starts the source afresh from `start`. The other settings keep its progress. The source keeps reading until you remove it.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

One worker of the group holds the source. Each poll runs your query inside a statement of Smeltr's own, which adds the position test, the order and the batch limit. After the example's first row, each of its polls runs:

```
SELECT * FROM (
SELECT event_id, occurred_at, user_name FROM events
) AS q
WHERE q.`event_id` > ?
ORDER BY q.`event_id`
LIMIT 5000
```

The form shows the exact statement for your settings under **what smeltr runs instead**. The query is one `SELECT` or `WITH`, with no `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` or placeholders of its own. The source runs the statement in a read-only transaction, with the session's time zone set to UTC, and reads a time without a zone as UTC. The settle test compares with `NOW(6)`, the database's own clock.

A poll that fills `batch` reads the next at once. Otherwise the next poll starts `pollIntervalSecs` after this one. When **Run** checks a poll's plan and finds that each poll would read a whole table of more than about 100,000 rows, the form warns. Index the first field of `position`, or filter inside the query with `:last.<field>`.

A poll's result may hold up to 256 MiB. The source has the database stop a statement after 290 seconds, or sooner if the database's own limit is shorter, and drops a connection that has not answered in 300. After a failure, the source asks again after one second, then waits twice as long each time, up to five minutes. It opens a new connection after one breaks.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

1.  In the form, choose **Run**. It shows the first rows the query returns, the record the pipeline sees for the first, and, once you choose a position, whether a poll reads through an index.
2.  Once the source is deployed, add a row the query returns. It reaches the destination within `pollIntervalSecs`, plus `settleSecs` for a datetime position. On the Sources page, the **worker** column names the worker that holds the source.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

The form shows what the MySQL or MariaDB server answered to **Run**, and the worker log shows it for a poll.

**The MySQL password is in …, which this worker does not have**

The credential is not on the worker that holds the source. See [Credentials](/docs/secrets).

**Run fails with a refusal to read a table**

Grant the user `SELECT` on the table.

**The result has no column `x`, which the record declares**

An entry of `fields` names a column the query does not return. Rename the entry, or give the column that name with `AS` in the query.

**The result has two columns named `x`**

Give one of them another name with `AS` in the query.

**Each poll scans all of a table**

The database reads the whole table on each poll to find the new rows. Index the first field of `position`, or filter inside the query with `:last.<field>`.

**More rows share one position value than twice the batch**

Add a field to `position` that tells those rows apart, such as an id, or raise `batch`.

**Two rows have the key …**

In Comparing, `key` must be unique in the result. Add fields to `key` until it is.

**Every poll reads at most … rows**

In Every poll, the result holds more rows than `batch`. Raise `batch`, up to 100,000, or choose another mode.

**This poll's result holds more than 256 MiB**

Lower `batch`, or read fewer or narrower fields.

**The position's first column is of a type smeltr reads only as text**

Cast the column in the query to a type in the table under [Column types](#types).

sections.text:

-   [Credentials](/docs/secrets)

sections.heading: Okta System Log
sections.text:
# Okta System Log

Reads an Okta org's System Log, every event once, in the order Okta stored it.

The source polls Okta's [System Log API](https://developer.okta.com/docs/reference/api/system-log/).

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Reads the System Log of `acme.okta.com`. The source signs in as the service app `0oa1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8i9` and reads its private key from the worker-host variable `OKTA_PRIVATE_KEY`.

```
{
  "id": "okta-audit",
  "type": "oktaLogs",
  "org": "https://acme.okta.com",
  "clientId": "0oa1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8i9",
  "privateKey": "OKTA_PRIVATE_KEY"
}
```

![The Okta System Log form on the Sources page: id okta-audit, org https://acme.okta.com, sign in as a service app, client id 0oa1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8i9.](/okta-logs-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog, before you pick its private key.

The same source, signing in with an API token instead:

```
{
  "id": "okta-audit",
  "type": "oktaLogs",
  "org": "https://acme.okta.com",
  "token": "OKTA_TOKEN"
}
```

sections.heading: How it signs in
sections.text:
## How it signs in

The source signs in to Okta as a service app or with an API token. For a service app, set `clientId` and `privateKey`; for an API token, set `token`.

|  | Service app | API token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Settings | `clientId`, `privateKey`, and `keyId` when the app has several active keys | `token` |
| Acts as | The app, with only the scope and role you grant it | The admin who created the token, with all of that admin's rights |

Use a service app. Recommended because it keeps working after the person who set it up leaves. Use an API token for quick tests.

sections.heading: Set up a service app
sections.text:
## Set up a service app

Create an API Services app as Okta's [service app guide](https://developer.okta.com/docs/guides/implement-oauth-for-okta-serviceapp/main/) describes, with:

1.  Public key / private key client authentication, with DPoP on or off.
2.  The `okta.logs.read` scope.
3.  The Read-only Administrator role.

Copy its client ID into `clientId`, put its active private key in a [credential](/docs/secrets) named in `privateKey`, and set `keyId` when the app has more than one active key.

The source takes an RSA key in PKCS#8 PEM, which begins `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`. If your key begins `-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----`, convert it first:

```
openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt -in key.pem -out key-pkcs8.pem
```

sections.heading: Set up an API token
sections.text:
## Set up an API token

Create an API token as Okta's [API token guide](https://developer.okta.com/docs/guides/create-an-api-token/main/) describes, signed in as an admin who can read the System Log, such as a Read-only Administrator. Put it in a [credential](/docs/secrets) and name it in `token`.

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

Set `org` to the address your users sign in at, such as `https://acme.okta.com`, or to the org's custom domain. The source also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`org`  string required

The org's address, with no path. It sends the token only over `https://`, or to this host.

Examples:

- `https://acme.okta.com`
- `https://login.acme.com`

`token`  credential default the service app's sign-in

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding an Okta API token that can read the System Log. It is sent as `Authorization: SSWS <token>`. Give a token, or `clientId` and `privateKey`, never both.

Examples:

- `OKTA_TOKEN`
- `{"secret": "okta-token","version": 1}`

`clientId`  string default none

The client id of a service app granted the `okta.logs.read` scope and the Read-only Administrator role. The source signs in as the app with a signed key assertion and reads with a token bound to the source's own key by DPoP when Okta binds it. Set both `clientId` and `privateKey`, or neither.

Example:

- `0oa1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8i9`

`privateKey`  credential default none

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the service app's private key, an RSA key as PEM PKCS#8 (`BEGIN PRIVATE KEY`), whose public half the app holds.

Examples:

- `OKTA_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `{"secret": "okta-key","version": 1}`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`keyId`  string default none

The `kid` naming `privateKey`, for a service app with several keys.

Example:

- `k1`

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under, for a proxy's private CA.

Examples:

- `okta-client`
- `corp-proxy`

`start`  string default `everything`

What its first poll asks for.

`everything`

Asks from what Okta lists with no start: its last seven days.

`new`

Asks from the first poll's start.

`pollIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

Seconds from the start of one poll to the start of the next. At least 1. A rate limit is waited out until the reset Okta names.

Examples:

- `30`
- `60`

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

Each record is one event, exactly as Okta sends it. `__source.url` holds the address of the page the source read it from.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.url` | `str` | The address of the page an API source read the record from. |
| `__source.bytes` | `bytes` | The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text. |

sections.heading: Where it starts
sections.text:
## Where it starts

The first poll asks for the last seven days of events. With `start` set to `new`, it asks only for events from the first poll onward. After that, the source resumes at the last page every destination took, so a restarted worker neither skips nor repeats events, and changing `start` does not replay anything. The source keeps reading until you remove it.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

One worker of the group holds the source. Each poll asks the System Log API for events in ascending order and follows Okta's next links until a page holds nothing new, then waits `pollIntervalSecs` from the poll's start. When the source reaches Okta's rate limit, it waits until the reset time Okta names.

As a service app, the source signs a key assertion with `privateKey` and asks the org's token endpoint, `/oauth2/v1/token`, for a token for the `okta.logs.read` scope. The source makes its own DPoP key when it starts, and proves each request with it when the app requires DPoP. The source renews the token shortly before it expires, and signs in again when Okta refuses a token it has already used.

The source follows no redirects, because it sends its credentials with every request.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Sign in to the org, then look at the destination for an event with `eventType` `user.session.start`. It arrives within a poll interval after Okta lists it.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

The worker log shows Okta's answer, followed by what to check.

**The client\_assertion signature is invalid**

The app holds no active key that matches `privateKey`. Check that the app holds the key's public half and that the key is **Active**.

**kid is invalid**

The app has several active keys. Set `keyId` to the key's **KID**, or deactivate the other keys.

**Refused the credentials (403), E0000006**

Check that the app, or the token's admin, has the Read-only Administrator role.

**Refused the sign-in (400), invalid\_scope**

Check that the app has the `okta.logs.read` scope.

**Refused the sign-in (302)**

`org` names the `-admin` address. Remove `-admin` from it.

**The private key is not PKCS#8**

Convert it with `openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt`, as shown above.

**Refused the credentials (401) with an API token**

Okta no longer accepts the token. Create a new token, or switch to a service app.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text:
## See also

-   [Sources](/docs/sources)
-   [Credentials](/docs/secrets)
-   [Okta: Implement OAuth for Okta with a service app](https://developer.okta.com/docs/guides/implement-oauth-for-okta-serviceapp/main/)
-   [Okta: System Log API](https://developer.okta.com/docs/reference/api/system-log/)

sections.heading: OTLP receiver
sections.text:
# OTLP receiver

Takes one signal OpenTelemetry exporters send over OTLP to its port, logs, metrics or traces: over HTTP, as protobuf or JSON, and over gRPC. It answers each export once every destination has its records.

Receivers of different signals may share one port. Each signal is records of its own fields, which its own pipelines read.

OpenTelemetry SDKs, Collectors and other OTLP clients send to it. Every worker in the group listens on its port, and the sender, or a balancer in front of the workers, picks a worker for each export. Add workers to take more.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Takes OTLP logs on port 4318, over TLS with the [identity](/docs/secrets#identities) `receiver-tls`. Senders present the token held in the worker-host variable `OTEL_TOKEN`.

```
{
  "id": "otel-logs",
  "type": "otlpReceiver",
  "port": 4318,
  "tokens": {
    "collectors": "OTEL_TOKEN"
  },
  "identity": "receiver-tls"
}
```

![The OTLP receiver form on the Sources page: id otel-logs, port 4318, signal logs, no tokens yet.](/otlp-receiver-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog, before you add its token and identity.

Takes traces on the same port, from the same senders:

```
{
  "id": "otel-traces",
  "type": "otlpReceiver",
  "port": 4318,
  "signal": "traces",
  "tokens": {
    "collectors": "OTEL_TOKEN"
  },
  "identity": "receiver-tls"
}
```

A sender posts an export of logs like this:

```
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $OTEL_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"resourceLogs":[{"resource":{"attributes":[{"key":"service.name","value":{"stringValue":"demo"}}]},
       "scopeLogs":[{"logRecords":[{"severityText":"INFO","body":{"stringValue":"hello"}}]}]}]}' \
  https://workers.example.com:4318/v1/logs
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Pick a port no other receiver in the group uses. The one port takes both HTTP and gRPC. Point each sender at the port you pick.
-   Decide how senders prove who they are: a token, a client certificate, or both. See [Tokens and certificates](#senders).
-   Put each token in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
-   Open the port on every worker, and give senders one address that reaches them all. See [Open its port](#port).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`port`  integer required

The port it listens on. Every worker of the group binds it, so no two receivers share one, but OTLP receivers of different signals may, with the same `identity` certificate.

Examples:

- `4318`
- `14318`

`signal`  string default `logs`

The signal it takes, each a record of its own fields.

`logs`

Gives one record per log record, from `/v1/logs` and the logs gRPC service.

`metrics`

Gives one record per metric data point, from `/v1/metrics` and the metrics gRPC service.

`traces`

Gives one record per span, from `/v1/traces` and the trace gRPC service.

`tokens`  map default none

Each token's name to the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding it. An exporter presents one as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, and any other request is refused `401`. A receiver with no token needs an `identity` with authorities.

Examples:

- `collectors = OTEL_TOKEN`
- `{"apps": {"secret": "otlp-apps","version": 1}}`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`identity`  identity default plain HTTP

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it serves TLS under: its certificate and key. With authorities, a sender must present a certificate that chains to one of them.

Example:

- `receiver-tls`

`maxRequestBytes`  integer default `10485760`

The largest request body it reads, between 1024 and 67108864. A larger one is refused `413`. A body sent as gzip is held to it as it inflates.

Examples:

- `1048576`
- `67108864`

sections.heading: Paths it serves
sections.text:
## Paths it serves

**POST** `/v1/logs`, `/v1/metrics`, `/v1/traces`

OTLP over HTTP: the body is an `Export*ServiceRequest` of its signal, protobuf with `Content-Type: application/x-protobuf`, or OTLP's JSON with `Content-Type: application/json`. The receiver answers in the encoding the export was sent in, and inflates a body sent with `Content-Encoding: gzip`.

**POST** `/opentelemetry.proto.collector.logs.v1.LogsService/Export`, and the `MetricsService` and `TraceService` methods

OTLP over gRPC, over HTTP/2 in the clear or through TLS: one message per call, plain or gzipped as `grpc-encoding` names it.

**GET** `/health`

Says whether the port's receivers take exports. See [Health check](#health).

An export of a signal no receiver on the port takes is refused 404, or `UNIMPLEMENTED` over gRPC.

sections.heading: Records it gives
sections.text:
## Records it gives

Each log record, metric data point or span of an export becomes one record, its fields typed as OTLP types them. A field it leaves unset is null. Times are datetimes, to the microsecond; IDs lowercase hex, and an ID that is all zero, or not 16 and 8 bytes long, is null; an enum is its number. `attributes` and the other variants keep each value's own type: a string, an int, a double, a bool, bytes, a list or a map. Read an attribute as text with `attributes["http.method"] as str`.

sections.heading: Logs
sections.text:
### Logs

`time`, `observedTime`

When it happened, and when it was seen.

`severityNumber`, `severityText`

The severity as OTLP's number, 1 to 24, and as the sender's text.

`body`, `attributes`

Variants.

`traceId`, `spanId`, `flags`

The span it was written in.

`eventName`, `droppedAttributesCount`

As the log record gives them.

sections.heading: Metrics
sections.text:
### Metrics

One record per data point, each with its metric's fields.

`name`, `description`, `unit`, `metadata`

Its metric's.

`type`

`gauge`, `sum`, `histogram`, `exponentialHistogram` or `summary`.

`aggregationTemporality`, `isMonotonic`

1 for delta and 2 for cumulative, where its type has one; whether a sum only grows.

`startTime`, `time`, `attributes`, `flags`

The point's.

`value`

A gauge's or sum's number, an int or a double as it was sent.

`count`, `sum`, `min`, `max`

A histogram's, exponential histogram's or summary's. Counts are doubles.

`bucketCounts`, `explicitBounds`

A histogram's buckets: each one's count and each one's upper bound, both arrays of doubles.

`scale`, `zeroCount`, `zeroThreshold`, `positive`, `negative`

An exponential histogram's; `positive` and `negative` each hold `offset` and an array of doubles, `bucketCounts`.

`quantileValues`

A summary's, an array of `quantile` and `value`, both doubles.

`exemplars`

A variant list of the point's exemplars.

sections.heading: Traces
sections.text:
### Traces

`traceId`, `spanId`, `parentSpanId`, `traceState`, `flags`

Where the span sits in its trace.

`name`, `kind`

Its name, and OTLP's kind: 1 internal, 2 server, 3 client, 4 producer, 5 consumer.

`startTime`, `endTime`

When it started and ended.

`attributes`, `events`, `links`

Its attributes, and lists of its events, each with its `time`, `name` and `attributes`, and of the spans it links to.

`statusCode`, `statusMessage`

1 ok, 2 error, and why.

`droppedAttributesCount`, `droppedEventsCount`, `droppedLinksCount`

As the span gives them.

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

The resource and instrumentation scope a record came under are `__source` fields, which every record of that scope shares. `__source.remote` holds the IP address the export came from: the balancer's, when one is in front of the workers.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.remote` | `str` | The address of the sender that delivered the record to a receiver. |
| `__source.resource` | `variant` | The resource an OTLP log record came under: its attributes, each keeping its own type, or null where the export named none. Read one as text with `__source.resource["service.name"] as str`. |
| `__source.scope.name` | `str` | The name of the instrumentation scope an OTLP log record came under, the library that wrote it, or null where the export named none. |
| `__source.scope.version` | `str` | The version of that instrumentation scope, or null where the export named none. |
| `__source.scope.attributes` | `variant` | That instrumentation scope's attributes, each keeping its own type, or null where the export named none. |

sections.heading: Tokens and certificates
sections.text:
## Tokens and certificates

Anyone a receiver admits can put records into the group's pipelines, so a receiver needs `tokens`, an `identity` with authorities, or both. The leader refuses a receiver with neither.

-   **Tokens:** a sender presents one as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, set as a header on its exporter. The receiver refuses any other request before reading its body. Without an identity, the token crosses the network in the clear, so use a token alone only behind a balancer that terminates TLS.
-   **Client certificates:** with an [identity](/docs/secrets#identities), the receiver serves TLS with the identity's certificate and key. If the identity has authorities, every connection, health checks included, must present a certificate that chains to one of them.

With both, a sender presents a certificate and a token.

sections.heading: What it answers
sections.text:
## What it answers

The receiver answers success only once every destination has the export's records, so an exporter that retries an unanswered export loses nothing. Each refusal below carries an OTLP `Status` whose message says why. The receiver takes an export whole or refuses it whole. Over gRPC, the same answers are [gRPC status codes](#grpc).

**200**

Every destination has the export's records. The body is an empty `Export*ServiceResponse`, `{}` in JSON.

**503**, with `Retry-After`

The receiver is full, [blocked](/docs/delivery#hold) or stopping, or the sender took more than 30 seconds to send the whole body. It refuses a new export at once, and a stopping receiver answers every export it holds. An exporter may send it again.

**401**

The request has no token, gives one other than as `Bearer <token>`, or gives one the receiver does not hold.

**400**

The body is not an OTLP export of the receiver's signal. An exporter may drop it.

**413**

The body, or what it inflates to, is larger than `maxRequestBytes`, or its records hold more decoded than a receiver holds at once. Send smaller exports.

**404**

No receiver on the port takes the export's signal. An exporter may drop it.

**415**

The body's `Content-Type` is neither `application/x-protobuf` nor `application/json`, or its `Content-Encoding` is other than `gzip` or `identity`.

Over gRPC, an export is answered `OK` once every destination has it, with an empty `Export*ServiceResponse`. A refusal is `UNAVAILABLE` where HTTP says 503, which an exporter may send again; `UNAUTHENTICATED` where it says 401; `INVALID_ARGUMENT` where it says 400, 413 or 415, which an exporter may drop; and `UNIMPLEMENTED` where it says 404, and for a `grpc-encoding` other than `gzip` or `identity`. Its `grpc-message` says why. A request whose `content-type` is not `application/grpc` is a plain 415.

sections.heading: Health check
sections.text:
## Health check

`GET /health` on the receiver's port answers 200 while every receiver on it takes exports and 503 while one is full, blocked or stopping. It needs no token. Point a balancer's health check or a readiness probe at it, so a busy worker gets no exports until it can take them. Under an identity with authorities it needs a client certificate like any other request.

sections.heading: Senders it takes
sections.text:
## Senders it takes

Any sender of OTLP works: over HTTP, as protobuf or JSON, or over gRPC, plain or gzipped. Over gRPC, a sender presents its token as the `authorization` metadata, `Bearer <token>`.

-   The OpenTelemetry Collector's `otlphttp` and `otlp` exporters.
-   OpenTelemetry SDKs, with their exporters on any OTLP protocol.
-   Fluent Bit's `opentelemetry` output, and Vector's `opentelemetry` sink.

This OpenTelemetry Collector configuration sends logs and traces to the port of the [example](#example)'s two receivers, with `OTEL_TOKEN` set in the collector's environment:

```
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
      http:

exporters:
  otlphttp:
    endpoint: https://workers.example.com:4318
    headers:
      Authorization: Bearer ${env:OTEL_TOKEN}

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlphttp]
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlphttp]
```

An SDK reads the same from its environment:

```
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://workers.example.com:4318
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Bearer%20$OTEL_TOKEN"
```

sections.heading: Open its port
sections.text:
## Open its port

Every worker in the group listens on the receiver's `port`. Open that port to senders on each worker, and give senders one address that reaches them all, such as a balancer's. On a Unix host, an export sent while a worker deploys a new configuration waits, and the new configuration answers it.

-   On Kubernetes, add the port to the worker pods and put a Service in front of them: [Expose a receiver](/docs/enroll-worker/kubernetes#receiver).
-   On a host or in a container, open the host's firewall or publish the container's port: [Enroll a worker on a host](/docs/enroll-worker/host).

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

POST an export you can recognize, as in the [example](#example). The receiver answers 200 with `{}` once every destination has it. Then find it at the destination.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**The sender cannot connect**

Check that the port is open on every worker, that the sender's address reaches them, and that its endpoint names the receiver's port. An identity with authorities refuses a connection without a certificate that chains to one of them.

**Every export gets 401**

Check that the sender presents `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, with a token one of the receiver's credentials holds.

**Every export gets 404**

No receiver on the port takes the signal it sends: add one for it, or stop sending it. Or the sender posts to a path other than its signal's, such as `/v1/logs`.

**Every export gets 503**

Check the source's status. A blocked receiver takes nothing until its destinations take records again. A full one takes more with more workers.

**The same records arrive twice**

An exporter that hears no answer may send the export again. Give the exporter a timeout longer than its destinations take to deliver.

sections.heading: PostgreSQL
sections.text:
# PostgreSQL

Runs a query you write against a PostgreSQL database every poll, and reads each row of its result as one record.

Use it for what an application keeps in its own tables, such as an audit table or a sign-in history. The source reads only what your query returns, and its mode decides which of those rows are new.

sections.heading: Example
Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Create a user that can connect to the database and read the tables the query reads, and nothing more. See PostgreSQL's [CREATE ROLE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createrole.html) and [GRANT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-grant.html).
-   Let the user connect from the workers' addresses in [pg\_hba.conf](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auth-pg-hba-conf.html), and allow workers to reach the server's port.
-   With `tls` `require`, the default, the server needs [SSL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ssl-tcp.html) on, with a certificate that names `host`. For a certificate from a private authority, give the source a [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) that trusts it.
-   Put the password in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
-   For Incrementing or Updated at, index the first field of `position`, so each poll reads only the new rows. See [CREATE INDEX](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

The form on the Sources page asks for the connection first, then the query. Its **Run** button runs the query on a worker of the group and shows the rows it read, so you choose the mode and the fields from the real result. The source also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`host`  string required

The database server's host name or address.

Examples:

- `db.internal`
- `10.4.0.12`

`database`  string required

The database the query runs in.

Examples:

- `auth`
- `shop`

`user`  string required

The user it connects as. Give it read access and nothing more: the query runs in a read-only transaction, but only the user's own grants keep a source from writing.

Example:

- `smeltr_reader`

`password`  credential default none, for a server that asks for no password

The [credential](/docs/secrets) holding the user's password.

Examples:

- `PG_PASSWORD`
- `{"secret": "auth-db-reader","version": 1}`

`query`  string required

A `SELECT` or a `WITH`, with no `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT` of its own: the statement around it orders by the position and sets the batch. `:last.<field>` is the value that field held in the last row sent, `NULL` before the first, for a filter the statement's own cannot reach, such as one inside a `GROUP BY`. The statement still reads past the last row sent, so the filter keeps the last value (`>=`) and rows sharing it are not lost.

Examples:

- `SELECT event_id, occurred_at, user_name FROM auth.events`
- `SELECT event_id, occurred_at, user_name FROM auth.events WHERE (:last.occurred_at IS NULL OR occurred_at >= :last.occurred_at)`

`mode`  mode required

How it knows a row is due. `position` is the field rows are read in the order of, then the fields that tell apart rows with the same value in it. A position that starts with a datetime waits `settleSecs` (default 30) behind the database's clock for late commits. A source with no progress begins where `start` says: `"now"` (default) at the largest position the query returns on its first poll, `"beginning"` at every row, or `"from"` at `startFrom`, an integer or an ISO 8601 time with its offset.

`incrementing`

Each row once, by a field that only grows as rows are added: an id, or the time it was inserted. Reads only the new rows.

`updatedAt`

Each row when it is added and again each time it changes, by a datetime every insert and update sets. A deleted row is not seen.

`comparing`

Each row when its `key` is new or its values changed, by reading the whole result every poll. Up to a million rows; the leader keeps an entry for each.

`everyPoll`

The whole result every poll. Nothing is remembered.

`fields`  list of fields required

Each field of the record: the result column of the same `name`, and its `type` as a pipeline spells one, such as `i64`, `datetime`, `str`, `bytes` or `array<str>`. A column the fields do not name is not read.

Example:

- `[{"name": "event_id","type": "i64"},{"name": "occurred_at","type": "datetime"},{"name": "user_name","type": "str"}]`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`port`  integer default `5432`

The server's port.

Examples:

- `6432`
- `5433`

`tls`  string default `require`

Whether the connection is encrypted.

`require`

Encrypts, and verifies the server's certificate and its name.

`disable`

Sends everything in the clear, the password too.

`identity`  identity default none

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it connects under: the authorities it trusts for the server's certificate, and a certificate to present. Only with `tls` `require`.

Examples:

- `auth-db-client`
- `corp-ca`

`pollIntervalSecs`  integer default `60`

Seconds from the start of one poll to the start of the next. At least 1. A poll that reads a full batch reads the next at once.

Examples:

- `30`
- `300`

`batch`  integer default `5000`

The most rows one poll reads by a position. With no field after the first in `position`, a full poll leaves its last rows sharing one value to the next, which reads up to twice `batch` when they fill a poll; past that, the rest of the rows sharing that value are skipped with a warning. In `everyPoll`, a result with more fails the poll. Between 1 and 100000.

Examples:

- `1000`
- `20000`

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

Each record is one row. It holds a field for each entry of `fields`, read from the result column of the same name and held as the type the entry declares. A column no entry names is not read.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.database` | `str` | The database an SQL source read the record from, as `host:port/database`. |

sections.heading: How it finds new rows
sections.text:
## How it finds new rows

`mode` says which rows a poll sends. The form lists the modes cheapest first, and suggests one from the result of **Run**.

**Incrementing**

Sends each row once. `position` names a field whose value only grows as rows are added, such as an id or the time a row was inserted. Each poll reads the rows past the last row sent, in the order of `position`. A row added later with a smaller value than one already sent is never read.

**Updated at**

Sends each row when it is added and again each time it changes. `position` starts with a datetime that every insert and every update sets. A deleted row sends nothing.

**Comparing**

Sends each row whose `key` is new, or whose fields changed since the last poll. Each poll reads the whole result, up to 1,000,000 rows, and the leader keeps a hash of each row. Use it for a table with no column that grows, such as a list of accounts. A deleted row sends nothing; a row whose key comes back is sent again.

**Every poll**

Sends the whole result on every poll, and remembers nothing. Use it for a small table read as a whole, such as current settings.

In `position`, the fields after the first tell apart rows that share a value in it, such as an id after a time. When many rows share one time, add such a field. Without one, a poll that fills `batch` leaves its last rows sharing one value to the next poll, which reads up to twice `batch`. Past that, the rest of the rows sharing the value are skipped, and the worker log says so.

A position that starts with a datetime reads only rows at least `settleSecs` behind the database's clock. A transaction that commits after a later one is then still read, as long as it commits within `settleSecs`. Rows arrive that much later.

`:last.<field>` in the query is the value that field held in the last row sent, and `NULL` before the first. Use it to filter where the statement's own test cannot reach, such as inside a `GROUP BY`. Keep rows with the last value (`>=`, not `>`), because rows sharing it may not all have been sent.

sections.heading: Column types
sections.text:
## Column types

**Run** suggests each field's type from its column's type. A column of a type not listed here is read as its text.

| PostgreSQL type | Field type |
| --- | --- |
| `boolean` | `bool` |
| `smallint`, `integer`, `bigint`, `oid` | `i64` |
| `real`, `double precision` | `f64` |
| `text`, `varchar`, `char`, `numeric`, `uuid`, `inet`, `cidr`, an enum | `str` |
| `timestamptz`, `timestamp`, `date` | `datetime` |
| `time`, `interval` | `duration` |
| `json`, `jsonb` | `variant` |
| `bytea` | `bytes` |
| An array | `array<…>` of its element's type, or `variant` |
| A domain | Its base type's |

A `numeric` is read as its exact decimal text. An `interval` counts a month as 30 days. **Run** suggests an array of one dimension; declare an `array<…>` for each further one, or `variant`.

sections.heading: Where it starts
sections.text:
## Where it starts

A source in Incrementing or Updated at with no progress begins where `start` says:

-   `now`, the default: at the largest position the query returns on its first poll. It sends the rows that hold that value, then the rows added after them.
-   `beginning`: every row the query returns.
-   `from`: the rows whose position is at or past `startFrom`.

Comparing sends every row on its first poll. After that, the leader keeps how far every destination has taken, and a restarted worker, or another worker that takes the source over, resumes there. It may send a row twice and never skips one. Changing the connection's host, port or database, the query, the mode, or the fields of `position` or `key` starts the source afresh from `start`. The other settings keep its progress. The source keeps reading until you remove it.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text:
## How it works

One worker of the group holds the source. Each poll runs your query inside a statement of Smeltr's own, which adds the position test, the order and the batch limit. After the example's first row, each of its polls runs:

```
SELECT * FROM (
SELECT event_id, occurred_at, user_name FROM auth.events
) AS q
WHERE q."event_id" > $1
ORDER BY q."event_id"
LIMIT 5000
```

The form shows the exact statement for your settings under **what smeltr runs instead**. The query is one `SELECT` or `WITH`, with no `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` or placeholders of its own. The source runs the statement in a read-only transaction, with the session's time zone set to UTC, and reads a time without a zone as UTC. The settle test compares with `now()`, the database's own clock.

A poll that fills `batch` reads the next at once. Otherwise the next poll starts `pollIntervalSecs` after this one. When **Run** checks a poll's plan and finds that each poll would read a whole table of more than about 100,000 rows, the form warns. Index the first field of `position`, or filter inside the query with `:last.<field>`.

A poll's result may hold up to 256 MiB. The source has the database stop a statement after 290 seconds, or sooner if the database's own limit is shorter, and drops a connection that has not answered in 300. After a failure, the source asks again after one second, then waits twice as long each time, up to five minutes. It opens a new connection after one breaks.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

1.  In the form, choose **Run**. It shows the first rows the query returns, the record the pipeline sees for the first, and, once you choose a position, whether a poll reads through an index.
2.  Once the source is deployed, add a row the query returns. It reaches the destination within `pollIntervalSecs`, plus `settleSecs` for a datetime position. On the Sources page, the **worker** column names the worker that holds the source.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

The form shows what the PostgreSQL server answered to **Run**, and the worker log shows it for a poll.

**The PostgreSQL password is in …, which this worker does not have**

The credential is not on the worker that holds the source. See [Credentials](/docs/secrets).

**Run fails with a refusal to read a table**

Grant the user `SELECT` on the table, and `USAGE` on its schema.

**The result has no column `x`, which the record declares**

An entry of `fields` names a column the query does not return. Rename the entry, or give the column that name with `AS` in the query.

**The result has two columns named `x`**

Give one of them another name with `AS` in the query.

**Each poll scans all of a table**

The database reads the whole table on each poll to find the new rows. Index the first field of `position`, or filter inside the query with `:last.<field>`.

**More rows share one position value than twice the batch**

Add a field to `position` that tells those rows apart, such as an id, or raise `batch`.

**Two rows have the key …**

In Comparing, `key` must be unique in the result. Add fields to `key` until it is.

**Every poll reads at most … rows**

In Every poll, the result holds more rows than `batch`. Raise `batch`, up to 100,000, or choose another mode.

**This poll's result holds more than 256 MiB**

Lower `batch`, or read fewer or narrower fields.

**The position's first column is of a type smeltr reads only as text**

Cast the column in the query to a type in the table under [Column types](#types).

sections.heading: Prometheus receiver
sections.text:
# Prometheus receiver

Takes the samples Prometheus sends over remote\_write to its port. It answers each request once every destination has its samples.

Prometheus and any agent that speaks remote\_write 1.0 or 2.0 send to it. Every worker in the group listens on its port, and the sender, or a balancer in front of the workers, picks a worker for each request. Add workers to take more.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Takes remote\_write on port 9090, over TLS with the [identity](/docs/secrets#identities) `receiver-tls`. Senders present the token held in the worker-host variable `PROM_TOKEN`.

```
{
  "id": "prometheus",
  "type": "prometheusReceiver",
  "port": 9090,
  "tokens": {
    "prometheus": "PROM_TOKEN"
  },
  "identity": "receiver-tls"
}
```

![The Prometheus receiver form on the Sources page: id prometheus, port 9090, no tokens yet.](/prometheus-receiver-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog, before you add its token and identity.

Prometheus sends to it with a `remote_write` block like this:

```
remote_write:
  - url: https://workers.example.com:9090/api/v1/write
    authorization:
      credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/smeltr-token
    tls_config:
      ca_file: /etc/prometheus/smeltr-ca.pem
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Pick a port no other receiver in the group uses.
-   For native histograms, set `send_native_histograms: true` in the sender's [remote\_write](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/configuration/configuration/#remote_write) settings.
-   Decide how senders prove who they are: a token, a client certificate, or both. See [Tokens and certificates](#senders).
-   Put each token in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
-   For exemplars, set `send_exemplars: true` in the sender's [remote\_write](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/configuration/configuration/#remote_write) settings.
-   Open the port on every worker, and give senders one address that reaches them all. See [Open its port](#port).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`port`  integer required

The port it listens on. Every worker of the group binds it, so no two receivers share one.

Examples:

- `9090`
- `19291`

`tokens`  map default none

Each token's name to the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding it. A sender presents one as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, and any other request is refused `401`. A receiver with no token needs an `identity` with authorities.

Examples:

- `prometheus = PROM_TOKEN`
- `{"agents": {"secret": "prom-agents","version": 1}}`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`identity`  identity default plain HTTP

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it serves TLS under: its certificate and key. With authorities, a sender must present a certificate that chains to one of them.

Example:

- `receiver-tls`

`maxRequestBytes`  integer default `10485760`

The largest request body it reads, between 1024 and 67108864. A larger one is refused `413`, which a sender may drop.

Examples:

- `1048576`
- `67108864`

sections.heading: Paths it serves
sections.text:
## Paths it serves

**POST** `/api/v1/write`

A remote\_write 1.0 or 2.0 request, as the sender sends it.

**GET** `/health`

Says whether the receiver takes requests. See [Health check](#health).

sections.heading: Records it gives
sections.text:
## Records it gives

Each sample of a request becomes one record: a float sample, or a native histogram. A series of three samples is three records, each with the series' labels. Each field has the name and type of an [OTLP metric point's](/docs/sources/otlp-receiver#records) field, so a pipeline reads a metric from either receiver alike. A field a sample does not have is null.

`time`

A datetime, from the sample's milliseconds.

`name`

The series' metric name, its `__name__` label.

`value`

A variant holding the sample's double, bit for bit, so a staleness marker stays one. Read it as a number with `value as f64`.

`attributes`

The series' other labels, an object of strings, or null when the series has no label but `__name__`. Read one with `attributes["job"] as str`.

`type`

A native histogram's: `exponentialHistogram`, or `histogram` for one with custom buckets. Null for a float sample.

`aggregationTemporality`

2, cumulative, for a counter's histogram; null for a gauge histogram.

`count`, `sum`

A histogram's count and sum, doubles.

`scale`, `zeroCount`, `zeroThreshold`, `positive`, `negative`

An exponential histogram's, as [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/data-model/#exponentialhistogram) lays it out. `positive` and `negative` each hold `offset` and `bucketCounts`, an array of doubles.

`resetHint`

`yes` or `no` where the sender said whether the histogram's counter reset, and null where it did not say.

`bucketCounts`, `explicitBounds`

A histogram of custom buckets: its bucket counts and their bounds, as [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/data-model/#histogram) lays them out.

`exemplars`

The series' exemplars, on its last record of the request, each shaped as an OTLP point's exemplar: `time`, `value`, `traceId`, `spanId`, and its other labels in `filteredAttributes`. A series sent with exemplars alone is one record, its `value` null.

`startTime`

When the series started counting, which remote\_write 2.0 may send with a sample or histogram. Null from 1.0, and where the sender did not say.

Each metric family's metadata is a record of its own. Its `time` and `value` are null, `name` is the family's, `description` its help and `unit` its unit. Its `type` is as an OTLP metric's: a counter is `sum` with `isMonotonic` true. A pipeline that wants samples alone drops records with no `time`.

Over remote\_write 2.0, a family's metadata record comes once a request, ahead of the family's first series.

Classic histograms arrive as samples of their `_bucket`, `_sum` and `_count` series, as a [classic histogram](https://prometheus.io/docs/concepts/metric_types/#histogram) is laid out.

This pipeline keeps one metric and reads its job as text:

```
if (name != "http_requests_total") drop();
job = attributes["job"] as str;
```

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

`__source.remote` holds the IP address the request came from: the balancer's, when one is in front of the workers.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.remote` | `str` | The address of the sender that delivered the record to a receiver. |

sections.heading: Tokens and certificates
sections.text:
## Tokens and certificates

Anyone a receiver admits can put records into the group's pipelines, so a receiver needs `tokens`, an `identity` with authorities, or both. The leader refuses a receiver with neither.

-   **Tokens:** a sender presents one as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, Prometheus's `authorization` block. The receiver refuses any other request before reading its body. Without an identity, the token crosses the network in the clear, so use a token alone only behind a balancer that terminates TLS.
-   **Client certificates:** with an [identity](/docs/secrets#identities), the receiver serves TLS with the identity's certificate and key. If the identity has authorities, every connection, health checks included, must present a certificate that chains to one of them: Prometheus's `tls_config` with `cert_file` and `key_file`.

With both, a sender presents a certificate and a token.

sections.heading: What it answers
sections.text:
## What it answers

The receiver answers success only once every destination has the request's samples, so a sender that retries an unanswered request loses nothing. The receiver takes a request whole or refuses it whole, and each refusal's body says why.

**204**

Every destination has the request's samples.

**503**, with `Retry-After`

The receiver is full, [blocked](/docs/delivery#hold) or stopping, or the sender took more than 30 seconds to send the whole body. A sender may send it again.

**401**

The request has no token, gives one other than as `Bearer <token>`, or gives one the receiver does not hold.

**400**

The body does not read as remote\_write, or it holds a series or histogram remote\_write does not allow, such as a label with an empty name or a histogram whose count is not what its buckets hold. The answer's body names what is wrong. A sender may drop it.

**413**

The body is larger than `maxRequestBytes`, or what it holds decompressed and decoded is more than a receiver holds at once. Send smaller requests, or raise `maxRequestBytes`.

**415**

The request is neither remote\_write 1.0 nor 2.0. The answer's body names what is wrong.

sections.heading: Health check
sections.text:
## Health check

`GET /health` on the receiver's port answers 200 while the receiver takes requests and 503 while it is full, blocked or stopping. It needs no token. Point a balancer's health check or a readiness probe at it, so a busy worker gets no requests until it can take them. Under an identity with authorities it needs a client certificate like any other request.

sections.heading: Senders it takes
Open its port
sections.text:
## Open its port

Every worker in the group listens on the receiver's `port`. Open that port to senders on each worker, and give senders one address that reaches them all, such as a balancer's. On a Unix host, a request sent while a worker deploys a new configuration waits, and the new configuration answers it.

-   On Kubernetes, add the port to the worker pods and put a Service in front of them: [Expose a receiver](/docs/enroll-worker/kubernetes#receiver).
-   On a host or in a container, open the host's firewall or publish the container's port: [Enroll a worker on a host](/docs/enroll-worker/host).

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

Point a sender at the receiver and check in its own logs or metrics that its requests succeed. Then find its samples at the destination.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**The sender cannot connect**

Check that the port is open on every worker and that the sender's address reaches them. An identity with authorities refuses a connection without a certificate that chains to one of them.

**Every request gets 401**

Check that the sender presents `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, with a token one of the receiver's credentials holds.

**Every request gets 415**

The sender does not speak remote\_write 1.0 or 2.0. The answer's body names what is wrong.

**Every request gets 503**

Check the source's status. A blocked receiver takes nothing until its destinations take records again. A full one takes more with more workers.

**The same samples arrive twice**

A sender that hears no answer may send the request again. Give it a `remote_timeout` longer than its destinations take to deliver.

sections.heading: S2S receiver
sections.text:
# S2S receiver

Takes what Splunk forwarders send over Splunk-to-Splunk (S2S).

Every worker in the group listens on its port. Add workers to take more.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text:
## Example

Takes forwarders on port 9997, over TLS with the [identity](/docs/secrets#identities) `s2s-tls`. Forwarders present the token held in the worker-host variable `S2S_TOKEN`. An event of the sourcetype `java:app` starts at a line that starts with a date and holds the lines after it. The sourcetype `access_combined` breaks at every line end, as every sourcetype not named does, so its row is there only to show the default.

![The S2S receiver form on the Sources page: id forwarders, port 9997, no tokens yet, the sourcetype java:app with its date line breaker, and access_combined with ([\r\n]+).](/s2s-receiver-source-form-light.png)

The same source in the Sources page's add dialog, with its sourcetypes, before you add its token and identity.

A forwarder sends to it with this outputs.conf:

```
[tcpout]
defaultGroup = smeltr

[tcpout:smeltr]
server = worker1:9997, worker2:9997
useACK = true
token = 0d2a5f6c-4b1e-4c3a-9f7d-2e8b6a1c5d40
```

sections.heading: Before you start
sections.text:
## Before you start

-   Pick a port no other receiver in the group uses.
-   Decide how forwarders prove who they are: a token, a client certificate, or both. See [Tokens and certificates](#senders).
-   Put each token in a [credential](/docs/secrets).
-   List only the sourcetypes whose events span several lines, such as stack traces, or break somewhere other than a line end. Every other sourcetype is an event per line. See [How lines become events](#events).
-   Open the port on every worker, and give forwarders the address of each. See [Open its port](#port).

sections.heading: Settings
sections.text:
## Settings

It also takes the settings [every source](/docs/sources#settings) takes.

`port`  integer required

The port it listens on. Every worker of the group binds it, so no two receivers share one.

Examples:

- `9997`
- `9998`

`tokens`  map default none

Each token's name to the [credential](/docs/secrets) holding it. A forwarder presents one as its outputs.conf `token`, and one that presents none or another is cut off. A receiver with no token needs an `identity` with authorities.

Examples:

- `uf-fleet = S2S_TOKEN`
- `datacenter = DC_FORWARDER_TOKEN`
- `branches = BRANCH_FORWARDER_TOKEN`

`sourcetypes`  map default an event per line for every sourcetype

Each sourcetype's name to its `lineBreaker`, where an event ends. Its first capture group is the break and is dropped: the bytes before it end an event, line ends and all, and the bytes after it start the next. What follows the group is kept, so the pattern can say how an event starts: `([\r\n]+)\d{4}-` keeps a stack trace with the line that logged it, and `</event>(\s*)` cuts a stream of XML events with no line ends between them. It needs a capture group and must not match the empty string. A sourcetype not named, or named with no `lineBreaker` or with `([\r\n]+)`, is an event per line, a line ending at `\n`, `\r\n` or a lone `\r`. An event that arrives already broken is one record as it came.

Examples:

- `{"java:app": {"lineBreaker": "([\\r\\n]+)\\d{4}-"}}`
- `{"java:app": {"lineBreaker": "([\\r\\n]+)\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}"},"app:xml": {"lineBreaker": "</event>(\\s*)"}}`

sections.heading: Advanced
sections.text:
### Advanced

`identity`  identity default plain TCP

The [connection identity](/docs/secrets#identities) it serves TLS under: its certificate and key. With authorities, a forwarder must present a certificate that chains to one of them.

Example:

- `s2s-tls`

`maxRequestBytes`  integer default `10485760`

The largest frame it reads, and the most one record holds, between 1024 and 67108864.

Examples:

- `1048576`
- `67108864`

sections.heading: Point a forwarder at it
sections.text:
## Point a forwarder at it

In the forwarder's outputs.conf, a `[tcpout]` group's `server` names every worker on the receiver's port, as in the [example](#example). Splunk's [Configure forwarding with outputs.conf](https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/forward-and-process-data/universal-forwarder-manual/10.6/forward-data/configure-forwarding-with-outputs.conf) covers the file.

-   `useACK = true` makes delivery at-least-once. See [Acknowledgement](#acks).
-   `token` is the value one of the receiver's `tokens` holds. Leave it out when the receiver has no tokens.
-   `compressed = true`, when set, needs no change on the receiver: it takes compressed and uncompressed connections alike.

sections.heading: How lines become events
sections.text:
## How lines become events

The receiver breaks what a forwarder sends into events by the rule `sourcetypes` names for its sourcetype:

-   A sourcetype not named in `sourcetypes` is an event per line, so most need no row.
-   A line ends at `\n`, `\r\n` or a lone `\r`.
-   A sourcetype named in `sourcetypes` ends an event where its `lineBreaker`'s first capture group matches. What the group matched is dropped; what follows it starts the next event, so the pattern can say how an event starts. The pattern needs a capture group and must not match the empty string.
-   An event that arrives already broken is one record as it came.
-   A line still unfinished when its connection ends, or after 30 seconds with no more of it from a forwarder with `useACK`, is an event as it stands. A line longer than `maxRequestBytes` is cut at that length.

A sourcetype not named, or one whose line breaker is left blank, breaks as `([\r\n]+)` does: at every line end, with no event for a blank line.

The line breaker `([\r\n]+)\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}` keeps each Java stack trace with the log line above it: it breaks only at line ends followed by a date, and only the log line starts with one. The line breaker `</event>(\s*)` makes an event of each XML event in a stream that has no line ends between them.

sections.heading: Fields it gives
sections.text:
## Fields it gives

Each event is a record, its text in `_raw`. The host, source, sourcetype, index and time the forwarder files it under, and its indexed fields, become `__source` fields. `__source.remote` holds the IP address the forwarder's connection came from.

| Field | Type | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `__source.name` | `str` | The name of the source that read the record. |
| `__source.type` | `str` | The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`. |
| `__source.remote` | `str` | The address of the sender that delivered the record to a receiver. |
| `__source.host` | `str` | The host a HEC sender filed the event under, or null where it named none. |
| `__source.source` | `str` | The source a HEC sender filed the event under, or null where it named none. |
| `__source.sourcetype` | `str` | The sourcetype a HEC sender filed the event under, or null where it named none. |
| `__source.index` | `str` | The index a HEC sender filed the event under, or an Elasticsearch client's bulk action named for its document; null where it named none. |
| `__source.time` | `datetime` | The time a sender gave the event, null otherwise. |
| `__source.fields` | `variant` | The indexed fields a HEC sender gave the event, or null where it gave none. Read one as text with `__source.fields.env as str`. |
| `__source.bytes` | `bytes` | The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text. |

sections.heading: Tokens and certificates
sections.text:
## Tokens and certificates

Anyone a receiver admits can put records into the group's pipelines, so a receiver needs `tokens`, an `identity` with authorities, or both. The leader refuses a receiver with neither.

-   **Tokens:** a forwarder presents one as its outputs.conf `token`. The receiver closes the connection of a forwarder with no token or a wrong one before admitting any of its data. Without an identity, the token crosses the network in the clear.
-   **Client certificates:** with an [identity](/docs/secrets#identities), the receiver serves TLS with the identity's certificate and key. If the identity has authorities, every forwarder must present a certificate that chains to one of them.

With both, a forwarder presents a certificate and a token.

sections.heading: Acknowledgement
sections.text:
## Acknowledgement

The receiver acknowledges an event once every record holding its bytes has reached every destination. Set `useACK = true` on every forwarder whose events must all arrive; an event can then arrive twice, never be lost. Splunk's [Protect against loss of in-flight data](https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/forward-and-process-data/forwarding-and-receiving-data/10.2/perform-advanced-configuration/protect-against-loss-of-in-flight-data) covers the forwarder's side.

sections.heading: When it is full
sections.text:
## When it is full

A receiver that is full, or [blocked](/docs/delivery#hold), stops reading from its connections until its destinations take records again. Name every worker in the forwarder's `server`, so it has others to send to.

sections.heading: Forwarders it takes
sections.text:
## Forwarders it takes

-   A forwarder sending with `tcpout` and its default protocol, compressed or not.
-   A forwarder set to `enableOldS2SProtocol = true` is refused.
-   A forwarder's `httpout` posts S2S to `/services/collector/s2s`, which the [HEC receiver](/docs/sources/hec-receiver) serves.

sections.heading: Open its port
sections.text:
## Open its port

Every worker in the group listens on the receiver's `port`. Open that port to forwarders on each worker, and name every worker in the forwarder's `server`.

-   On Kubernetes, add the port to the worker pods: [Expose a receiver](/docs/enroll-worker/kubernetes#receiver).
-   On a host or in a container, open the host's firewall or publish the container's port: [Enroll a worker on a host](/docs/enroll-worker/host).

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text:
## Verify

1.  Point a forwarder at the receiver, as in the [outputs.conf above](#forwarder).
2.  Append a line you can recognize to a file the forwarder monitors.
3.  Find it at the destination, with its host, source and sourcetype.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting

**The forwarder cannot connect**

Check that the port is open on every worker and that the forwarder's addresses reach them. An identity with authorities refuses a connection without a certificate that chains to one of them.

**The receiver closes the forwarder's connections at once**

The forwarder has no token, or one no credential of the receiver's `tokens` holds. Set its outputs.conf `token` to one the receiver holds.

**The forwarder is refused on every connection**

Check its outputs.conf for `enableOldS2SProtocol = true`, and remove it. The receiver takes only the forwarder's default protocol.

**Nothing arrives**

Check the source's status. A blocked receiver reads nothing until its destinations take records again. A full one takes more with more workers.

**A multi-line event arrives as one record per line**

Name its sourcetype in `sourcetypes` with a `lineBreaker` that matches only line ends before an event's first line, such as `([\r\n]+)\d{4}-`.

**Many events arrive as one record**

No line end separates them. Name their sourcetype in `sourcetypes` with a `lineBreaker` that matches between two events, such as `</event>(\s*)`.

**A line arrives cut in two, and the worker warns that a line was cut**

No more of the line arrived for 30 seconds, as when its file stopped growing mid-line, or when the source's destinations are slow. A line longer than `maxRequestBytes` is cut at that length.

**Events are missing after a worker stopped**

Set `useACK = true` on the forwarder. See [Acknowledgement](#acks).

**The same events arrive twice**

With `useACK`, an event not acknowledged when its connection was cut can arrive again. See [Acknowledgement](#acks).

sections.text:
